Americans usually describe a believer by their doctrine, such as 'they hold a binitarian view,' rather than calling themselves a binitarian. Trinitarian Christians may treat the label as a sharp criticism of a view they consider heretical.

distinctions.note: A trinitarian affirms three persons in one God, while a binitarian affirms only two.
A unitarian holds that God is one person, while a binitarian holds that God is two persons; the two labels describe different doctrines.

examples.professional: In the seminar, the student defended a binitarian reading of the Gospel, and the class pushed back with questions about the Spirit.
examples.analytical: A binitarian reading may make the Spirit appear as an impersonal power, which many theologians argue does not fit the New Testament's language.

nuance.analogy: A binitarian is like someone who sets a three-legged table on two legs: it looks close to complete, but something essential is missing.
nuance.etymology: From Latin bini, meaning 'two by two' or 'two together,' combined with the 'trinitarian' pattern.
common_mistakes: Saying 'bin-ih-TAIR-ee-un' with the stress on the first syllable instead of the third.
Confusing binitarian with unitarian; a binitarian believes in two persons, a unitarian in one.
nuance.biblical_note: Binitarian views are read against passages that name the Father, Son and Holy Spirit together. Matthew 28:19 (RSV) has Jesus commanding baptism in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, which Trinitarian Christians cite as a basis for three persons. John 1:1 (RSV) calls the Word God, and binitarian readings focus on the Father and Son relationship described in the Gospel of John. John 14:26 (RSV) speaks of the Father sending the Holy Spirit in Jesus' name, which binitarians interpret differently from Trinitarians.

senses.definition: A measure of the equivalence of multiple formulations of a drug in terms of bioavailability.
senses.example: The generic manufacturer submitted bioequivalence data showing its tablets matched the brand-name drug's absorption.

core.definition: The condition in which two drug formulations deliver the same amount of active ingredient into the bloodstream at the same rate.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on -KWIV-, not on the bio- syllable, so the dictionary version with stress on the oh is wrong. The middle vowel of equivalence is reduced to a short uh sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It signals regulatory or scientific reassurance without any emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use bioequivalence mainly in pharmaceuticals, pharmacy, and FDA regulation. Patients hear it when a pharmacist explains that a generic works like the brand-name drug. Its opposite in everyday talk is simply saying a generic 'works the same.'

distinctions.note: Bioavailability describes how much and how fast one drug reaches circulation. Bioequivalence compares two formulations of the same drug against each other.
Therapeutic equivalence means two drugs have the same clinical effect. Bioequivalence is a narrower lab and pharmacokinetic measure that supports it.

examples.everyday: The pharmacist said the generic has proven bioequivalence, so it should work just as well as the brand.
examples.professional: Before we submit the application, we need bioequivalence data showing the new tablet matches the reference product.
examples.analytical: Regulators infer therapeutic equivalence from bioequivalence, which rests on comparing blood concentration curves rather than clinical outcomes.

nuance.analogy: Bioequivalence is like two keys cut to the same pattern: they may look different, but they open the lock in the same way.
nuance.etymology: From bio- (Greek bios, life) and equivalence (Latin aequivalens, of equal value).
common_mistakes: Stressing the bio- syllable instead of the -KWIV- syllable.
Confusing bioequivalence with bioavailability, which describes a single drug rather than a comparison.

senses.definition: Magic derived from evil forces, as distinct from good or benign forces; or magic performed with the intention of doing harm.
senses.example: The villagers whispered that the old widow practiced black magic against her rivals.

senses.definition: A technology, process, etc. that is mysterious, esoteric; anything which appears to be almost magic to those who do not understand it.
senses.example: To my grandmother, the smartphone was pure black magic she couldn't begin to understand.

core.definition: Magic drawn from evil forces or meant to harm others; figuratively, a technology or process that seems magical to outsiders.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the first syllable of magic (MAJ-ik), not on the second. Say black with a short a as in cat, not a long a as in lake.

nuance.connotation: Negative in the literal sense of harmful sorcery; playful or admiring when someone jokes that a complicated tool or skill is black magic.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use black magic in fiction, pop culture, and everyday jokes, and it can refer to a real belief in harmful sorcery. In tech and workplace talk, people use it humorously to describe something that works but that they do not understand. In religious settings, speakers more often say witchcraft or sorcery, and black magic can sound unserious when discussing actual spiritual practices.

distinctions.note: White magic is the benevolent or healing kind, so it is the direct opposite of black magic in intent.
Witchcraft is a broader term for folk or religious practices, and it is not always harmful; black magic is always the harmful or evil kind.
Sorcery is more formal and often appears in older or literary texts, while black magic is the everyday phrase in American English.

examples.everyday: My grandmother swears my pie crust is black magic.
examples.professional: Nobody on the sales team understands the model, so it looks like black magic to them.
examples.analytical: Medieval courts often treated black magic as a crime against church and state, not merely as superstition.

nuance.analogy: Like a card trick that looks supernatural until you learn the method, black magic seems dark to people who do not know how it works.
nuance.etymology: Black (Old English blæc) plus magic, from Greek magikos, from magos, a term for a Persian priest-magician.
common_mistakes: Saying black magic for any mysterious result when you mean only that you do not understand it; the figurative use is informal.
Stressing the second syllable of magic (ma-JIK) instead of MAJ-ik.
nuance.biblical_note: The phrase black magic is not biblical. Scripture forbids the practices it describes: the Hebrew kashaph (to practice sorcery) and the Greek mageuo (to practice magic). Deuteronomy 18:10-12 (RSV) forbids Israel to practice sorcery, divination and necromancy. Acts 8:9-24 (RSV) describes Simon the magician in Samaria, who tries to buy the power of the Spirit. Acts 19:18-19 (RSV) tells how new believers in Ephesus burn their magic books. Galatians 5:19-21 (RSV) lists sorcery among the works of the flesh.

senses.definition: Unimpressed, indifferent, especially because of overfamiliarity.

core.definition: Bored or unimpressed by things, especially because you have experienced or seen them too often.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, ZAY. In General American the first vowel sounds like the ah in father, because of the cot-caught merger, so don't say blay.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative, suggesting jaded coolness; it can sound sophisticated or dismissive depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use blasé for someone who acts unimpressed by something exciting, such as a famous view or a celebrity. It is common in conversation and writing, and it is not rude when describing a third person. Saying it directly to someone's face can sound snobbish, so it is safer to use about someone else's attitude.

distinctions.note: Bored means tired of something dull; blasé means unimpressed even by things that would normally excite people, which implies worldliness.
Indifferent is a general lack of interest or concern; blasé specifically suggests that so much has been seen that nothing surprises you.
Cynical implies distrust of other people's motives, while blasé is about lack of excitement; a person can be blasé without distrusting anyone.

examples.everyday: We saw the famous skyline from the hotel window, and my teenage son just gave a blasé shrug.
examples.professional: Our executives seemed blasé about the security breach, which worried the team even more.
examples.analytical: Simmel argued that the blasé attitude of the modern city dweller is a psychological defense against constant sensory overload.

nuance.analogy: Like a movie critic who has seen every film and can no longer be surprised by a plot twist.
nuance.etymology: From French blasé, meaning satiated or jaded, from the verb blaser, to satiate.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first syllable as blay instead of blah.
Dropping the accent mark in writing; the accented é is part of the standard spelling.

blasé.etymology: Borrowed from French *blasé* (“blasé, jaded”), past participle of *blaser* (“to blunt, dull”), from Middle Dutch *blâsen* (“to blow, sound, brag”), from **blāsan*, from **blāsan* (“to blow”), from Proto-Indo-European **bʰleh₁-* (“to blow; to bleat, cry”).

senses.definition: A machine with sharp rotating blades in a bowl, for mashing, crushing, or liquefying food ingredients.
senses.example: Pour the frozen strawberries and yogurt into the blender and pulse until smooth.

senses.definition: A piece of fabric sewn into the front of a theatrical wig to make it blend in with the performer's natural hair.
senses.example: The costume designer sewed a blender of sheer lace into the front of the wig.

senses.definition: A subtly patterned fabric printed in different shades of a single color, often used in place of a solid to create visual texture.
senses.example: The upholstery fabric is a blender printed in soft gray tones, hiding stains well.

senses.definition: To mix in a blender.
senses.example: Blend the spinach with the banana before you add the ice.

core.definition: A kitchen appliance with a jar and spinning blades that chops, mixes, or liquefies food and drinks such as smoothies and soups.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final '-er' is a reduced, rhotic American 'er' sound, not 'ah' or 'uh' pronounced separately.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical, everyday word with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'blender' for the jar appliance that makes smoothies, sauces, and frozen drinks. For chopping solid food like vegetables, people use a 'food processor.' A 'mixer' usually means a stand mixer or hand mixer for batters and doughs. In a recipe you might hear, 'Throw it in the blender.'

distinctions.note: A food processor chops, slices, and shreds solid food, while a blender is designed to liquefy liquids and soft ingredients.
A mixer, especially a stand mixer, is for batters and doughs, while a blender is for liquids and smooth mixtures.

collocations: make a smoothie in the blender

examples.everyday: Can you toss the banana in the blender with some milk and ice?
examples.professional: Our test kitchen ran the soup through a commercial blender to check the final texture.
examples.analytical: The blender reduces ingredients to a uniform texture by shearing them with rapidly rotating blades.

nuance.analogy: Like a tiny tornado inside a glass jar, pulling everything into a smooth swirl.
nuance.etymology: From 'blend' plus the suffix '-er,' meaning one that blends.
common_mistakes: Using 'mixer' for a blender; in American kitchens a mixer is a different appliance.
Pronouncing the final syllable as a separate 'dah' sound instead of a reduced 'er.'

senses.definition: In a blind manner; without sight.
senses.example: I stumbled blindly through the forest, branches whipping at my face.

senses.definition: Without consideration or question.

core.definition: Without thinking carefully or without knowing the facts, often trusting or obeying without question.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. Say the 'nd' cluster and then the 'l' clearly; the final 'ly' is pronounced as 'lee,' not 'lie.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests a lack of thought, judgment or care, though it can be neutral when describing physical movement without sight.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'blindly' most often to criticize someone for accepting something without checking, as in 'Don't just follow the GPS blindly.' Physically, it can mean moving without being able to see, as in 'He reached blindly into the dark drawer.' It sounds natural in both casual and professional speech.

distinctions.note: Blindly suggests trust or obedience without seeing the facts, while unthinkingly describes acting without thinking at all.
Blindly describes lack of awareness, while recklessly describes willful disregard of danger or consequences.

examples.everyday: Don't just follow the directions on your phone blindly; look at the map too.
examples.professional: We shouldn't adopt the vendor's model blindly without testing it on our own data.
examples.analytical: To accept the authority of tradition blindly is to surrender the very reason that makes faith intelligible.

nuance.analogy: Like a driver who follows the GPS voice into a lake without looking at the road.
nuance.etymology: From 'blind' (Old English 'blind,' without sight) plus the adverbial suffix '-ly.'
common_mistakes: Using 'blindly' to mean 'totally' or 'completely' without the sense of lacking judgment.
Pronouncing the 'd' as silent; in 'blindly' it is clearly pronounced before the 'l.'

blindly.etymology: From Middle English *blindly*, *blyndly*, from Old English *blindlīċe* (“in a blind manner; blindly; rashly”), equivalent to *blind* + *ly*.

core.definition: The major prophetic book of the Old Testament, named for the prophet Isaiah, which warns of judgment, comforts exiles and foretells a coming Messiah and servant.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on ZAY, the second syllable. The final -iah is one reduced syllable, 'uh,' not 'ah' or 'ee-uh.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It is a central book in Christian worship and teaching.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'the book of Isaiah' or just 'Isaiah' in Bible study and preaching. It is long, so people often refer to specific chapters such as Isaiah 40 or 53. Quoting a passage, say 'Isaiah chapter 53' or 'Isaiah 53:5' rather than 'the Isaiah part.'

distinctions.note: Both are major prophets, but Isaiah is known for visions of Zion and messianic prophecy, while Jeremiah is more personal and tied to the fall of Jerusalem.
A prophet is a person who speaks for God, while the Book of Isaiah is the written collection attributed to the prophet.

examples.everyday: My pastor's sermon this Sunday is from the book of Isaiah, so bring your Bible.
examples.professional: The commentary series treats Isaiah in three sections, which changes how we date the final chapters.
examples.analytical: Scholars debate whether the book of Isaiah has one author or several, given the shift in historical setting between chapters 39 and 40.

nuance.analogy: Like a long anthology with several voices, the book of Isaiah gathers warnings, comfort and hope across different times.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Yeshayahu, meaning 'YHWH is salvation'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as EYE-zay-uh
Pronouncing the ending as 'ah' instead of 'uh'
Assuming all sixty-six chapters come from one author
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew Yeshayahu, 'YHWH is salvation' or 'the LORD saves'. Isaiah 6:8 records Isaiah's response to God's call, saying he is ready to be sent. Isaiah 7:14 contains the sign of a young woman bearing a child called Immanuel. Isaiah 40:3 speaks of a voice crying in the wilderness to prepare the way of the LORD. Isaiah 53 describes the suffering servant who bears the sins of many.

senses.definition: A basket used for storing or carrying bread.
senses.example: She set the warm rolls in the breadbasket and carried them to the table.

senses.definition: A region which has favorable conditions to produce a large quantity of grain or, by extension, other food products; a food bowl.
senses.example: The Great Plains serve as the breadbasket for much of the world's wheat.

senses.definition: The abdomen or stomach, especially as a vulnerable part of the body in an attack.
senses.example: The linebacker's hit landed squarely in the breadbasket, and he doubled over.

core.definition: A region with ideal farmland and weather for growing large amounts of grain and other food. Also, a basket for holding bread, or (informal) the stomach.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, BRED, and the second part, basket, is pronounced BAS-kit with a reduced final t that sounds almost like a soft d. Do not stress the second syllable of basket as if it were 'bas-KET'.

nuance.connotation: Positive when describing a fertile farming region, since it suggests abundance and national importance. Informal when used to mean the stomach, as in a punch to the breadbasket in sports or fighting.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often use breadbasket for a farming region, as in 'The Midwest is the nation's breadbasket.' News articles use it for agricultural areas, and it often appears in discussions of food supply. In casual speech, 'breadbasket' for the stomach is slightly playful or slangy, and you will hear it mostly in sports commentary or movies. A bread box, a countertop container for loaves, is a different object, so use that term for the kitchen item.

distinctions.note: A bread box is a kitchen container for storing loaves; breadbasket for the object is more often a woven container for serving bread at a table.
A granary is a building for storing threshed grain, while breadbasket names a whole region that produces it.
A food bowl is a general container or a pet's dish, not a region, so it never means farmland.

examples.everyday: Iowa is a huge breadbasket, so you'll see corn fields for miles on that drive.
examples.professional: Our supply chain analysis shows the Central Valley is the breadbasket for most of our produce contracts.
examples.analytical: Historians have long argued that Ukraine's plains made it a breadbasket whose output shaped European grain markets.

nuance.analogy: A breadbasket region is like a kitchen pantry for a whole country, always stocked and ready to supply everyone else.
nuance.etymology: Bread (Old English brēad) plus basket (Middle English basket); the regional sense grew from the image of a basket full of bread.
common_mistakes: Saying 'bread box' for a basket on the table; in American English a basket for serving bread at dinner is simply a breadbasket.
Stressing the second syllable as 'bread-BAS-ket' rather than BRED-bas-kit.

senses.definition: Something that breaks (something else).
senses.example: a breaker of men's souls

senses.definition: A machine for breaking rocks, or for breaking coal at the mines.
senses.example: The mine's crew fed the coal into a big breaker that crushed it into smaller pieces.

senses.definition: The building in which such a machine is placed.
senses.example: at the coal breaker

senses.definition: A person or company that specializes in breaking things; their yard.
senses.example: The scrap yard is a breaker that takes apart old cars and sells the parts.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of shipbreaker, a shipbreaking company or its yard.
Ellipsis of car breaker, a car breaking company or its yard.
Ellipsis of horsebreaker.
A wave breaking into foam against the shore, or against a sandbank, or a rock or reef near the surface, considered a useful warning to ships of an underwater hazard.
senses.example: Surfers wait beyond the breakers, where the waves start curling before they reach the sand.

senses.definition: A breakdancer.
Ellipsis of circuit breaker.
senses.example: breaker panel

senses.definition: A small cask of liquid kept permanently in a ship’s boat in case of shipwreck.
senses.example: The captain ordered the breaker of fresh water lashed to the lifeboat before the storm hit.

senses.definition: A user of CB radio.
senses.example: Our neighbor is a breaker who talks to truckers on his radio every night.

senses.definition: Used to open a conversation or call for a response on CB radio.
senses.example: breaker one nine

core.definition: A switch that automatically cuts off electric power when a circuit is overloaded, or a wave that curls and breaks onto a shore.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on BRAY, and the final syllable is an unstressed r-colored schwa, so say it as 'kur' with the r clearly heard in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical, technical word with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'breaker' most often for a circuit breaker in a house, the switch box in the basement or garage, and for ocean waves at the beach. 'Breaker' alone as a machine for rock is specialized. Use 'circuit breaker' or 'fuse box' in everyday talk; 'breaker' alone can be understood in context, as in 'flip the breaker.'

distinctions.note: A fuse melts once and must be replaced, while a circuit breaker can be flipped back on after it trips.
'Wave' is general for any water motion, while 'breaker' specifically refers to a wave that collapses on shore.
A switch turns power on or off on purpose, while a breaker cuts power automatically when there is too much current.

examples.everyday: The lights went out, so I went to the basement to flip the breaker back on.
examples.professional: Facilities says the server room breaker keeps tripping, so we need an electrician to check the load.
examples.analytical: A breaker is designed to interrupt current at a threshold, protecting conductors from overheating, which makes it a standard example of a feedback safety device.

nuance.analogy: Like a safety valve on a pressure cooker: it releases the load before something dangerous happens.
nuance.etymology: From break plus -er, meaning something that breaks, with the electrical and wave senses developing later.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'breaker' with 'fuse': a breaker can be reset, while a fuse must be replaced.
Using 'breaker' for a person who breaks rules; the word refers to a device or wave, not a rule-breaker.
Pronouncing the final -er as a clear 'air'; the usual American sound is a soft 'ur.'

conversation.text: We sat on the beach and watched the breakers roll in.
The breakers were too big for the kids, so they played in the shallow water.
Try to dive under the breaker before it hits you.

senses.definition: Propagation of offspring through sexual reproduction.
senses.example: Careful breeding of the flock produced stronger lambs each spring.

senses.definition: The act of insemination by natural or artificial means.
senses.example: The veterinarian explained artificial breeding options to the dairy farmers.

senses.definition: The act of copulation in animals.
The good manners regarded as characteristic of the aristocracy and conferred by heredity.
senses.example: Her refined breeding was obvious the moment she greeted the duke's guests.

senses.definition: Nurture; education; formation of manners.
senses.example: Good breeding, not wealth, shaped the young man's manners at the dinner table.

senses.definition: Descent; pedigree; extraction.
senses.example: Your dog has good breeding.

senses.definition: Ejaculation inside the rectum during bareback anal sex.
Of, relating to or used for breeding.
senses.example: Your toothbrush is a breeding ground for bacteria.

core.definition: The process of producing offspring, especially by choosing animals or plants with desired traits to mate.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final '-ing' is a short 'ih' plus a velar 'ng,' with no 'g' sound. Keep the long 'ee' in the first syllable, not a short 'i.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral in farming, biology, and animal care; in older speech, 'good breeding' describes refined manners and can sound dated or snobbish.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'breeding' most often in discussions of animal husbandry, genetics, and conservation, such as 'captive breeding program.' As an adjective, it appears in 'breeding ground' or 'breeding season.' The phrase 'good breeding' for manners is old-fashioned, so 'upbringing' or 'manners' sounds more natural today.

distinctions.note: 'Reproduction' is the general biological term for making offspring; 'breeding' usually implies deliberate human selection or care.
'Upbringing' is the standard word for how someone was raised; 'breeding' in that sense sounds old-fashioned.

examples.everyday: Our neighbor's chickens are in breeding season, so the rooster crows at five every morning.
examples.professional: The breeding program improved the herd's milk yield significantly over the last five years.
examples.analytical: Selective breeding reshapes populations by privileging some heritable traits over others, often in ways the breeders did not fully foresee.

nuance.analogy: Like tending a garden where you keep only the strongest plants, breeding gradually shifts a population toward chosen traits.
nuance.etymology: From 'breed' (Old English brēdan) with the suffix '-ing' forming a noun.
common_mistakes: Using 'breeding' to refer to the animal type, as in 'a rare breeding'; the correct word is 'breed.'
Saying 'good breeding' for everyday manners, which sounds dated.

breeding.etymology: From Middle English *breedyng*, *bredynge* (“gestation, incubation, propagation, hatching; engineering, formation, development, growth”), equivalent to *breed* + *ing*.

senses.definition: To call up for consideration.
To make something happen earlier than originally planned.
senses.example: The meeting has been brought forward by one day.

core.definition: To move an event, meeting, or deadline to an earlier time. It can also mean to present a proposal or issue for consideration.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on the first syllable of 'forward,' FOR, and the final syllable is reduced to a weak 'wurd' sound. The 'r' after 'for' is pronounced in General American English.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a scheduling or procedural change and carries no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: In business and government, Americans use 'bring forward' for moving a meeting or deadline earlier, and for presenting a motion or proposal for a vote. In casual conversation, many Americans say 'move up' instead, as in 'Can we move up the dinner?' 'Bring forward' sounds more formal and procedural, so it fits meeting invitations, emails, and reports.

distinctions.note: 'Move up' is the more common, casual phrase in American speech for changing a time to an earlier one.
'Postpone' means to delay to a later time, so it is the opposite direction of 'bring forward.'
'Bring up' means to raise a topic in conversation, while 'bring forward' means to change a time or formally present an item.

examples.everyday: Could we bring our dinner reservation forward to six? My sister has to leave early.
examples.professional: Legal wants to bring the audit forward by two weeks so we have time to fix the findings before the board meets.
examples.analytical: The committee chose to bring forward the vote, which compressed the debate and reduced the time available for public comment.

nuance.analogy: Like moving a train's departure time earlier on the schedule, so everyone has to get to the platform sooner.
nuance.etymology: Bring is from Old English bringan; forward is from Old English foreweard, 'toward the front'.
common_mistakes: Using 'bring forward' in casual conversation where Americans would more naturally say 'move up.'
Stressing the second syllable of 'forward' instead of the first, which makes it sound like 'for-WARD.'

senses.definition: Random motion of particles suspended in a fluid, arising from those particles being struck by individual molecules of the fluid.
senses.example: Under the microscope, the pollen grains showed Brownian motion as they jittered endlessly in water.

senses.definition: Synonym of Wiener process.
senses.example: In the pricing model, stock returns are approximated by Brownian motion over short intervals.

senses.definition: A state of chaos or disarray.
senses.example: After the reorg, the department was pure Brownian motion, with memos crisscrossing and no one in charge.

core.definition: The random, zigzag movement of tiny particles suspended in a fluid, caused by constant collisions with fluid molecules.

pronunciation.tip: Stress BROW in Brownian and MO in motion, and make the -ian ending a quick, weak syllable. The ending is pronounced 'shun', not 'shee-un'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise scientific term with no emotional sense.
nuance.usage_note: Brownian motion is used in physics, chemistry, statistics, and finance, where it describes random fluctuations in a model. Americans capitalize Brownian because it comes from the name Robert Brown. In everyday talk, the figurative sense of chaos is rare, and people usually say chaos, disorder, or a mess.

distinctions.note: A random walk is a discrete, step-by-step model, while Brownian motion usually refers to the continuous-time limit or the physical phenomenon.
The Wiener process is the mathematical model of Brownian motion, named after Norbert Wiener, used in probability and stochastic calculus.
Diffusion describes the large-scale spreading of particles, while Brownian motion describes the random movement of each individual particle.

examples.everyday: My friend who works in physics said that the pollen in the water was moving because of Brownian motion.
examples.professional: We model the stock's log returns as geometric Brownian motion, which assumes continuous random changes.
examples.analytical: Einstein's explanation of Brownian motion gave strong evidence that matter is made of discrete atoms and molecules.

nuance.analogy: Brownian motion is like a crowd of people in a dark room bumping into each other and moving in random directions.
nuance.etymology: Named after Robert Brown, the Scottish botanist who described the motion of pollen particles in 1827.
common_mistakes: Writing it in lowercase as 'brownian motion', since it is a proper adjective and should be capitalized.
Using it to mean chaos in ordinary conversation, when most Americans would say chaos or disorder.

brownian-motion.etymology: who investigated the movement of pollen suspended in water.

senses.definition: A slight correction or modification.
A review of a topic to be learned.
senses.example: Before the job interview, I needed a brush-up on spreadsheet formulas.

core.definition: A quick review or refresher of a subject or skill, or a slight correction or improvement made to something.

pronunciation.tip: As a noun, the stress falls on the first word, 'BRUSH', unlike the verb phrase 'brush UP', where the stress falls on 'up'. Keep the vowel short in both syllables.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It suggests a helpful, practical review rather than a serious failure.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use brush-up as a noun in work and school: 'I need a brush-up on Excel before the meeting.' It is friendly and practical. Many Americans also say 'refresher' or 'review'. The verb form, 'brush up on', is more common in daily speech than the noun.

distinctions.note: A refresher is often a course or practice meant to restore skills; a brush-up is usually a quicker, informal review.
Review is a broader and more formal word for examining material again; brush-up suggests a lighter, personal effort to get back up to speed.

examples.everyday: I'm rusty on my Spanish, so I'm doing a quick brush-up before our trip.
examples.professional: The team scheduled a brush-up on our data pipeline tools before the new hires start next week.
examples.analytical: A brush-up of the argument in the second chapter would clarify how the author moves from premise to conclusion.

nuance.analogy: A brush-up is like tuning a guitar before a concert: nothing is broken, but it sounds better after a little attention.
nuance.etymology: From the phrasal verb brush up, meaning to smarten or refresh something, with the noun formed from it.
common_mistakes: Using brush-up as a verb; say 'brush up on' instead.
Forgetting 'on' after the verb: say 'brush up on Python', not 'brush up Python'.

senses.definition: Synonym of build on.

core.definition: To use something that already exists as a foundation for further growth or improvement; the same as build on.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, pon, which has the open ah vowel of cot. The word upon is weak, so do not say up-ON with equal stress.

nuance.connotation: Positive. The phrase suggests careful progress from an existing base.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say build on far more often in conversation. Build upon is correct and common in American writing, speeches, reports and academic prose, but it sounds stiff in casual talk. For example, Let's build on that idea sounds more natural than Let's build upon that idea.

distinctions.note: Build on is the everyday form and sounds more natural in conversation.
Expand on means adding more detail to an idea, while build upon means using an idea as a foundation for something new.

examples.everyday: Let's build upon what we talked about at dinner and plan the trip for next spring.
examples.professional: The second phase will build upon the data cleaning work we completed last quarter.
examples.analytical: Later theologians built upon Augustine's account of grace, but they also revised it in ways he would not have accepted.

nuance.analogy: Like a second story added to a finished house, it rests on something already complete.
nuance.etymology: From build (Old English byldan) and upon, from up and on.
common_mistakes: Using build upon in casual speech, where build on sounds more natural.
Pronouncing upon as up-ON with equal stress on both syllables.

senses.definition: To make a joke concerning; to ridicule or make fun of.
senses.example: Her roommates busted on her for wearing a bathrobe to the job interview.

senses.definition: To hit or attack (someone); to insult (someone); to snitch on (someone).
senses.example: Don't bust on your brother just because he told Mom about the broken vase.

core.definition: To tease or make fun of someone, often harshly; in some regions, to criticize or hit someone.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the particle ON, which is pronounced 'ahn' with the open vowel of 'father'. Americans with the cot-caught merger say the same vowel in both 'on' and 'cot'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests mocking or ridicule, and it can hurt feelings.
nuance.usage_note: Bust on is informal American slang used mostly among friends, teenagers, and in some regions. Friends may say 'Don't bust on me' when they tease each other, but saying it to a stranger or a colleague can sound rude. In formal or polite speech, use 'make fun of,' 'tease,' or 'criticize.' A natural reply is 'Okay, okay, I get it' or 'Fine, you got me.'

distinctions.note: Tease is usually playful and friendly, while bust on can be harsher and more hostile.
Pick on suggests repeatedly targeting someone, often in a bullying way.
Rib means to joke gently with someone you like, which is usually more affectionate than bust on.

collocations: bust on him for being late

examples.everyday: My roommates busted on me for wearing my bike helmet to dinner, but they were only joking.
examples.professional: I'd avoid busting on a colleague's slide deck in front of the team, even if the chart is messy.
examples.analytical: Commentators who bust on younger readers' tastes often mistake their own irritation for critical judgment.

nuance.analogy: Busting on someone is like a comedian's roast: the joke can land as fun or as an insult, depending on the room.
nuance.etymology: From bust (verb) plus on; American slang with an uncertain exact origin.
common_mistakes: Using bust on in formal writing, where criticize or make fun of is better.
Saying the particle on with a long o sound, as in 'bust OHN.'

senses.definition: Having a certain type of bust (breasts; cleavage).
senses.example: The fashion critic called the dress flattering for a busted figure, with its deep sweetheart neckline.

senses.definition: Broke; having no money.
senses.example: I'd like to help you, but I'm busted.

senses.definition: Caught in the act of doing something one shouldn't do.
senses.example: I saw you take that cookie from the cookie jar! You're busted!

senses.definition: Extremely ugly.
senses.example: She was cute, but all her friends were busted.

senses.definition: Tired.
senses.example: After a double shift, I was busted and could barely keep my eyes open.

senses.definition: Broken.
senses.example: The busted water heater flooded the basement, so we called a plumber this morning.

senses.definition: Extremely overpowered.
senses.example: That new champion is busted in ranked matches, so everyone is playing him.

core.definition: Caught doing something wrong, such as lying, cheating, or breaking a rule, often in a playful way.

pronunciation.tip: It has two syllables, with stress on the first, and the ending -ed is pronounced as a separate syllable 'id' because it follows the t. Do not add an extra vowel between s and t.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to playful. When said to a child or friend, it sounds teasing; in a serious situation, it can sound harsh.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often shout 'Busted!' playfully when they catch someone doing something small, like eating a cookie before dinner. In casual speech, 'busted' also means 'broken,' as in 'My phone is busted,' which is informal. In serious situations, use 'caught' or 'found out' instead. A natural reply is 'Okay, you got me.'

distinctions.note: Caught is neutral and suits any situation; busted is informal and often playful.
Found out is a neutral way to say someone discovered a secret or lie, and it is more appropriate in serious talk.
Exposed is formal and suggests that a hidden wrong has been publicly revealed.

examples.everyday: You had a cookie before dinner, so you're busted!
examples.professional: The vendor got busted for sending duplicate invoices, so we're now checking all their billing records.
examples.analytical: The official's claim collapsed when the reporter showed the statistics were fabricated, so he was busted in front of the entire press corps.

nuance.analogy: Being busted is like a magician's trick suddenly becoming visible to the audience.
nuance.etymology: Past participle of bust, probably from burst; the exact origin is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Using busted for broken in formal writing, where broken or damaged is better.
Confusing busted with the noun bust, which can mean a sculpture or a woman's chest.

senses.definition: Of a result, one that remains constant or the same regardless of the criteria one uses for measuring.
senses.example: The recovery was successful by any measure, with sales up and costs down.

core.definition: Judged by any reasonable standard; no matter how the result is measured or compared. Used to say a result is clearly true.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable of 'measure'. The final 'ure' is pronounced as the 'zh' sound followed by a reduced 'er', so do not say 'mez-ur' with a hard s.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It is used to make a strong, confident judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'by any measure' in reviews, business reports and everyday evaluations to say something is clearly good or bad. In everyday talk, 'by any standard' is a close alternative. It sounds confident, so it is best used when you can support the claim.

distinctions.note: The two are very similar, but 'by any measure' suggests quantities or results, while 'by any standard' suggests a general set of criteria.
'In every respect' covers all aspects, while 'by any measure' focuses on how the result is judged.

examples.everyday: The trip was a success by any measure, even with all the rain.
examples.professional: By any measure, our customer churn rate improved this quarter, and the trend is holding.
examples.analytical: The theory is parsimonious by any measure we can define, which is why it is widely preferred.

nuance.analogy: Like a ruler that gives the same reading no matter who holds it.
nuance.etymology: 'Measure' comes from Latin mensura, meaning 'a measuring'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'by any measurement' instead of 'by any measure', which is less idiomatic.
Stressing the second syllable as 'meh-ZHUR', which sounds unnatural in American speech.

senses.definition: A convenience store, originally one that sold coffee and similar basic items.
senses.example: Late at night, we bought ice and cold drinks at the cafe on the corner.

senses.definition: Alternative form of café.

core.definition: A small place that serves coffee, tea and light food such as sandwiches, pastries and salads, often with a relaxed atmosphere.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the final syllable, 'FAY', and the first vowel is the short 'a' of 'cat', not 'ah' or 'kaf'.

nuance.connotation: Positive and friendly. It suggests a relaxed place to meet, work or chat over coffee.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say cafe in everyday speech for a small coffee place, and it is often written without the accent mark. You might hear 'Let's meet at the cafe on Main Street.' Many Americans say coffee shop for a place focused on coffee drinks. The first dictionary sense about a convenience store is dated and regional, so do not use it in ordinary conversation.

distinctions.note: A coffee shop focuses on coffee drinks and may have only pastries. A cafe usually also serves full light meals.
A cafeteria is self-service with a tray and a food line. A cafe usually has table service or simple ordering at a counter.

examples.everyday: Let's meet at that little cafe on Main Street before the movie.
examples.professional: I'll book a table at the cafe near the office for the client lunch on Thursday.
examples.analytical: The neighborhood cafe has long been studied as a public space where people discuss politics and community life.

nuance.analogy: A cafe is like a living room that sells coffee, where strangers and friends can sit together without being asked to leave.
nuance.etymology: From French café, coffee, from Italian caffè, from Turkish kahve, from Arabic qahwa.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'KAF-ay' with the stress on the first syllable; the stress falls on the final syllable.
Using cafe for a self-service food line; that is a cafeteria.

senses.definition: A colorless or white inorganic compound, CaCO3, occurring as chalk, limestone, marble etc. Reacts with acids to liberate carbon dioxide.
senses.example: Vinegar fizzed when poured onto the chalk, which is mostly calcium carbonate.

core.definition: A white mineral compound, CaCO3, found in chalk, limestone, and marble; also used in antacids and calcium supplements.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'KAR' in 'carbonate', and 'calcium' gets a lighter stress with a reduced final syllable. Pronounce the 'r' clearly, and do not add an extra syllable in 'carbonate'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical term in chemistry and geology but is also a familiar supplement ingredient.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'calcium carbonate' in chemistry, geology, and nutrition. On supplement and antacid labels it is common, and an everyday person might say 'I take calcium carbonate for heartburn.' In casual talk, people often just say 'calcium' or name a brand such as Tums.

distinctions.note: Calcium carbonate needs stomach acid and food to absorb well, while calcium citrate is absorbed more easily on an empty stomach.
Limestone is a rock that is mainly calcium carbonate, while calcium carbonate is the pure chemical compound.

examples.everyday: I chew a calcium carbonate tablet when my stomach feels sour after dinner.
examples.professional: The lab report says the sample is mostly calcium carbonate, so it should fizz when we add the acid.
examples.analytical: Calcium carbonate appears in both seashells and limestone, showing how living organisms build mineral structures.

nuance.analogy: Calcium carbonate is like the chalk on a blackboard: the same stuff that forms the great cliffs of limestone and the shells on a beach.
nuance.etymology: Calcium from Latin calx, lime; carbonate from carbon, from Latin carbo, charcoal, with the chemical suffix -ate.
common_mistakes: Putting the main stress on 'cal' in 'calcium' as in 'kal-SEE-um', instead of the lighter stress used in compounds.
Pronouncing 'carbonate' with an extra syllable, as in 'CAR-bun-ate'.

senses.definition: Checking your audio on a call.

core.definition: A question to check that the other person can hear your voice clearly enough, used at the start of a meeting or call.

pronunciation.tip: 'Okay' is pronounced 'oh-KAY' in American English, with the stress on the second syllable. Many learners say 'OH-kay' or 'oh-KAH', but the vowel is the long /eɪ/ as in 'day'. The word 'hear' has secondary stress, and 'can' reduces to /kən/.

nuance.connotation: Polite and considerate. It shows you care that the others can follow you.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this in video calls and conference calls, often right after joining, or when the audio seems off. It is friendly and workplace-appropriate. A common reply is 'Yes, loud and clear' or 'Mostly, but you're a little quiet.'

distinctions.note: Adding 'okay' makes the question softer and invites a quality check, not just a yes or no about audibility.
'Is my audio working?' is more technical and suits a troubleshooting moment; the 'okay' version is a social check during a meeting.

collocations: can you hear me okay in the back
can you hear me okay with the mic on
everyone, can you hear me okay

examples.everyday: Can you hear me okay? My phone keeps cutting out when I walk.
examples.professional: Good morning, everyone. Can you hear me okay? Let me know if the audio sounds off.
examples.analytical: A presenter who asks whether the room can hear them is already practicing a kind of accountability, because clarity depends on the listener as much as the speaker.

nuance.analogy: It works like a pilot asking the cabin, 'Can you all hear me okay?' before takeoff.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'okay' as 'OH-kay', which sounds unnatural; the American stress is oh-KAY.
Using 'Are you hearing me okay?' with a continuous form, which is less common in US meetings than the simple 'can you hear me'.

conversation.text: Hi, I'm using a new headset. Can you hear me okay?
Can you hear me okay? My internet is a little slow today.
"Can you hear me okay?" "Yeah, loud and clear."

senses.definition: The quality of being capacious.

core.definition: The quality of being roomy, spacious, or able to hold a great deal, whether a space, container, or mind.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on PAY, the second syllable. The final syllables are reduced, so say -shus-nus quickly, with the sh sound and little vowel weight at the end.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises generous room or breadth, though it can sound stiff in casual speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use capaciousness mostly in formal writing, literary description, reviews, and academic prose. In everyday talk, people usually say roominess or just that a thing is big or roomy. The word is a good choice when you want an elegant description of space or breadth.

distinctions.note: Capacity is the maximum amount something can hold, while capaciousness describes how roomy or generous that space feels.
Spaciousness is the more common word for open room in a home or building, while capaciousness suggests a container or a mind that holds a lot.
Roominess is informal and everyday, while capaciousness is more formal and literary.

examples.everyday: I love the capaciousness of this old station wagon, since we can fit all the camping gear in the back.
examples.professional: The venue's capaciousness made it a good choice for the eight-hundred-person conference.
examples.analytical: Her theology has a capaciousness that holds mystery without collapsing it into a fixed doctrine.

nuance.analogy: Capaciousness is like a well-designed backpack that holds far more than its size suggests.
nuance.etymology: From capacious, from Latin capax, able to hold much, from capere, to take or hold.
common_mistakes: Confusing capaciousness with capacity, which is the limit or ability to hold, rather than the roomy quality.
Stressing the first syllable, as in KAP-uh-shus-ness, when the stress is on PAY.

senses.definition: In a captious manner.

core.definition: In a way that criticizes or finds fault with small, petty details, often in a deliberately argumentative manner.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, KAP. The ending -ious becomes shus, and the final -ly is a clear lee. Avoid saying kap-tee-OUS-lee.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes petty, nitpicking criticism that is more interested in faults than in the real issue.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use captiously mainly in formal writing, literary criticism or a discussion of argument. In everyday speech they would say nitpicky, picky or fussy. Using captiously in casual talk may sound overly bookish, so save it for analysis of how someone argued.

distinctions.note: Critically can mean thoughtfully or seriously evaluating, while captiously means finding fault in trivial points.
Skeptically means doubting a claim, while captiously means picking at small flaws even when the main point is sound.
Nitpicky is the everyday informal equivalent, while captiously is formal and more precise about deliberate fault-finding.

examples.everyday: Don't answer her captiously; she only wants a simple yes or no about dinner.
examples.professional: The reviewer commented captiously on every comma but missed the central flaw in our sampling method.
examples.analytical: Socrates' interlocutors often argue captiously, seizing on wording rather than engaging the substance of the claim.

nuance.analogy: It is like a referee who calls every tiny foul and never notices what happens in the game.
nuance.etymology: From Latin captiosus, deceptive or fault-finding, from captio, a trick or sophism.
common_mistakes: Confusing captious (fault-finding) with capricious (unpredictable or whimsical).
Dropping the i in the spelling or saying the ending as tee-us instead of shus.

senses.definition: In a captivating manner.

core.definition: In a way that strongly holds attention, usually in an appealing, charming or fascinating manner.

pronunciation.tip: Stress KAP, and keep the middle syllables quick and reduced. The -ing is a nasal ting, and the ending -ly is a clear lee.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises something that is highly engaging or attractive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use captivatingly mostly in writing, especially in reviews, essays and literary description, as in captivatingly beautiful. In speech they usually say really captivating or so captivating. The adverb sounds polished, so use it when you want precision rather than casual talk.

distinctions.note: Charmingly stresses pleasantness and grace, while captivatingly stresses strongly holding someone's attention.
Fascinatingly emphasizes curiosity and interest, while captivatingly emphasizes that the attention is held completely.

examples.everyday: She sang the old song so captivatingly that the whole table went quiet.
examples.professional: The presenter explained the model captivatingly, so the executives kept asking questions for the full hour.
examples.analytical: Augustine writes captivatingly about his restless heart, making the reader feel the pull of desire from within.

nuance.analogy: Like a song you cannot stop humming, it keeps pulling your attention back to itself.
nuance.etymology: From captivate, from Late Latin captivare, to take captive, plus the suffix -ingly.
common_mistakes: Using captivatingly in casual speech where really captivating sounds more natural.
Confusing captivating (interesting, attractive) with captive (a prisoner).

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to the making of maps.

core.definition: Relating to the making of maps, or to the design and accuracy of maps.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on GRAF, and the unstressed syllables are reduced to a short 'tuh' and 'ik.' Keep the r clear in the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical adjective without emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use cartographic in geography, GIS, urban planning, and academic writing. It appears in phrases such as cartographic standards or cartographic projection. In everyday speech people usually say map or mapping instead, so cartographic sounds specialized.

distinctions.note: Geographic describes places and features of the earth in general, while cartographic describes the making or design of maps.
Topographic refers to the shape and elevation of land. Cartographic is broader and covers the whole process of mapmaking.

examples.everyday: My hiking app has great cartographic details, so I rarely get lost.
examples.professional: The GIS team updated the cartographic layers before we shared the dashboard with the city.
examples.analytical: Every cartographic projection distorts some feature of the earth, which means the choice of projection is itself an argument.

nuance.analogy: Cartographic thinking is like drawing a sketch of a house so others can find their way around it without visiting.
nuance.etymology: From cartography, with the adjective suffix -ic.
common_mistakes: Using cartographic for geographic in general contexts, as in cartographic features of a country; geographic is usually better.
Stressing the wrong syllable as kar-tuh-GRAF-ick or kar-TOG-ruh-fik.

senses.definition: A shortened or incomplete last foot at the end of a verse.
Truncation at the close of a line of poetry by omission of one or two final syllables.

core.definition: The omission of one or two syllables at the end of a line of verse, leaving the final foot incomplete.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, 'KAT'. The middle vowels are reduced to 'uh' and the final -sis is a short 'sis', rhyming with 'miss'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a technical term in prosody.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term in classes on poetry, meter, and prosody, and in scholarly writing about verse. It is not used in everyday conversation. In speech, people usually describe the effect rather than naming it.

distinctions.note: Elision omits a sound within a word or between words, while catalexis omits syllables at the end of a line.
Ellipsis is the omission of words in a sentence for grammatical or stylistic reasons, not a metrical feature.
Truncation is the general word for cutting something short; catalexis is its specific metrical form in verse.

examples.professional: For the anthology, the editors note catalexis in several lines where the poet drops the final syllable.
examples.analytical: The poet's repeated catalexis gives the closing couplets a clipped, unfinished sound that matches the theme of silence.

nuance.analogy: Like a sentence that ends one word early, leaving the listener waiting for the last beat.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin catalexis, from Greek katalēxis 'a stopping short', from katalēgein 'to leave off'.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'catalysis', the chemical process.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in 'kuh-TAL-ih-sis'.
Using it outside poetry where 'omission' or 'cut' is the natural word.

senses.definition: To focus one's emotional energies on someone or something.

core.definition: To invest emotional energy or attention in a person, object or idea, especially in psychoanalysis.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, THEKT. The th is voiceless, and the final -ect sounds like 'ekt', as in expect, not as separate letters.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical psychological term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use cathect mainly in psychology, psychoanalysis and academic writing. In everyday speech, they would say invest emotionally in or put a lot of energy into. Using it in casual talk will sound like jargon.

distinctions.note: Invest is an everyday word for putting time or feeling into something, while cathect is a technical term from psychoanalysis.
Cathect is the verb for the act of investing emotional energy, while cathexis is the noun for that investment itself.

examples.everyday: My therapist says I have been cathecting too much of my energy into my job and not enough into my friends.
examples.professional: Some engineers cathect so strongly to one architecture that they resist any alternative proposal.
examples.analytical: In Freud's account, the child first cathects the mother as an object of libidinal energy and later redirects that investment.

nuance.analogy: Like pouring water into one container until it becomes the main vessel for your attention, cathecting focuses emotional energy on a single object.
nuance.etymology: From cathexis, from Greek kathexis, meaning holding, chosen by James Strachey as the English translation of Freud's German Besetzung.
common_mistakes: Using cathect in everyday conversation where invest or put energy into would be natural.
Confusing the verb cathect with the noun cathexis.

senses.definition: Without an end.
Without stop or pause, incessant.
senses.example: The ceaseless rain flooded the streets of the town throughout the entire week.

core.definition: Never stopping or pausing; continuing without any break.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The second syllable is a light 'less' ending, and the final 's' is voiceless.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It can describe admirable endurance or an exhausting, unpleasant condition.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'ceaseless' in writing and formal speech to describe something that never stops, such as noise, effort, or rain. In everyday talk people say 'nonstop' or 'constant.' It sounds dramatic if used for small, ordinary annoyances.

distinctions.note: 'Incessant' often implies something annoying that keeps going, while 'ceaseless' can be neutral or even admirable.
'Constant' is everyday and general, while 'ceaseless' is more formal and emphasizes that something has no pause at all.

examples.everyday: The ceaseless beeping from the construction site gave me a headache all morning.
examples.professional: The team faced ceaseless pressure to deliver the model before the quarter closed.
examples.analytical: Augustine describes God's love as ceaseless, a grace that does not withdraw even when the human heart fails to notice it.

nuance.analogy: A ceaseless sound is like a faucet that never fully shuts off.
nuance.etymology: From cease (from Old French cesser) and the suffix -less, meaning without.
common_mistakes: Using 'ceaseless' for small, short-term problems; it implies something that never stops.
Mispronouncing the first syllable as 'seh' instead of 'see'.

senses.definition: Addicted to censure and scolding; apt to blame or condemn; severe in making remarks on others, or on their writings or manners.
senses.example: Her censorious father criticized every grade on my report card and every friend I brought home.

senses.definition: Implying or expressing censure.
senses.example: censorious remarks

senses.definition: Tending to engage in or support censorship.
senses.example: The senator was censorious about film content and pushed to ban several movies from schools.

core.definition: Quick to criticize or condemn others harshly, especially over small matters of behavior, taste, or morality.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the SOR syllable, the second one. The -ious ending is usually two syllables, ee-us, not shus.

nuance.connotation: Negative. Calling someone censorious criticizes their judgmental attitude; it is never a neutral description.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use censorious in writing, news, or serious conversation to describe a harsh, judgmental tone, often about personal behavior or online comments. In casual talk, people say judgmental or critical instead. Do not use it to mean subject to censorship; it describes an attitude, not an official action.

distinctions.note: Critical can be neutral or constructive, as in a critical review; censorious always implies harsh, disapproving judgment.
Judgmental is more common and casual in American speech; censorious is more formal and literary and suggests a moral tone.
Censorial is a rare adjective meaning relating to censors or censorship; censorious describes a critical attitude.

examples.everyday: My neighbor gave me a censorious look when I parked my car in front of the mailbox.
examples.professional: Please avoid a censorious tone in code review; focus on what the change should do rather than what the author should have known.
examples.analytical: Many nineteenth-century reformers wrote with a censorious tone that exposed real abuses but also hardened their contempt for ordinary people.

nuance.analogy: A censorious person is like a referee who blows the whistle on every small move and never lets the game flow.
nuance.etymology: From Latin censorius, from censor, plus the English -ious suffix.
common_mistakes: Using censorious to mean subject to censorship; it describes a judgmental attitude.
Stressing the first syllable instead of sen-SOR-ee-us.

censorious.etymology: From Latin *cēnsōrius* (“of or pertaining to a censor; severe”).

senses.definition: Relating to, or associated with, the commemoration of an event that happened a hundred years before.
senses.example: a centennial ode

senses.definition: Happening once in a hundred years.
senses.example: a centennial jubilee a centennial celebration

senses.definition: Lasting or aged a hundred years.
senses.example: The centennial oak in the courthouse yard has shaded visitors for generations.

senses.definition: The hundredth anniversary of an event or happening.

core.definition: The hundredth anniversary of an event, such as the founding of a city, company, or university, or its celebration.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, -TEN-. The ending -ial is two syllables, 'ee-ul', so do not pronounce it as 'ee-al' with a long a.

nuance.connotation: Positive, suggesting celebration and pride in history.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use centennial often for the hundredth birthday of towns, universities, companies, and buildings. It also appears in names such as the Centennial State, Colorado's nickname. For a 150th anniversary, Americans say 'sesquicentennial', and for 200 years they say 'bicentennial'.

distinctions.note: Centenary is the British equivalent; Americans normally use centennial.
A centenarian is a person who is one hundred years old, not an event.
Bicentennial means two hundred years, so it is not the hundredth anniversary.

examples.everyday: The whole town is throwing a parade for its centennial next summer.
examples.professional: Our company's centennial report goes out to clients in June, so please send your sections by Friday.
examples.analytical: The centennial of a founding is less a measure of time than an occasion for a community to retell its origin story.

nuance.analogy: A centennial is like a hundredth birthday cake for an institution: everyone gathers to celebrate how long it has lasted.
nuance.etymology: From Latin centum 'hundred' and annus 'year', formed on the model of 'biennial'.
common_mistakes: Using centennial for a 200th anniversary, which is bicentennial.
Writing centenial with one n, which is a common spelling error.

senses.definition: Indicating a distinguishing feature of a person or thing; typical.
(rare) Describing or pertaining to personal characters or character types; characterful.
senses.example: Her grandmother's characteristic bluntness made every visitor feel welcome and slightly unsettled.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: A distinguishing feature of a person or thing, a part of mental or physical behavior.
senses.example: Patience is a characteristic of good teachers, and mine rarely lost her temper.

senses.definition: The integer part of a logarithm.
senses.example: For log base ten of 350, the characteristic is 2, and the mantissa is about 0.544.

senses.definition: For a given field or ring, a natural number that is either the smallest positive number n such that n instances of the multiplicative identity (1) summed together yield the additive identity (0) or, if no such number exists, the number 0.
senses.example: The characteristic of a field, if non-zero, must be a prime number.

senses.definition: The distinguishing features of a navigational light on a lighthouse etc by which it can be identified (color, pattern of flashes etc.).
senses.example: Each lighthouse on the coast has a distinct characteristic, so sailors can identify it at night.

core.definition: Typical of a particular person, place, or thing; a feature that clearly distinguishes it from others.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on RIS, and the first three syllables are weak, so say them quickly. Many learners stress the first syllable or pronounce the middle vowels fully, which makes the word sound clumsy.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a trait without judging it, though it can be used positively ('her characteristic kindness').
nuance.usage_note: Americans use characteristic in both speech and writing to say that something is typical of someone or something, as in 'That's characteristic of him.' In casual conversation, people often prefer 'typical' or 'so him,' which sound more natural. As a noun, the everyday sense is 'a trait,' and the mathematical senses appear only in technical contexts.

distinctions.note: Typical emphasizes what is usual or average, while characteristic emphasizes the defining mark that makes a thing recognizable.
Distinctive stresses that something sets a thing apart, often in an attractive way, while characteristic implies a regular, expected trait.

examples.everyday: It's very characteristic of her to bring cookies to a potluck.
examples.professional: A characteristic of this dataset is that the outliers cluster around weekends.
examples.analytical: The argument treats moral goodness as a characteristic of persons rather than of acts, which changes what counts as a virtue.

nuance.analogy: Like a fingerprint: it marks one thing out from the rest.
nuance.etymology: From Greek kharaktēr, 'a mark or engraving tool,' via Latin and French.
common_mistakes: Misspelling it as 'charactaristic' or 'charactoristic' by dropping the second 'e' sound in the middle.
Stressing the first syllable (KAIR-ik-tuh-ris-tik) instead of RIS.
Using 'characteristic for' where Americans say 'characteristic of.'

characteristic.etymology: From Ancient Greek *χαρακτηριστικός*, from *χαρακτηρίζω* (“to designate by a characteristic mark”), from *χαρακτήρ* (“a mark, character”).

core.definition: The national god of the Moabites, to whom sacrifices were offered and whom Israel's prophets condemned.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, with a long 'ee' vowel. The 'ch' is pronounced as a hard k, and the final syllable rhymes with 'wash' in General American. Avoid a soft 'ch' as in 'cheese'.

nuance.connotation: Negative in biblical context, since the god is presented as a false deity.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly encounter Chemosh in Bible study, history, or archaeology. It is not used in everyday speech. Use a neutral, careful tone when discussing the god, since he appears in sacred texts.

examples.everyday: In church we read about how Solomon built a high place for Chemosh.
examples.professional: In my lesson on Moab, I explained that Chemosh was the national god whose worship shaped the kingdom's identity.
examples.analytical: The prophetic critique of Chemosh exposes the idolatry of Moab, presenting national deities as powerless before the God of Israel.

nuance.analogy: Chemosh is like a national mascot raised to the level of a god: a symbol of a people's identity that the prophets refuse to honor.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Kĕmōsh, the name of the Moabite national god, of uncertain meaning.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the initial 'ch' as in 'cheese' instead of a hard k sound.
Confusing Chemosh with Molech, who was a different god worshiped by Ammonites.
nuance.biblical_note: Chemosh was the national god of the Moabites, and the Hebrew name is Kĕmōsh. Numbers 21:29 refers to the people of Chemosh, and 1 Kings 11:7 says that Solomon built a high place for Chemosh on the hill east of Jerusalem. Jeremiah 48:46 declares that the people of Chemosh are undone, because their sons and daughters have been taken into exile.

core.definition: The ninth month of the Hebrew calendar, roughly November to December, named in the Bible as a time of specific events.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable is a short 'lev', not 'lehv'. Many Americans hear it as close to 'KIS-lev' in church settings.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a technical or historical term used in Bible study and calendar discussions.
nuance.usage_note: Americans encounter 'Chislev' mainly in Bible reading, scholarship, or Jewish calendar discussions, and it is unusual in everyday conversation. In Hebrew it is spelled Kislev, and some English Bibles use that form. Use it when discussing dates in the Bible, such as in a sermon or a study group.

distinctions.note: 'Kislev' is the Hebrew spelling and most modern Jewish calendar sources; 'Chislev' is the spelling used in the RSV Bible.

examples.everyday: The Bible study group argued about whether the month Chislev falls in November or December.
examples.professional: The timeline in Nehemiah is dated to the month Chislev, so we need the Babylonian calendar to align the dates.
examples.analytical: The dating of Nehemiah's prayer to Chislev of the twentieth year of Artaxerxes anchors the narrative in a precise historical moment.

nuance.analogy: Chislev is like a calendar page that the Bible tears off to mark a specific season of the year.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Kislev, the name of a month of Babylonian origin.
common_mistakes: Assuming Chislev is a person or place, when it is a month of the Hebrew calendar.
Spelling it 'Kislev' in an English essay that follows the RSV, or mixing the two forms in one document.
nuance.biblical_note: Chislev is the ninth month of the Hebrew calendar. It appears in Nehemiah 1:1, where Nehemiah hears news of Jerusalem in the month Chislev of the twentieth year of Artaxerxes, and in Zechariah 7:1, which dates a message from the word of the LORD to the fourth day of the ninth month, Chislev. Jeremiah 36:9 also refers to the ninth month, which is the same month in the Hebrew calendar.

senses.definition: A free peasant (as opposed to a serf) of the low rank, below an earl and a thane; a freeman; also, a person without royal or noble status; a commoner.
senses.example: In Anglo-Saxon England, a churl owned his own land and paid taxes but ranked below the thanes.

senses.definition: A bondsman or serf.
senses.example: The charter freed the churl from bondage, though he still owed labor to the manor lord.

senses.definition: A rough, surly, ill-bred person; a boor.
senses.example: Ignoring the waiter's request, the churl stared at his phone and grunted at the bill.

senses.definition: A countryman, a peasant, a rustic.
senses.example: The old churl hauled his cart of turnips down the muddy lane to market.

senses.definition: A freedman, rank below a thane but above a thrall.
senses.example: Under the old law, a churl freed from servitude enjoyed rights above a thrall but below a thane.

core.definition: A rude, surly, ill-mannered person who is mean or ungracious toward others.

pronunciation.tip: Say it as one stressed syllable, with the r-colored vowel of fur. The r is pronounced in American English, so do not drop it to a short uh sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative. Calling someone a churl is a sharp insult implying coarse, grudging bad manners.
nuance.usage_note: Churl is literary and rarely used in everyday American speech. You will meet it in novels, poetry or formal criticism, and it can sound theatrical if used in casual conversation. For everyday speech, say jerk, boor or rude person.

distinctions.note: A boor is a crude, socially clumsy person, while a churl is more surly and ungenerous in attitude.
Jerk is common, informal American slang for an unkind person; churl is formal and literary.

examples.everyday: Don't be a churl about it, just say thanks when someone holds the door.
examples.professional: The vendor's replies were so curt that our project lead called him a churl in the meeting notes.
examples.analytical: Medieval texts often contrast the courtly knight with the churl, whose lowly status is treated as a moral failing.

nuance.analogy: A churl is like a grumpy shopkeeper who grudges every smile and every favor.
nuance.etymology: From Old English ceorl, a free peasant of low rank; the meaning shifted to a rude person over time.
common_mistakes: Confusing churl with churn; they sound similar but churn means to stir or to lose customers.
Using churl for a mild annoyance; it is a strong insult and too literary for casual use.

churl.etymology: *churle* (“person not of the nobility or clergy; serf, servant, simpleton, fellow”), from Old English *ċeorl* (“freeman ranking below a thane but above a thrall; commoner, peasant; countryman, husbandman; man; husband”), from **kerl*, from Proto-Germanic…

senses.definition: A strong fortress that sits high above a city.
A stronghold or fortified place.
An armored portion of a warship, housing important equipment.
senses.example: The shells struck the ship's citadel, but the armored core kept the engines running.

senses.definition: A Salvation Army meeting place.
senses.example: Every Sunday the family walked to the citadel for the morning service and hymn singing.

core.definition: A fortified place built high over a city to defend it, or a stronghold that protects something valuable.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The second syllable is a reduced 'uh', and the final syllable is a light 'dul', not 'DEL' as in 'delight'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive, suggesting strength, protection, and endurance, though it can be used figuratively to describe a place that resists outside influence.
nuance.usage_note: Most Americans encounter 'citadel' in history, travel writing, or literature, such as 'the citadel of Quebec' or a military academy named The Citadel in South Carolina. In everyday speech, people would more likely say 'fortress', 'stronghold', or 'castle'. Figuratively, 'citadel' appears in phrases like 'a citadel of learning' in formal writing.

distinctions.note: A fortress is a general term for a large fortified structure, while a citadel is typically the strongest fortified core of a city or town.
Stronghold is broader and often figurative, used for groups or places that hold power, while citadel more often describes a physical fortress.

examples.everyday: We walked up to the old citadel on the hill and looked out over the whole town.
examples.professional: The company's headquarters functioned as a citadel, with its own security and backup power.
examples.analytical: Many Enlightenment thinkers treated the university as a citadel of reason against superstition.

nuance.analogy: A citadel is like the castle keep in a video game: the strongest, highest point that defenders retreat to when everything else falls.
nuance.etymology: From Italian cittadella, a diminutive of città, city, from Latin civitas.
common_mistakes: Putting the stress on the second syllable, as in 'si-TA-del'.
Pronouncing the final syllable as 'DEL' instead of a reduced 'dul'.

citadel.etymology: From French *citadelle*, from Italian *cittadella*, diminutive of *città* (“city”), from Latin *cīvitās*.

senses.definition: In a civic manner.

core.definition: In a way that involves a person's duties and participation as a member of a community or citizen.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle vowel is a short i, and the ending is a light lee, not a separate syllable like lee-kuh-lee. Say SIV-ik-lee with a clear k.

nuance.connotation: Positive; suggests responsibility, participation, and community spirit.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use civically mostly in writing about schools, neighborhoods, and public life, such as civically engaged students. In casual talk they would more likely say get involved in your community. The word is somewhat formal, so it fits essays, mission statements, and school applications better than everyday chat.

distinctions.note: Civilly means politely or courteously, as in speaking civilly to an opponent, while civically means relating to citizenship and community duties.
Politically refers to government, parties, and power, while civically focuses on community participation and public responsibility, often without partisan meaning.

examples.everyday: My neighbor is really civically active, so she goes to every school board meeting.
examples.professional: Our mission statement says we want employees to act civically, not only as workers but as members of the neighborhoods we serve.
examples.analytical: A liberal education is meant to form students who think and act civically, not merely as consumers of public services.

nuance.analogy: Acting civically is like being a good member of a potluck: you bring something for the group, not just for yourself.
nuance.etymology: From civic, from Latin civicus, of a citizen, from civis, citizen, plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Confusing civically with civilly; civilly means politely, while civically means as a citizen.
Using it in casual speech where Americans would say get involved in your community.

senses.definition: Able to be claimed.
Something that can be claimed.
senses.example: The unclaimed property office lists every claimable item, from forgotten bank accounts to old tax refunds.

core.definition: Able to be claimed, such as a tax deduction or a benefit a person is entitled to request.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, KLAY. The middle syllable is reduced to uh, and the ending -able sounds like buhl, not ayb-ul.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and administrative. It is used for money or benefits, not for emotional claims.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use claimable mostly in taxes, insurance, employee benefits, and government programs, as in claimable expenses. In casual speech, people usually say you can claim it or you can get reimbursed. The word is correct but more formal than everyday conversation.

distinctions.note: Eligible means a person meets the requirements for something, while claimable means a specific expense or benefit can be requested.
Refundable means money can be returned to you, while claimable means you can request it as a benefit or deduction.

examples.everyday: Are the gym fees claimable through the company, or do I have to pay them myself?
examples.professional: Travel costs are claimable only if you attach the original receipts to the expense report.
examples.analytical: The rights claimable under the statute are limited to those specifically listed in its text.
