core.definition: Too vague, subtle, or complex to be precisely defined or described in words.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'FY', the third syllable, as in 'define'. The final -able is a reduced 'uh-bul', not 'ay-bul'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it suggests a special quality that resists description.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this in writing, reviews, and conversation about a feeling, a flavor, or an atmosphere that is hard to name. In casual speech people often say 'I can't put my finger on it'. It can sound a little dramatic if overused.

distinctions.note: Indescribable stresses that words fail to capture something; indefinable stresses that its boundaries or nature cannot be fixed.
Vague is a general negative term about unclearness; indefinable is more neutral and often used for subtle qualities.

examples.everyday: This little café has an indefinable charm that makes you want to stay all afternoon.
examples.professional: The product has an indefinable quality that customers love, but it is hard to write into the spec.
examples.analytical: Aristotle's concept of virtue remains indefinable in purely quantitative terms, which is part of its appeal.

nuance.analogy: Like a smell in a room: you notice it clearly, but you cannot name its exact ingredients.
nuance.etymology: From in- 'not' + definable, from Latin definire 'to define'.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'undefinable' in formal writing; both are used, but 'indefinable' is more common.
Putting stress on 'in' rather than 'FY'.

senses.definition: The principle that if two objects are absolutely identical then they must be indistinguishable from one another with respect to all of their properties.
senses.example: Leibniz's indiscernibility of identicals rules out two distinct objects sharing every property.

core.definition: The philosophical principle that if two things are truly identical, they cannot differ in any property, so no property can tell them apart.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on BIL in indiscernibility and on DEN in identicals. Say 'of' as a weak 'uv', and link the words smoothly in fast speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a precise technical term used in logic and metaphysics with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Philosophers and logicians use this phrase, usually in its shorter form 'Leibniz's Law', when arguing about identity and properties. Americans in conversation rarely say it, so in ordinary talk you would say 'if two things are exactly the same, they have all the same properties'. It is often paired with the converse, the identity of indiscernibles.

distinctions.note: The converse principle: things with all the same properties must be identical. Leibniz held both principles, but they are logically distinct claims.
Another name for the same principle, used more often in American philosophy classrooms.

examples.professional: In the model specification review, we used the indiscernibility of identicals to argue that the two feature sets were redundant.
examples.analytical: The argument from the indiscernibility of identicals presupposes that every property is an intrinsic or relational feature that can be included in a complete description of an object.

nuance.analogy: Like two copies of a key cut from exactly the same mold: if they match in every measurement, there is no way to tell which one is which.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'indiscernibilis' (not distinguishable), from 'in-' (not) plus 'discernere' (to separate, distinguish) and 'identicus' (the same).
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, saying 'in-dis-ser-NIB-il-ity' instead of 'in-dih-sur-nuh-BIL-ih-tee'.
Confusing the principle with the converse, which is the identity of indiscernibles.

senses.definition: The tendency for a person to act without reference to others, particularly in matters of style, fashion or mode of thought.
senses.example: Her grandmother's disdain for fashion trends reflected a fierce individualism in her wardrobe choices.

senses.definition: The moral stance, political philosophy, or social outlook that promotes independence and self-reliance of individual people, while opposing the interference with each person's choices by society, the state, or any other group or institution.
senses.example: Many Americans see individualism as the foundation of a government that should stay out of their lives.

senses.definition: The doctrine that only individual things are real.
senses.example: In his seminar, the professor argued that metaphysical individualism leaves no room for abstract universal categories.

senses.definition: The doctrine that nothing exists but the individual self.
senses.example: Some strands of solipsism push individualism so far that the outside world seems to vanish.

core.definition: The belief that people should act independently and make their own choices, valuing personal freedom over group or state control.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on VIH, the third syllable. Keep the middle syllables quick and reduced, and the final '-ism' is a short 'izm' with a reduced vowel.

nuance.connotation: Often positive, linked to freedom and self-reliance; can be negative when it suggests selfishness or disregard for others.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often discuss individualism as a core national value, linked to independence, the frontier and the self-made person. In casual talk, calling someone an individualist can be a compliment or a criticism, depending on tone. In politics and academic debate, it is central, often contrasted with collectivism or community.

distinctions.note: Individualism is a belief or philosophy; individuality is the quality of being distinct from others.
Selfishness is a negative focus on oneself; individualism is a principled stance that emphasizes personal choice and independence.

examples.everyday: My brother is all about individualism; he refuses to follow any trend.
examples.professional: Our team culture values individualism in problem solving, but we still expect everyone to share their code.
examples.analytical: Tocqueville saw American individualism as a double-edged virtue, fostering independence while weakening civic bonds.

nuance.analogy: Like a lone tree on a hill that grows its own shape, unlike trees planted in a row.
nuance.etymology: Formed from individual plus the suffix -ism; the word appeared in the 19th century.
common_mistakes: Using it to mean 'individuality' (the quality of being unique), when it refers to a belief or social outlook.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in in-dih-vih-DJOO-uh-lizm.

senses.definition: Someone who believes in individualism as a sociopolitical system.
Someone who believes in the philosophy of individualism; a solipsist.
Someone who does as they wish, unconstrained by external influences.
senses.example: My sister is a fierce individualist who refuses to follow any trend her friends start.

core.definition: A person who believes in individualism and acts independently, valuing personal freedom and self-reliance over group or government direction.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on VIJ, the same syllable as in individual. The ending -ist is a short 'ist', not 'eest', and the final syllable is not stressed.

nuance.connotation: Mixed. In American culture it can praise independence and self-reliance, but it can also describe someone who ignores teamwork or group rules.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use the phrase 'rugged individualist' to praise self-reliance, a value deeply rooted in the country's history. It can also describe someone who refuses to cooperate, which sounds like criticism at work. In political talk, 'libertarian' is the closer term for someone who favors minimal government. Be careful when describing a colleague as an individualist, since it may suggest they work alone.

distinctions.note: Individualist is the person; individualistic is the adjective describing a trait, idea or style.
A libertarian is someone who favors minimal government; an individualist may be an artist, a thinker or an ordinary person with no political view.
A loner prefers to be alone and often avoids people; an individualist values personal independence and may work well with others.

examples.everyday: My uncle is a real individualist; he would rather fix his own roof than call a contractor.
examples.professional: Our lead engineer is an individualist who likes to design solutions alone, so we pair her with a reviewer.
examples.analytical: Critics of modern liberalism often portray the individualist as a self-made agent who owes nothing to the community that formed him.

nuance.analogy: An individualist is like a solo sailor: independent by choice, but still steered by the same wind as everyone else.
nuance.etymology: From individual plus -ist, from Latin individuus 'undivided'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'individualist' with 'individualistic'; say 'She is an individualist' for the person and 'individualistic' for the trait.
Assuming it is always positive; in a team setting it can suggest someone who ignores group goals.
Putting stress on the last syllable; say in-dih-VIJ-oo-uh-list.

senses.definition: The condition of being inevitable.
An inevitable condition or outcome.
senses.example: Given the rising interest rates, the recession seemed like an inevitability to most economists.

core.definition: The quality of being certain to happen and impossible to prevent; a situation or outcome that cannot be avoided.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on BIL, the third-from-last syllable. The 'ta' in the middle is reduced to a weak 'tuh', and the 't' in '-ity' is a flapped t sounding like a soft 'd' in American speech. Do not say 'ih-nev-ih-TAB-ih-tee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to somewhat negative; it often implies that something unwelcome cannot be stopped, though it can also describe a positive outcome.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use inevitability in discussions about trends, politics, sports, and history, such as 'the inevitability of change.' In everyday talk they more often say 'it was bound to happen' or 'there was no way around it.' Use the noun in writing or formal speech.

distinctions.note: Certainty is confidence that something is true or will happen; inevitability is the fact that it cannot be avoided, regardless of what anyone thinks.
Probability measures how likely an event is, from 0 to 1; inevitability describes an event that has probability 1 and cannot be prevented.

examples.everyday: After three late nights in a row, I could feel the inevitability of getting sick.
examples.professional: Given the budget cuts, there was a growing inevitability about the layoffs.
examples.analytical: Hegel's account of history rests on a claimed inevitability that many philosophers find hard to defend.

nuance.analogy: Like a train on a fixed track, its arrival is certain; nothing on the platform can change it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin inevitabilis, 'unavoidable', from in- 'not' plus evitabilis, from evitare 'to avoid'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable (ih-NEV-ih-tuh-bil-ih-tee) instead of BIL.
Using inevitability as a verb-like action; it names a quality or a condition, so say 'the inevitability of' rather than 'to inevitability'.

senses.definition: An illness caused by a specific infectious agent (bacterium, virus, fungus, protozoa, prion etc.), that results from transmission of that agent from an infected person, animal, or reservoir to a susceptible host.
senses.example: Measles is a highly infectious disease that spreads quickly through crowded classrooms.

senses.definition: A medical specialty dealing with the diagnosis, control and treatment of infections.
senses.example: She chose infectious disease as her specialty after working in tropical clinics.

core.definition: An illness caused by a microorganism, such as a bacterium, virus, or fungus, that spreads from one host to another.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on -FEK- in infectious and on -ZEEZ in disease, where the s is voiced like a z. Do not pronounce the final -ious as a full 'ee-us'; it reduces to 'shus'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. The phrase is a factual medical term and does not carry emotional weight by itself.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase in doctors' offices, news reports, and public health discussions, often as 'an infectious disease' or 'infectious diseases' as a plural. It is also the name of a medical specialty, so 'She's an infectious disease doctor' is common hospital talk. For everyday speech, Americans often just say 'it's contagious' or 'it's going around'.

distinctions.note: Contagious means spread by direct or close contact, while infectious covers any transmission route, including air, water, insects, or contaminated surfaces.
Communicable is a formal public health term for diseases that can be passed from person to person, and is less common in everyday American speech.

examples.everyday: My doctor said it's an infectious disease, so I need to stay home for a few days.
examples.professional: The infectious disease team traced the outbreak to a contaminated water supply at the plant.
examples.analytical: Koch's postulates were designed to link a specific microbe to a particular infectious disease.

nuance.analogy: Think of the agent as a seed and the host as soil: the disease is what grows once the seed is planted in a receptive body.
nuance.etymology: From Latin inficere, 'to put in, stain, infect', from in- plus facere, 'to make'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'contagious disease' for any illness; contagious is narrower and refers mainly to direct contact.
Stressing the second word on its first syllable, as in 'DIS-ease' instead of 'dih-ZEEZ'.
Using the phrase for non-infectious conditions such as heart disease or diabetes.

senses.definition: The act of entering.
A permission to enter.
senses.example: All ingress was prohibited.

senses.definition: A door or other means of entering.
The entrance of the Moon into the shadow of the Earth in eclipses, or the Sun's entrance into a sign, etc.
senses.example: Astronomers timed the ingress of the Moon into Earth's shadow, which began just after ten o'clock.

senses.definition: To intrude or insert oneself.
senses.example: She didn't want to ingress into their conversation, so she quietly walked away.

senses.definition: To enter into a zodiacal sign.
senses.example: The Sun will ingress into Aries next month, marking the start of the astrological spring season.

senses.definition: To manifest or cause to be manifested in the temporal world; to effect ingression.
senses.example: Her seminar paper argued that divine grace could ingress into human history through ordinary acts of mercy.

senses.definition: To enter (a specified location or area)
senses.example: The protesters attempted to ingress the building through a side door before police arrived.

core.definition: The act of entering a place, or a way or means of entering it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, IN, and the g is hard. The final -ess is short, like the word yes, not the long ee of egress.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a formal, descriptive term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ingress mostly in legal, architectural, security, and technical writing, such as ingress and egress in building codes or ingress traffic in networks. In everyday speech people say 'entrance,' 'way in,' or 'door.' The word sounds stiff if used casually.

distinctions.note: Entrance is the everyday word for a door or place of entering, while ingress is more formal and often refers to the act of entering or to access rights.
Access emphasizes the ability to reach or use something, while ingress emphasizes the physical or technical act of getting in.

examples.everyday: Please keep the ingress clear so people can get in and out safely.
examples.professional: The network team blocked unwanted ingress traffic at the firewall before it reached the database.
examples.analytical: The philosopher used the ingress of new ideas into a culture as a metaphor for gradual intellectual change.

nuance.analogy: Ingress is the doorway of a building: the way in that must be kept open for people to enter.
nuance.etymology: From Latin ingressus, past participle of ingredi, to go into.
common_mistakes: Confusing ingress with egress: ingress means entering, and egress means exiting.
Stressing the second syllable (in-GRESS) instead of the first syllable, IN.

senses.definition: A similar period of play.
senses.example: We batted around in our half of the inning.

senses.definition: A player (or team)'s turn at the table to make shots until ended by a miss or a foul.
senses.example: In the match, she ran sixty points in one inning before missing an easy bank shot.

senses.definition: A chance or opportunity to perform some deed or act.
senses.example: We are in just the second inning of our quest to enter this new market.

senses.definition: A period of play in which members of a visiting baseball team attempt to hit a baseball pitched by the opposing home team until three players are called out, followed by a similar attempt by members of the home baseball team against the visiting team's pitching. There are nine or more innings in a regulation baseball game.
senses.example: It is a baseball tradition to sing "Take Me Out To the Ball Game" during the seventh inning stretch.

core.definition: One of the main divisions of a baseball game, in which each team gets a turn to bat and try to score runs.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle vowel is short and quick, and the -ing ending is a light nasal sound, not a long 'eeng'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a standard sports term, often used in casual conversation about games.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'inning' mainly for baseball, and fans often talk about 'the seventh inning stretch'. In cricket or other sports, the word has different meanings, so say 'baseball inning' if you want to be precise. In a bar or at a game, people say 'bottom of the ninth' or 'top of the third'.

distinctions.note: 'Period' is general and used for hockey or school; 'inning' is specific to baseball.
'Turn' is a general word for taking a chance, while 'inning' is the formal term for a unit of a baseball game.

collocations: the bottom of the ninth inning

examples.everyday: We left the stadium in the seventh inning because the traffic was terrible.
examples.professional: Our marketing campaign has entered its final inning, so we need to lock in the results this week.
examples.analytical: A baseball game is structured in innings, and each inning divides the contest into two halves, one for each team.

nuance.analogy: An inning is like a round in a boxing match, a fixed portion of the game that repeats until the end.
nuance.etymology: From Old English 'innung', meaning a putting in, or a getting in, with reference to taking one's turn.
common_mistakes: Saying 'inning' for a single pitch or at-bat; an inning includes three outs for each team.
Confusing 'innings' (plural) with the singular form when speaking about a single turn.

inning.etymology: mistaken to be plural of the time period, not the entries of the batters/batsmen.

conversation.text: It's the bottom of the ninth inning, and the score is tied.
We got there in the third inning because of traffic.
They scored five runs in one inning.

senses.definition: Causing harm in a stealthy, often gradual, manner.
senses.example: The insidious spread of debt quietly eroded the family's savings over many years.

senses.definition: Intending to entrap; alluring but harmful.
senses.example: Hansel and Gretel were lured by the witch’s insidious gingerbread house.

core.definition: Harmful in a hidden or gradual way, so that the danger is hard to notice until serious damage has been done.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SID, the second syllable. The middle 'i' is a short 'ih' and the 'ee' sound is light, so the word has three syllables with the final 'us' reduced. Avoid stressing the last syllable.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. It describes a danger that is hidden, treacherous and hard to resist or detect.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'insidious' to describe slow, hidden threats such as disease, corruption, bias or addiction, especially in news, medicine and social commentary. It is a strong word, so it sounds dramatic in casual talk. Americans might say 'sneaky' or 'creeping' in everyday speech.

distinctions.note: Sneaky is casual and often about small deceptions. Insidious describes serious, gradual harm that is hard to detect.
Subtle means delicate or hard to perceive, and can be neutral or positive. Insidious always implies harm.
Dangerous describes obvious risk. Insidious describes risk that hides behind an appearance of safety.

examples.everyday: My doctor warned me that high blood pressure is insidious because you often feel fine until something goes wrong.
examples.professional: Data drift is an insidious problem, since model accuracy can decline slowly without any obvious error.
examples.analytical: Bentham's panopticon exerts an insidious power, because the subject internalizes surveillance and disciplines himself.

nuance.analogy: An insidious problem is like a slow leak in a roof: nothing looks wrong until the ceiling collapses.
nuance.etymology: From Latin insidiosus, from insidiae, ambush, from insidere, to sit in or upon.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'invidious', which means unfairly causing resentment or unpleasant.
Stressing the final syllable, as in in-sid-ee-US.

insidious.etymology: From Middle French *insidieux*, from Latin *īnsidiōsus* (“cunning, artful, deceitful”), from *īnsidiae* (“a lying in wait, an ambush, artifice, stratagem”) + *-ōsus*, from *īnsideō* (“to sit in or on”), from *in* (“in, on”) + *sedeō* (“to sit”).

senses.definition: To hold up a claim emphatically.
senses.example: The defendant insisted on his innocence.

senses.definition: To demand continually that something happen or be done; to reiterate a demand despite requests to abandon it.
senses.example: The Prime Minister insisted on his Chancellor's resignation.

core.definition: To state something firmly, or demand that something happen, refusing to back down or drop the point.

pronunciation.tip: The single syllable is stressed and has a short 'ih' vowel. Make the final -st a clear, sharp sound and do not add a vowel after the t.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative. It can be friendly when you are being generous ('I insist'), but it can sound pushy when used to override someone's objections.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'I insist!' when they want to pay for something or when refusing a polite no, as in 'No, I insist, let me get that.' It can also mean stubbornly demanding something. Use 'insist on' with a noun or -ing form, and 'insist that' with a clause; in 'insist that' clauses, Americans usually use a base verb (insist that she leave).

distinctions.note: Persist means to keep doing something despite difficulty over time; insist is about firmly stating or demanding something in words or action.
Demand is a direct request, often with authority; insist adds the sense that you refuse to accept a refusal.
Assert is a neutral, formal word for stating a claim confidently; insist implies more force and sometimes stubbornness.

examples.everyday: I told you I'd pay for dinner, but you insisted on getting the check, so thanks.
examples.professional: I insist that we review the security findings before the release goes out, even if it slips a week.
examples.analytical: Kant insists that moral duty must be grounded in reason rather than in inclination, and the argument turns on that claim.

nuance.analogy: To insist is to plant your feet on a point and refuse to be moved, like a tree that stays rooted through a storm.
nuance.etymology: From Latin insistere 'to stand upon, persist', from in- 'on' plus sistere 'to stand'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'insist for' something; use 'insist on' with a noun or -ing form.
Using 'insist that' with a past or present verb form where Americans use a base verb, as in 'insist that she leave' rather than 'insist that she leaves'.

insist.etymology: Partly from Middle French *insister*, from Latin *īnsistō*; and partly from a.

senses.definition: An organization founded to promote a cause.
senses.example: I work in a medical research institute.

senses.definition: An institution of learning; a college, especially for technical subjects.
senses.example: She earned her master's degree at a technical institute known for its engineering labs.

senses.definition: The building housing such an institution.
senses.example: We met for coffee in the old institute across from the public library.

senses.definition: To begin or initiate (something); to found.
senses.example: He instituted the new policy of having children walk through a metal detector to enter school.

senses.definition: To nominate; to appoint.
senses.example: The council voted to institute Maria as the new chair of the library board.

senses.definition: To invest with the spiritual charge of a benefice, or the care of souls.
senses.example: The bishop will institute the new rector to the parish, entrusting him with its souls.

core.definition: An organization or school dedicated to research, education, or promoting a field, such as a specialized technical college.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, IN-. Americans say the -tute ending as toot, without a y sound. As a verb, the stress shifts to the second syllable: in-STOOT.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it suggests a serious, established body with a specific purpose.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use institute for a specialized organization or school, such as a research institute, a policy think tank, or a technical college. Large general schools are usually called universities. As a verb, institute is formal and common in news and law, as in 'institute a new policy' or 'institute proceedings.'

distinctions.note: An institute is usually smaller and focused on one field, while an institution is a broader term for any large, established organization.
Establish is the everyday verb for creating something; institute as a verb is more formal and often used for policies or legal actions.

examples.everyday: My cousin works at a research institute in Boulder, studying climate models.
examples.professional: We will institute a two-factor login requirement next quarter, so please update your accounts.
examples.analytical: Rawls argued that a just society must institute fair rules before individuals pursue their own aims.

nuance.analogy: Think of an institute as a focused workshop inside the larger city of knowledge, built for one kind of work.
nuance.etymology: From Latin institutum, 'arrangement, custom,' from instituere, 'to set up, establish.'
common_mistakes: Confusing institute with institution: a university is an institution, but a smaller research body is usually called an institute.
Stressing the verb on the first syllable as IN-stitute; the verb is in-STOOT.

institute.etymology: From French *institut*, from Middle French, from Latin *īnstitūtum*.

senses.definition: Capable of being understood; clear to the mind.
senses.example: Italian and Spanish are partially mutually intelligible languages.

core.definition: Clear enough to be understood; able to be grasped by the mind.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TEL. The middle syllables are reduced to schwa, and the ending is a syllabic 'bul,' so there is no separate 'ee' or 'ih' vowel at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes whether something can be understood, without praising or criticizing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use intelligible in formal writing, academic work, and speech about clarity, such as 'an intelligible explanation.' In casual speech they would more often say 'understandable' or 'clear.' It is also used with a negative, as in 'barely intelligible,' to describe unclear speech.

distinctions.note: Understandable is everyday and common; intelligible is more formal and often describes speech or writing that can be decoded with effort.
Clear can describe anything easy to see or hear; intelligible focuses on whether meaning can be grasped.
Comprehensible is nearly the same but more formal and less common in American speech.

examples.everyday: The recording was so noisy that I could barely make out what he said, and it wasn't intelligible at all.
examples.professional: Please make the dashboard labels intelligible to non-technical managers, because they are the ones signing off on it.
examples.analytical: Wittgenstein suggests that a language is intelligible only when its rules can be shared within a community of speakers.

nuance.analogy: An intelligible message is like a clear window: you can see through it to the meaning behind the words.
nuance.etymology: From Latin intelligibilis, from intelligere, 'to understand,' from inter- and legere, 'to choose, read.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable, as in 'in-tel-uh-JUH-bul.'
Confusing intelligible with 'intelligent,' which describes a mind rather than clarity of speech.
Using it as a noun; the noun form is intelligibility.

intelligible.etymology: From Middle French *intelligible*, from Old French, from Latin *intelligibilis*.

senses.definition: In an interesting way.
It is interesting to note that…

core.definition: In a way that holds your attention. Also used to introduce a surprising or notable fact, as in 'Interestingly, nobody noticed.'

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, IN. The middle 'ter' is often reduced to a quick r-colored syllable, so many Americans say it almost like IN-tres-ting-lee, and the final -ly is a light 'lee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. As a sentence opener it flags a mildly surprising point without judgment, though overuse can sound like a filler word.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often open a sentence with 'Interestingly,' in conversation, presentations and writing to flag a surprising point. In casual talk, 'The weird part is...' or 'Funny thing is...' sounds more natural. 'It is interesting to note that...' is wordy and academic; in a meeting, state the point directly.

distinctions.note: Interesting is an adjective describing something that holds attention; interestingly is an adverb that describes how something is done or introduces a surprising point.
Curiously often signals strangeness or puzzlement, while interestingly is milder and more neutral.

examples.everyday: Interestingly, the café on Fifth Street doesn't take cards, only cash.
examples.professional: Interestingly, churn dropped only in the two regions that got the new onboarding flow, so let's test it company-wide.
examples.analytical: Interestingly, Augustine's later writings on grace treat it as the source of the will's desire to do good, not merely a reward for it.

nuance.analogy: Like a side street that turns out to be the fastest route, it points you somewhere you didn't expect.
nuance.etymology: From interesting plus -ly; interesting comes from Latin interesse, 'to be between, concern, make a difference'.
common_mistakes: Starting every paragraph with 'Interestingly,' which sounds repetitive; vary it with 'What stood out was...'
Saying 'I am interesting in it' instead of 'I am interested in it'; the adjective 'interesting' describes the thing, 'interested' describes the person.

senses.definition: Acting or tending to interrupt.

core.definition: Tending to interrupt or break into something, especially in a way that disturbs the flow.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the 'RUP' syllable, with the short 'uh' vowel. The ending '-tive' is reduced to 'tiv', with no long 'ee' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It suggests something that disturbs or breaks the flow of an activity.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use interruptive. In conversation, they say 'interrupting' or 'disruptive'. The word appears mostly in formal writing or literary prose about speech, sound, or events.

distinctions.note: Disruptive is far more common and suggests a larger, more damaging break in order, while interruptive is rare and describes a simple breaking-in.
Interrupting is an everyday participle used to describe an action, while interruptive describes a quality or tendency.

examples.everyday: My little brother's questions are so interruptive when I'm on a call.
examples.professional: The alarm's interruptive tone pulls everyone out of their focus, so we should use a softer sound.
examples.analytical: The author treats the phone's interruptive ring as a symbol of constant demands on attention.

nuance.analogy: An interruptive sound is like a doorbell in the middle of a sentence: it breaks the thought without meaning to.
nuance.etymology: From interrupt plus the suffix -ive, from Latin interrumpere, to break apart.
common_mistakes: Using interruptive to mean interrupted; interrupted describes something that has been broken, while interruptive describes a tendency to break in.
Choosing this rare word in everyday speech where 'disruptive' or 'interrupting' sounds more natural.

senses.definition: A small opening or space between objects, especially adjacent objects or objects set closely together, such as between cords in a rope, components of a multiconductor electrical cable or atoms in a crystal.
A fragment of space.
An interval of time required by the Roman Catholic Church between the attainment of different degrees of an order.
senses.example: Canon law required a set interstice between receiving minor orders and the subdiaconate.

senses.definition: A small interval of time free to be spent on activities other than one's primary goal.
senses.example: In the brief interstice between meetings, she answered email and grabbed a sandwich.

core.definition: A small opening or narrow space between closely set objects, such as the gaps between threads, cords, or atoms in a crystal.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, and the ending sounds like 'iss,' not 'ace.' The middle vowel is a short 'i,' so avoid saying 'in-ter-STEES.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. The word is descriptive and carries no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'interstice' mainly in scientific, technical, or literary writing about small gaps. In everyday talk they say 'gap,' 'crack,' or 'space between.' Using it in casual conversation may sound overly bookish.

distinctions.note: 'Gap' is the everyday word for any opening or missing space; 'interstice' is more precise and specialized, usually for tiny spaces between closely packed parts.
A 'crevice' is a deep, usually rocky crack; an 'interstice' is a small space between adjacent things.

collocations: the interstices of a crystal lattice
through the interstices of the wall

examples.everyday: Sand had worked its way into every interstice between the deck boards.
examples.professional: The technician checked the interstices between the cable conductors for moisture before sealing the connector.
examples.analytical: Kant locates the interstices of human reason, the spaces where experience cannot fully determine knowledge.

nuance.analogy: Like the tiny spaces between bricks in a wall, where mortar goes.
nuance.etymology: From Latin interstitium, 'a space between,' from inter- 'between' and sistere 'to stand.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the stress on the first syllable (IN-ter-stice).
Using 'interstice' for a large gap or a break in time, where 'gap' or 'interval' is more natural.

interstice.etymology: From late Middle English *interstice*, from Old French *interstice* or directly from Latin *interstitium* (“a space between, gap, interval”), ultimately from *intersistō* (“to stand in between, to stop in the middle”), from *inter* + *sistō*.

senses.definition: In an intolerable manner; beyond endurance.
senses.example: The summer heat in the apartment became intolerably hot by midafternoon, so we left.

core.definition: In a way that is so extreme or unpleasant that it cannot be endured.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TAH, as in intolerable. The middle syllables reduce to a quick 'luh-ruh', and the ending is 'blee', so avoid saying 'in-tol-ER-ab-ly'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it is an intensifier used to express strong frustration.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use intolerably as an intensifier in complaints: 'intolerably hot,' 'intolerably slow.' It is more formal than 'really' but natural in casual speech about annoying situations. A natural reply is 'Tell me about it.'

distinctions.note: Nearly interchangeable; unbearably is slightly more common in casual speech.
Extremely is a neutral intensifier; intolerably signals the situation is actually impossible to endure.

examples.everyday: The traffic on the bridge was intolerably slow, so we took the back road.
examples.professional: The dashboard loads intolerably slowly on mobile, and customers have started to leave.
examples.analytical: Such a reading makes the text intolerably vague, reducing a precise command to a platitude.

nuance.analogy: Intolerably is like a sound so loud that you cannot stop hearing it.
nuance.etymology: Formed from intolerable (from Latin intolerabilis) plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Using intolerably as a verb or for a person; it modifies adjectives and verbs.
Stressing the wrong syllable; keep the main stress on TAH.

senses.definition: The state or quality of being intricate or entangled.
senses.example: the intricacy of a knot

senses.definition: Perplexity.
senses.example: The intricacy of the tax code left even experienced accountants completely confused.

senses.definition: Something which is intricate or complex.
senses.example: There are many intricacies in the plot of this novel.

core.definition: The quality of having many small, interrelated parts or details that make something complex.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, IN. The middle vowels are reduced, and the final -cy is pronounced 'see'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It can admire fine detail or complain about something overly complicated.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use intricacy for designs, machines, systems, stories and arguments with many interlocking parts. It is common in both professional and general writing. In casual speech people often say the complexity or all the details. The word can be admiring, as in the intricacy of the carving, or critical, as in the intricacies of the tax code.

distinctions.note: Complexity is the general quality of having many parts; intricacy stresses fine, interlocking detail that requires care to understand.
Detail is a single small item; intricacy describes the whole pattern of many connected details.

examples.everyday: I love the intricacy of my grandmother's quilt, with hundreds of tiny stitches in every corner.
examples.professional: The intricacy of the billing rules makes the pipeline hard to maintain, so we should simplify it.
examples.analytical: The novel's power lies in the intricacy of its moral arguments, which resist any single reading.

nuance.analogy: Intricacy is like a watch movement: each small gear matters, and the beauty and difficulty come from how they all fit together.
nuance.etymology: From intricate, from Latin intricatus (entangled), from intricare (to entangle).
common_mistakes: Using intricacy as a countable noun without the plural intricacies when meaning several details.
Stressing the second syllable as in-TRIK-uh-see.
Confusing it with intricate, the adjective, in sentences that need a noun.

senses.definition: The act of invalidating, or the state of being invalidated.

core.definition: The act of making something invalid, or the state of having been made invalid, such as a result, a contract, or stored data.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on DAY, and the earlier syllables are weaker, with a reduced 'uh' in the third syllable. Learners often confuse it with 'invalidity' and stress the wrong syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a neutral process, though the result may be negative for whoever loses the thing being invalidated.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use invalidation most in technical and legal writing, such as cache invalidation in software, patent invalidation in law, and contract invalidation. In everyday conversation people say 'canceling' or 'voiding' instead. In computing, cache invalidation is a very common phrase that English speakers in tech will hear often.

distinctions.note: Invalidation is the act of making something invalid, while invalidity is the state of being invalid.
Cancellation is the everyday word for calling something off, while invalidation focuses on the thing losing its validity.

examples.everyday: The bank's invalidation of my old card came with a text saying a new one was on the way.
examples.professional: The cache invalidation logic was buggy, so users kept seeing stale prices for hours.
examples.analytical: The court's invalidation of the statute rested on a narrow reading of the constitutional text.

nuance.analogy: Like crossing out a line on a form and writing VOID beside it: the form is still there, but it no longer counts.
nuance.etymology: From invalidate, from Medieval Latin invalidare, 'to make void,' with the noun suffix -ation.
common_mistakes: Using invalidation when you mean the state of being invalid, where invalidity is the correct noun.
Stressing the first syllable instead of DAY, which makes the word sound unnatural to American ears.

senses.definition: Synonym of arctangent.

core.definition: The angle whose tangent equals a given number; written tan^-1 or arctan.

pronunciation.tip: Stress IN in 'inverse' and TAN in 'tangent'. The final syllable of 'tangent' is a weak, reduced 'jent', not 'jont'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise mathematical term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'inverse tangent' in math courses, physics, and calculators, and 'arctangent' or 'arctan' is equally standard. In code, the function is often called atan or atan2. The two-argument version atan2 is widely used in engineering to find the correct quadrant.

distinctions.note: The two names mean the same thing; 'arctangent' is common in higher math and programming, while 'inverse tangent' is common in textbooks and calculators.
Atan2 takes two arguments and returns the correct angle in all four quadrants, while the inverse tangent takes one ratio and returns an angle between minus pi over two and pi over two.

collocations: principal branch of the inverse tangent
use atan2 instead of the inverse tangent

examples.everyday: I was trying to figure out the slope of the roof, and my neighbor said I needed the inverse tangent on my phone calculator.
examples.professional: The gyroscope code takes the inverse tangent of the ratio, but we switch to atan2 so the heading comes out in the right quadrant.
examples.analytical: Because the inverse tangent has a range limited to an open interval, it cannot distinguish angles that differ by pi unless we use the two-argument form.

nuance.analogy: The inverse tangent is like reading a slope gauge backward: you start with the steepness and find the angle that gives that steepness.
nuance.etymology: 'Inverse' comes from Latin inversus, 'turned upside down'; 'tangent' comes from Latin tangens, 'touching'.
common_mistakes: Reading tan^-1 x as 1/tan x; the -1 means inverse function, and 1/tan x is cotangent.
Using the single-argument inverse tangent for direction in code instead of atan2, which gives the wrong quadrant.

senses.definition: Lack of relationship with the topic at hand; lack of importance.

core.definition: The quality of not being connected to the topic at hand, or of not being important.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on REL, the first full syllable. The 'ir-' is 'ih-', and the unstressed middle vowels reduce to a quick schwa, so it sounds like 'ih-REL-uh-vuhns'.

nuance.connotation: Negative or dismissive. It suggests something does not matter to the discussion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use irrelevance in meetings, debates, and writing when they want to say a point does not apply. In everyday conversation people usually say 'That doesn't matter' or 'That's beside the point.' Saying a person is an irrelevance can sound harsh, so use it carefully.

distinctions.note: Triviality is about something small or unimportant in itself; irrelevance is about something not connected to the matter at hand.
Unimportance describes low significance; irrelevance describes lack of connection, even if the thing is important elsewhere.

examples.everyday: Let's stop talking about his old job, because that's total irrelevance to what we're deciding.
examples.professional: The committee rejected the proposal on grounds of irrelevance to our quarterly goals.
examples.analytical: Frege's argument turns on the irrelevance of psychological states to the logical truth of a proposition.

nuance.analogy: Like a key that is shaped for a different lock: it may be a fine key, but it does not open this door.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin irrelevans, from in- 'not' plus relevare 'to lift up, relieve, bear upon'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable; the stress is on REL.
Using relevance and irrelevance interchangeably when describing a point.

senses.definition: A small island.
senses.example: There is an islet on the other side of this body of water.

senses.definition: An isolated piece of tissue that has a specific function.
senses.example: Researchers isolated insulin-producing islet cells from the pancreas to study how diabetes develops.

core.definition: A very small island, often rocky or uninhabited, that is surrounded by water.

pronunciation.tip: The s is silent, and the stress falls on the first syllable. The final -et is reduced to a light schwa or a short -it sound, so avoid pronouncing the t with a strong burst.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can suggest small, quiet, or isolated places, sometimes with a poetic tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use islet for small rocky or sandy islands, often in travel writing, geography, and coastal survey reports. In biology, the term islets of Langerhans refers to clusters of cells in the pancreas, which is a different sense. In everyday talk, many Americans just say small island.

distinctions.note: An islet is much smaller and often uninhabited. An island can be large enough for towns and roads.
A cay is a small sandy island common in the Caribbean and the Florida Keys. An islet can be rocky or sandy.

examples.everyday: We anchored near a tiny islet and swam over to the beach.
examples.professional: The survey team mapped every islet in the bay for the coastal erosion study.
examples.analytical: The islet becomes a symbol of isolation, a fragment of land the sea has not yet claimed.

nuance.analogy: Like a single stepping stone in a river, small enough to stand on but surrounded by water.
nuance.etymology: From French ilet, a diminutive of ile 'island', from Latin insula.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the s, as in EYE-slet. The s is silent.
Confusing islet with isle, which is a poetic word for island.

senses.definition: A descendant of Issachar, ninth son of Israel.
A descendant or member of the tribe of Issachar.
Of or pertaining to Issachar, or to the tribe of Issachar.
senses.example: The genealogy listed each Issacharite family that settled in the northern hills of Canaan.

core.definition: A member or descendant of Issachar, one of the twelve tribes of Israel, traditionally named for a son of Jacob.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the first syllable, IS-, and the -ite ending sounds like 'bite'. The 'ch' in Issachar is a hard 'k' sound, and the 'ar' in the middle is the American r-colored vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, with a religious or historical tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Issacharite mainly in Bible study, theology, and historical writing about the twelve tribes. In everyday speech they say 'from the tribe of Issachar' or 'a descendant of Issachar' instead. The word is rare outside scholarly or church contexts.

distinctions.note: Israelite refers to any member of the twelve tribes or the people as a whole, while Issacharite names only the descendants of one tribe.
Tribe of Issachar is a noun phrase used in everyday or scholarly speech, while Issacharite is a single word that describes the people.

examples.everyday: My Sunday school teacher said the tribe of Issachar was known for understanding the times.
examples.professional: The Bible study handout describes the Issacharite tribe as skilled at reading the signs of their era.
examples.analytical: The adjective Issacharite is rarely needed, but it marks tribal descent, as in Jacob's blessing of Issachar in Genesis 49:14-15.

nuance.analogy: An Issacharite is to Israelite as a Texan is to American: the same larger family, but with a specific local identity.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Yissakhar, usually glossed as 'there is reward' or 'hire', in connection with Genesis 30:18.
common_mistakes: Placing the stress on the second or third syllable instead of the first.
Pronouncing the ch in Issachar as 'sh' or 'ch' as in 'church' instead of a hard 'k'.
Using Issacharite for all Israelites, when it refers only to the tribe of Issachar.
nuance.biblical_note: Issachar is the ninth son of Jacob, born to Leah (Genesis 30:18, RSV), and Jacob's blessing of him in Genesis 49:14-15 describes him as a strong donkey who settles among the sheepfolds. First Chronicles 12:32 (RSV) praises men of Issachar who understood the times, which gives the tribe a reputation for wisdom.

senses.definition: It irritates me, especially when repeated.

core.definition: Saying that something a person does or a noise irritates you, especially when it keeps happening.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on NURVZ, and 'on' is reduced to 'ahn' or even 'un.' The words run together, so say it as one flowing phrase, and keep the r in 'nerves' American.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It expresses mild to strong annoyance, but it is casual and not usually cruel.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this expression in casual conversation about habits, noises or people's behavior. It is a soft criticism, so you can say it to a friend or roommate, but avoid using it with a boss or a stranger. A natural reply is 'Oh, sorry, I'll stop' or 'I didn't know, I'll try to be quieter.'

distinctions.note: Bug is even more casual and lighter; it is common among friends.
This is stronger and suggests the annoyance is almost unbearable.
Irritate is more formal and sounds clinical, so Americans rarely say it in casual talk.

collocations: that tapping gets on my nerves

examples.everyday: Your dog barking at the mailman every morning really gets on my nerves.
examples.professional: The constant pings from the chat tool get on my nerves, so I've muted it during focused work blocks.
examples.analytical: Dostoevsky's narrators often show how small irritations get on people's nerves until they turn into cruelty.

nuance.analogy: Like a sound that keeps tapping on a sensitive tooth, small and steady, until you can't ignore it.
common_mistakes: Saying 'gets to my nerves' or 'annoys on my nerves'; the natural phrase is 'gets on my nerves.'
Pronouncing 'on' as a full 'ON' in fast speech; it usually reduces to 'ahn' or 'un.'

conversation.text: He chews with his mouth open, and it gets on my nerves.
The dog is sweet, but when it barks all night, it gets on my nerves.
"Does the noise bother you?" "Yeah, it gets on my nerves after a while."

senses.definition: Used as a polite reply after being thanked.
Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see it's,‎ nothing.

core.definition: A polite reply to thanks, meaning you were glad to help and do not want the other person to feel they owe you.

pronunciation.tip: Say 'its' lightly, with the stress on NUTH. The 'th' is voiceless, with the tongue between the teeth, and the final -ing is a light 'ing', not 'in'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It is warm and modest, though it can sound dismissive if the favor was big.
nuance.usage_note: Americans reply to 'Thanks for helping me move!' with 'Oh, it's nothing,' or more often 'No problem' or 'Happy to help.' Use 'it's nothing' for small favors. For a large favor, 'it was no trouble' or 'I was glad to do it' sounds warmer and more sincere.

distinctions.note: No problem is the most common casual reply in American service and daily talk, while it's nothing is slightly more personal and warm.
You're welcome is the standard, neutral reply to thanks, while it's nothing signals that you are downplaying your effort.
Don't mention it is polite but a little more formal or old-fashioned, and it sounds more like a request to stop talking about the favor.

examples.everyday: When my neighbor thanked me for shoveling her driveway, I just said, 'Oh, it's nothing.'
examples.professional: When my manager thanked me for covering the late deploy, I said it's nothing and we moved on to the sprint review.
examples.analytical: A modest reply like it's nothing can reveal how people measure their debts of gratitude, since a favor done freely may feel like nothing to the giver.

nuance.analogy: It's nothing is like a shrug with words: it shows you did the favor gladly and do not expect a reward.
nuance.etymology: From it is plus nothing, from Old English nan 'not one' and thing.
common_mistakes: Using 'it's nothing' for a large favor, where it may sound dismissive; 'I was glad to do it' is warmer.
Mispronouncing 'nothing' as 'nuh-fing' or 'no-ting', with a 'f' or 't' instead of the voiceless 'th'.
Confusing 'it's' with 'its', which is a possessive pronoun with no apostrophe.

senses.definition: The hard white form of dentin which forms the tusks of elephants, walruses and other animals.
A creamy white color, the color of ivory.
senses.example: ivory:

senses.definition: Something made from or resembling ivory.
senses.example: The antique dealer showed us a delicate ivory carved with a horse.

senses.definition: The teeth.
senses.example: He flashed his ivories in a grin after winning the card game.

senses.definition: The keys of a piano; or, the white keys, as opposed to the black keys (ebonies).
senses.example: to tickle the ivories

senses.definition: A white person.
A die (object bearing numbers, thrown in games of chance).
senses.example: She rolled the ivory across the table and groaned at the result.

senses.definition: Made of ivory.
senses.example: Her grandmother's ivory chess set sits in a glass case.

senses.definition: Resembling or having the color of ivory.
senses.example: She painted the nursery walls a soft ivory to brighten the room.

core.definition: The hard, creamy-white material from the tusks of elephants, walruses and similar animals, used for carvings and piano keys.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, EYE. The middle vowel is a reduced schwa that many speakers drop, so the word sounds like two syllables, and the final r is pronounced in American English.

nuance.connotation: Neutral as a material; positive when describing a color, where it suggests warm, soft elegance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ivory for the material and for the color, as in a cream-colored wedding dress. Because elephant ivory is restricted, the US has largely banned commercial ivory sales since 2016, so you may hear it discussed in news about wildlife conservation. Calling an antique piano key ivory is normal, but calling a modern one ivory may prompt a question about whether it is real or plastic.

distinctions.note: A tusk is the whole elongated tooth of the animal, while ivory is the dense material that the tusk is made of.
Off-white is a broad term for any slightly tinted white, while ivory names a specific warm, creamy shade.

examples.everyday: Her grandmother gave her a little ivory box that had been in the family for years.
examples.professional: Our design team chose an ivory background for the website because it looks softer than pure white.
examples.analytical: Ivory in the Hebrew Bible signals wealth and royal display, rather than the animal itself.

nuance.analogy: Ivory is like the warm, slightly yellowed white of an old piano, not the stark white of a new sheet of paper.
nuance.etymology: From Old French ivurie, from Latin ebur, ivory, related to the Egyptian word for elephant.
common_mistakes: Saying the first syllable as EYE-vor-ee with a strong second syllable instead of a quick, reduced middle.
Using ivory as a countable noun, as in an ivory for one tusk; the material is uncountable, so say a piece of ivory.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word is shen (שֵׁן), meaning tooth, used for ivory. Scripture mentions ivory as a costly luxury of royal and wealthy households. In 1 Kings 10:18 Solomon's great throne is made of ivory and overlaid with gold. In Psalm 45:8 the king's garments are described as coming from ivory palaces. In Amos 6:4 the wealthy of Samaria lie on beds of ivory, a sign of their indulgence that the prophet condemns.

ivory.etymology: From Middle English *yvory*, *ivorie*, from Anglo-Norman *ivurie*, from Latin *eboreus* (“in or of ivory”) adjective of *ebur* (“ivory”) (genitive *eboris*), from *yb* (“ivory, Elephantine”), from *ꜣbw* (“elephant, ivory, Elephantine”), from **leb-*.

senses.definition: Factually right, correct; factual.
senses.example: It is a just assessment of the facts.

senses.definition: Rationally right, correct.
Morally right; upright, righteous, equitable; fair.
senses.example: It looks like a just solution at first glance.

senses.definition: Proper, adequate.
Only, simply, merely.
senses.example: Just plant a few tomatoes, unless you can freeze or dry them.

senses.definition: Introduces a disappointing or surprising outcome that renders futile something previously mentioned.
senses.example: I spent two hours cooking my favorite recipe, just to burn the rice and ruin the meal.

senses.definition: Used to reduce the force of an imperative; simply.
senses.example: Just follow the directions on the box.

senses.definition: Used to increase the force of an imperative; simply, without questioning.
senses.example: I'm tired of playing games – just get it done.

senses.definition: Used to convey a less serious or formal tone. (Can we verify this sense?)
senses.example: I just called to say "hi".

senses.definition: Absolutely, positively.
senses.example: It is just splendid!

senses.definition: Barely, hardly, scarcely.
senses.example: They just left, but you may leave a message at the desk.

senses.definition: Moments ago, only very recently.
senses.example: They just left, but you may leave a message at the desk.

senses.definition: By a narrow margin; closely; narrowly; almost not.
senses.example: The fastball just missed my head!

senses.definition: Exactly, precisely, perfectly.
senses.example: He wants everything just right for the big day.

senses.definition: Expressing dismay or discontent.
A joust, tournament.
To joust, fight a tournament.

core.definition: Only; simply or merely. Also means exactly or precisely, as in just right.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a short u, like the vowel in 'but'. Pronounce the final t clearly, and do not make it sound like 'jest' or 'jist'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It softens statements and requests, so it can sound friendly or dismissive depending on tone.
nuance.usage_note: Just is one of the most frequent words in American speech. Americans say 'I just finished' in conversation, and 'Can I just ask a question?' to soften requests. In formal writing, 'I have just finished' is standard. The word can also mean 'exactly' in phrases like 'just right', and 'just' in the sense of fair is a separate, more formal meaning.

distinctions.note: Only is precise and neutral, while just is more casual and can also mean exactly, as in 'just right'.
Merely is more formal and emphasizes that something is small or unimportant, while just is everyday and flexible.
Fair describes something equitable in treatment, while the adjective just is more formal and often refers to moral rightness or legal fairness.

examples.everyday: Can I just have a glass of water, please?
examples.professional: We just need one more signoff before we can ship the release.
examples.analytical: The proof is just one step away from a contradiction, so the whole argument stands or falls on that lemma.

nuance.analogy: Like a pinch of salt: just a small amount can change the whole dish.
nuance.etymology: From Latin justus, meaning lawful or right, via Old French juste.
common_mistakes: Placing just in the wrong spot, which changes the meaning: 'I wanted just one' is not the same as 'I just wanted one'.
Confusing the adverb just (only) with the adjective just (fair), and using fair and just interchangeably in formal writing.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture, the adjective just translates the Greek dikaios, which means righteous or upright before God, as in Matthew 1:19, where Joseph is called a just man. Romans 3:26 says God is just and the justifier of those who have faith in Jesus, linking the idea of justice with his act of making people right with him. See also justification for the theological use of this idea.

just.etymology: From Middle English *juste*, from Old French *juste*, from Latin *iūstus* (“just, lawful, rightful, true, due, proper, moderate”), from Proto-Italic **jowestos*, related to Latin *iūs* (“law, right”); ultimately from Proto-Indo-European **h₂yew-*.

senses.definition: Of a person's beard or hair: combed.
Of wool or other fibres: combed.
senses.example: The kempt wool was spun into a smooth yarn for the weaver's new sweater.

senses.definition: Neat and tidy.

core.definition: Neat, combed and tidy, especially of a person's hair, beard or overall appearance.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with no stress to place. The p is often silent, so many Americans say it almost like 'kemt'; either pronunciation is acceptable.

nuance.connotation: Positive: it describes someone who looks carefully groomed. It appears most often as 'well-kempt' or as the opposite of unkempt.
nuance.usage_note: Americans meet kempt mostly in writing and formal description, such as a well-kempt lawn or a neatly kempt beard. In everyday speech they say neat, put-together or well-groomed instead. It sounds stiff in casual conversation but works well in an essay, a novel or a polished description.

distinctions.note: Neat is everyday and general, while kempt is more formal and suggests hair or fibers combed smooth.
Unkempt means messy and untidy; kempt is its positive counterpart, though it is much less common.

examples.everyday: He looks sharp tonight, with his beard neatly kempt for the wedding.
examples.professional: The keynote speaker was impeccably kempt, though her slides were a mess.
examples.analytical: Her prose is kempt: every clause is combed into place, leaving no loose threads.

nuance.analogy: Like a comb drawing tangled wool into smooth, parallel lines.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English kemben, from Old English cemban, meaning 'to comb'.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with kept, the past tense of keep.
Using it in casual speech where neat or well-groomed sounds more natural.

kempt.etymology: Partly from both of the following:

senses.definition: Christ's voluntary abasement consisting of humanity and the simultaneous occultation of the Divinity.
senses.example: In her seminar paper, she traced the theme of kenosis through Philippians 2 and Christian ethics.

core.definition: In Christian theology, the self-emptying of Christ in becoming human, taking the form of a servant and setting aside divine privileges.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, 'NOH', as in 'go'. The first vowel is a short 'ih', and the ending is 'sis' as in 'diagnosis'.

nuance.connotation: Positive and reverent in theology, suggesting humility and self-giving love. Some debates about its meaning are contested.
nuance.usage_note: This is a specialist term used in theology, seminary, and philosophy. Americans may use it more broadly for self-giving love. The related verb in Greek is 'ekenosen,' but English uses 'empty oneself.'

distinctions.note: Incarnation is God the Son becoming flesh, while kenosis describes the self-emptying or humility in that act.
Humility is a general virtue, while kenosis is the specific self-emptying of Christ.
In theology, condescension means God's gracious stooping down, without the negative modern sense of looking down on others.

examples.everyday: In our Bible study we talked about kenosis, how Jesus gave up status to serve others.
examples.professional: I'll teach a seminar on Philippians 2 that explores what kenosis means for Christology.
examples.analytical: Kenotic theologies debate whether Christ gave up divine attributes or simply refrained from using them, a tension shaping modern Christology.

nuance.analogy: Kenosis is like a king taking off his crown to wash the feet of his servants.
nuance.etymology: From Greek kenosis, 'emptying', from kenoo 'to empty', from the verb ekenosen in Philippians 2:7.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable ('KEN-uh-sis').
Thinking it means Christ ceased to be divine, which most traditions deny.
Confusing it with 'genesis' or 'necrosis' in sound.
nuance.biblical_note: Philippians 2:5-8 says Christ, though in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. The Greek verb is ekenosen, 'he emptied.' Other passages on the Son's humility include 2 Corinthians 8:9, where he became poor for our sake, and John 1:14, where the Word became flesh.

traditions.view: Kenosis is Christ's voluntary humility in the Incarnation, in which he remains fully God while taking human nature and suffering. Orthodox theologians reject any loss of divinity.

Kenosis is understood as Christ's humbling in assuming human nature and the form of a servant, without relinquishing divine nature, as taught by Chalcedon. The Church rejects views that Christ lost divine attributes.

Views differ. Some nineteenth-century Lutheran and Anglican kenoticists held that the Son gave up certain divine attributes, while Reformed and most evangelicals hold that he veiled or voluntarily limited their use without losing them.

kenosis.etymology: From Ancient Greek *κένωσις* (“emptying”) (see *keno-* and *κενό*), from *κενόειν* (“to empty”) (with reference to Philippians 2.vii, "But he emptied himself, taking the form of a slave, becoming as human beings are" – New Jerusalem Version).

senses.definition: To solve two problems with one single action.
senses.example: Biking to work kills two birds with one stone. It saves money traveling and will help to lose weight.

core.definition: To solve two problems or achieve two goals with a single action.

pronunciation.respelling: kil too burdz with wun STOHN
pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on STONE, the last word. 'With one' runs together as 'wi-thwun', and the z in 'birds' is voiced.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests efficiency and good planning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this idiom about efficiency in meetings, errands and budgeting, for example 'If we merge these two meetings, we'll kill two birds with one stone.' A natural reply is 'Nice, that works.' Avoid it when discussing actual harm, because the image is violent.

distinctions.note: Multitask means handling several tasks at once; kill two birds with one stone means one action solves two problems.

collocations: kill two birds with one stone
a plan that kills two birds

examples.everyday: If you're going to the store anyway, grab my prescription too. Kill two birds with one stone.
examples.professional: Combining the sprint review with the stakeholder demo will kill two birds with one stone and save everyone an hour.
examples.analytical: Instrumental reasoning often promises to kill two birds with one stone, yet the trade-off between the two goals is rarely measured.

nuance.analogy: Like using one trip to the hardware store to buy both paint and brushes.
nuance.etymology: Recorded in English from the 1600s; the exact origin is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Omitting 'with', as in 'kill two birds one stone'.
Using 'a stone' instead of 'one stone'.

conversation.text: I'll stop by the bank on my way to the gym and kill two birds with one stone.
Let's kill two birds with one stone and review both proposals in one meeting.
We visited my aunt during our Boston work trip, killing two birds with one stone.

inflections: kills two birds with one stone
killed two birds with one stone
killed two birds with one stone
killing two birds with one stone

senses.definition: A female relative.

core.definition: A female relative, especially one who belongs to the same extended family or clan.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, KINZ, with a light secondary stress on 'woo'. The final syllable is a reduced 'mun', not 'man'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to formal. It sounds old-fashioned and appears mostly in biblical, literary or historical writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely say kinswoman in everyday speech; they say 'cousin', 'aunt', 'relative' or 'family member'. You will see it in older translations and historical novels. In casual talk it may sound stiff, so use it only when you want a formal or literary tone.

distinctions.note: Relative is the everyday word for any family member, while kinswoman is formal or literary and specifically refers to a female relative.
Kinsman is the male counterpart, and kinswoman is specifically female.

examples.everyday: My aunt is my mother's kinswoman, but we just call her family.
examples.professional: The foundation's board included a kinswoman of the founder, so the committee disclosed the relationship.
examples.analytical: The Lukan narrative calls Elizabeth Mary's kinswoman, which places the two women within a shared family network.

nuance.analogy: A kinswoman is like a leaf on the same branch as you: different in shape, but growing from the same root.
nuance.etymology: From Old English cynn 'kin' and wif 'woman', meaning a female member of one's kin.
common_mistakes: Using kinswoman as a casual synonym for friend; it refers only to blood or marriage relations.
Stressing the second syllable (kinz-WOO-man); the main stress is on the first syllable.
nuance.biblical_note: In Luke 1:36 the angel tells Mary that her kinswoman Elizabeth has conceived in her old age, which connects the two women as relatives. The Greek word syngenis means a relative or kinswoman. The passage shows family ties shaping the story of John the Baptist's birth.

senses.definition: To put together, fabricate, or assemble, particularly if done hastily or temporarily.
senses.example: I'll just knock up a quick demo for the sales presentation.

senses.definition: To impregnate, especially out of wedlock or accidentally. See knocked up.
senses.example: I guess his summer plans are shot now that he knocked his girlfriend up.

senses.definition: To make even at the edges, or to shape into book form.
senses.example: to knock up printed sheets

senses.definition: To gently hit the ball back and forth before a tennis match, as practice or warm-up, and to gauge the state of the playing surface, lighting, etc. See knock-up.
senses.example: Before the match, the players knocked up for ten minutes to test the court.

senses.definition: To straighten up a stack of paper.
senses.example: Before the meeting, she knocked up the stack of printouts so they lined up neatly.

senses.definition: (dated) To exhaust; wear out; tire out; to fatigue until unable to do more.
senses.example: Three hours of hauling drywall had knocked me up completely by noon.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: (dated) To become exhausted or worn out; to fail of strength; to become wearied, as with labor; to give out.
senses.example: By the seventh mile, our hiking group had knocked up and was dragging behind.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: Informal and crude: to make a woman pregnant, usually by accident. The past participle knocked up is common in this slang sense.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on UP, since the particle usually carries the main stress in phrasal verbs. The k in knock is silent, and the vowel in up is the short STRUT sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative and crude. It is considered vulgar in polite company and can be offensive.
nuance.usage_note: In American English, knock up is informal slang for making someone pregnant, often in a joking or gossipy way. It is considered crude and should be avoided at work, in formal writing, or around children. The sense of quickly making or assembling something, as in knock up a meal, is mainly British, and Americans would say throw together instead. A neutral alternative is get pregnant or expecting.

distinctions.note: Get pregnant is neutral and standard, while knock up is crude slang that can sound mocking.
Expecting is polite and common in conversation, while knock up is informal and rude.
Throw together means to make or assemble something quickly; it is the American equivalent of the British sense of knock up.

examples.everyday: Did you hear Jess got knocked up? Her boyfriend is totally freaking out.
examples.professional: Please don't use the phrase knocked up in the client presentation; it's too crude for that room.
examples.analytical: The phrase knock up shows how slang can make a serious biological event sound casual, sometimes even comic, which reveals social attitudes about responsibility.

nuance.etymology: Knock comes from Old English cnocian, an imitation of the sound of striking; up comes from Old English upp.
common_mistakes: Using knock up in formal settings, where it sounds vulgar.
Using knock up to mean make a quick meal, which is mainly British; Americans say throw together.

senses.definition: A lapidary.

core.definition: A person who cuts, polishes, engraves, or sets gemstones; a lapidary.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the third syllable, DAIR, with the first syllable carrying a lighter stress. The -ist ending is a short 'ist', not 'eest'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a craft or trade term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'lapidarist'. The standard word is 'lapidary', which is used both for the person and for the craft. Use 'lapidarist' only when you want a rare or literary variant, or when a text uses it. In jewelry trades, you will hear 'gem cutter' or 'lapidary' far more often.

distinctions.note: Lapidary is the standard term for the person and the craft; lapidarist is a rarer, nearly synonymous variant.
A jeweler sells and often designs jewelry; a lapidarist specifically cuts and polishes the stones.

examples.everyday: My grandfather worked as a lapidarist and could tell a fake stone by the way it caught the light.
examples.professional: We hired a certified lapidary to recut the stone before setting it in the new ring.
examples.analytical: The ancient lapidarist treated each gem as a text, reading its flaws the way a scholar reads a manuscript.

nuance.analogy: Like a sculptor who works on stone, but smaller and more precise, polishing gems to show their light.
nuance.etymology: From Latin lapidarius, meaning of stones, from lapis, meaning stone.
common_mistakes: Using 'lapidarist' where Americans would say 'lapidary' or 'gem cutter'.
Stressing the first syllable (LAP-ih-dair-ist).
Confusing the person (lapidary) with the adjective meaning elegantly concise, as in lapidary prose.

senses.definition: To have a consequence or remnant.
senses.example: I left my car at home and took a bus to work.

senses.definition: To cause or allow (something) to remain as available; to refrain from taking (something) away; to stop short of consuming or otherwise depleting (something) entirely.
senses.example: I left my car at home and took a bus to work.

senses.definition: To cause, to result in.
senses.example: The lightning left her dazzled for several minutes.

senses.definition: To put; to place; to deposit; to deliver, with a sense of withdrawing oneself.
senses.example: Leave your hat in the hall.

senses.definition: To depart; to separate from.
senses.example: I left him to his reflections.

senses.definition: To let be or do without interference.
senses.example: I left him to his reflections.

senses.definition: To depart from; to end one's connection or affiliation with.
senses.example: His bow and arrow never leaves him.

senses.definition: To end one's membership in (a group); to terminate one's affiliation with (an organization); to stop participating in (a project).
senses.example: I left the band.

senses.definition: To die (the object denotes those affected by the death).
senses.example: He left his wife and two small children after a sudden heart attack at forty.

senses.definition: To depart; to go away from a certain place or state.
senses.example: I think you'd better leave.

senses.definition: To transfer something.
senses.example: When my father died, he left me the house.

senses.definition: To transfer possession of after death.
senses.example: When my father died, he left me the house.

senses.definition: To intentionally place (something) to be received by another; to deliver (something) to a repository; to deposit.
senses.example: I'll leave the car in the station so you can pick it up there.

senses.definition: To transfer responsibility or attention of (something) (to someone); to stop being concerned with.
senses.example: Can't we just leave this to the experts?

senses.definition: To give leave to; allow; permit; let; grant.
senses.example: My dad would not leave me stay out past midnight, no matter how I begged.

senses.definition: (rare) To produce leaves or foliage.
senses.example: The oaks leave early this year, so the forest looks green by March.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: The arrangement of balls in play that remains after a shot is made (which determines whether the next shooter — who may be either the same player, or an opponent — has good options, or only poor ones).
senses.example: After my bank shot, the leave was poor, so I played a defensive safety.

senses.definition: The tiles remaining on a player's rack after his or her turn.
senses.example: I didn't score much, but LING was a good leave.

senses.definition: Permission to be absent; time away from one's work.
senses.example: I've just been given three weeks' leave by my boss — I don't think I still have some leave owing to me.

senses.definition: The action of the batsman not attempting to play at the ball.
senses.example: He made 45 leaves in his innings of 64.

senses.definition: (dated) Permission.
senses.example: Might I beg leave to accompany you?
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: (dated) Farewell, departure.
senses.example: I took my leave of the gentleman without a backward glance.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: To go away from a place or person, so that you are no longer there.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is a long ee, and the word rhymes with 'weave'. Do not shorten it to the short i of 'live', which is a different verb with a different meaning.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. The tone depends on context: 'I'm leaving now' is neutral, while 'Just leave' can sound angry.
