senses.definition: Any of the 12 principal gods and goddesses of the Greek pantheon (Zeus, Hera, Poseidon, Ares, Hermes, Hephaestus, Aphrodite, Athena, Apollo, Artemis, Demeter, and Hades); preceded by the: Zeus, the supreme ruler of the Greek deities.
senses.example: Zeus was the king of the Olympians, ruling the other gods from Mount Olympus.

senses.definition: In the Platonist theology of Plethon, a god in one group of supercelestial gods, the other group of such gods being the Tartareans or Titans.
senses.example: In Plethon's theology, the supercelestial Olympians stand above the Titans in the divine hierarchy.

senses.definition: A person with superior talents or towering achievements.
senses.example: Everyone in the department agrees she is an Olympian when it comes to statistical modeling.

senses.definition: An inhabitant of the city of Olympia, the capital of Washington, United States.
senses.example: Every Olympian I met at the farmers market was proud of the city's waterfront.

senses.definition: A sportsperson competing in the modern Olympic Games.
(historical) A sportsperson competing in the ancient Olympic Games.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: An athlete who has competed in the Olympic Games, or a person of extraordinary excellence in a field.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on LIM, the second syllable. The final -ian is pronounced 'un', and the 'pi' is 'pee', not 'pih'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises elite athletic ability or outstanding achievement.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'Olympian' most often to mean an athlete who has competed in the Olympics, as in a former Olympian coaching at a local gym. It can also describe superhuman effort or a grand, lofty manner, and in mythology it refers to the gods of Mount Olympus. Friends might say 'an Olympian' to joke about someone with amazing stamina.

distinctions.note: Olympic is the adjective for the Games themselves, as in Olympic trials, while Olympian refers to a person or a lofty quality.
A Paralympian competes in the Paralympic Games for athletes with disabilities, while an Olympian competes in the Olympic Games.

examples.everyday: My neighbor is a former Olympian who still runs five miles every morning before work.
examples.professional: Our keynote speaker is a two-time Olympian who now runs a sports analytics firm and works with national teams.
examples.analytical: The ancient Olympians were the gods said to live on Mount Olympus, and the word later came to describe anyone who seems to rise above ordinary human limits.

nuance.analogy: Like a champion chess player who has reached the highest level and is recognized everywhere as a master.
nuance.etymology: From Latin Olympius, from Greek Olympios, meaning of Olympus, the mountain where the gods lived.
common_mistakes: Using Olympian as an adjective for the Games, as in an Olympian event; the correct adjective is Olympic.
Saying oh-LIM-pee-un with the stress on the wrong syllable or pronouncing -ian as 'ee-an'.

olympian.etymology: From Late Middle English *Olympyan*, from Latin *Olympius* (“of or relating to Mount Olympus”) and its etymon Ancient Greek *Ὀλῠ́μπῐος* (“of or relating to Mount Olympus; living on Mount Olympus; Olympian”) + English *-an*.

senses.definition: Located within the premises of a military base.
senses.example: Most families on base share a playground and a commissary near the main gate.

senses.definition: Flying the base leg of an approach.
senses.example: The Piper was on base for a landing on runway 9.

senses.definition: Having reached a base in an inning.
senses.example: One run, two hits, one walk, no errors; two left on base.

core.definition: In baseball, having reached first, second, or third base safely, so the batter or runner is not out.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'base', and 'on' is weak. Americans link the two words smoothly, so say it as 'ah-NBAYS' in quick speech.

nuance.connotation: Positive when describing a player or team doing well, neutral in statistics.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'on base' most often in baseball talk: 'He got on base three times tonight'. Fans and announcers use it for both single game and season play. In analytics, 'on-base percentage' is a standard statistic, usually written with a hyphen. The phrase is rarely used outside sports.

distinctions.note: 'Reach base' is the more verbal form, while 'on base' describes the state of being safely on a base.
'Batting average' measures hits per at-bat, while 'on base' counts all ways of reaching base, including walks.

examples.everyday: He got on base twice tonight, so the team is in good shape.
examples.professional: Our analytics team tracks on-base percentage because it predicts run scoring better than batting average.
examples.analytical: On-base percentage counts walks and hit batters, which is why sabermetricians value it more than batting average.

nuance.analogy: Being on base is like getting a seat on a train: you have reached a stop and are still in play.
nuance.etymology: 'Base' comes from Latin 'basis', meaning 'foundation'; in baseball it refers to the bags the runner touches.
common_mistakes: Saying 'in base' instead of 'on base'.
Confusing 'on base' with 'out' or 'in the base' (a military or location meaning).

senses.definition: Also, additionally, moreover.
senses.example: They were holding hands and, on top of that, they were kissing.

core.definition: In addition; also, and what is more, used to add another point, often an extra problem or complaint.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TOP, while of is reduced to uhv and the and that flow quickly. Say the th in that as a voiced sound with a short, relaxed vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in function; often signals frustration when adding a problem, but can be positive when adding a benefit.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it in everyday speech and meetings to add a point, often to stack complaints, as in 'The flight was delayed, and on top of that my bag got lost.' In professional settings it sounds natural and conversational, while moreover sounds more formal. A natural reply is 'Oh no, that's rough' or 'Sorry to hear that.'

distinctions.note: Moreover is formal and mostly used in writing; on top of that is conversational and common in speech.
Besides can mean in addition or apart from; on top of that is more emphatic and usually adds a problem or burden.

examples.everyday: The internet's been out all day, and on top of that, the power went out last night.
examples.professional: The release slipped two weeks, and on top of that, QA found a regression in the API.
examples.analytical: The model underperforms on minority subgroups; on top of that, its confidence scores are poorly calibrated, which undermines its use in high-stakes decisions.

nuance.analogy: Like adding one more box to a pile that is already tall.
common_mistakes: Adding an extra the and saying on the top of that
Using it for physical position, when it only adds a point

senses.definition: One and only one time.
senses.example: I have only once eaten pizza.

senses.definition: Formerly; during some period in the past.
senses.example: He was once the most handsome man around.

senses.definition: Multiplied by one: indicating that a number is multiplied by one.
senses.example: Once three is three.

senses.definition: As soon as; when; after.
senses.example: We'll get a move on once we find the damn car keys!

core.definition: One time only; on a single occasion, as opposed to repeatedly.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable, pronounced 'wuns' with a w sound at the start, not 'ohnss'. The spelling o is pronounced like the u in 'cup'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it simply counts occurrences.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use once constantly in everyday speech, as in 'I've been there once.' It also appears as a conjunction in speech, as in 'Once you finish, call me.' In formal writing, many prefer 'when' or 'after' to the conjunction. 'Once' can also point to the past, as in 'Once, this town had a mill.'

distinctions.note: Means the same thing and is more emphatic when counting, while once is more natural and conversational.
Refers to a past state or period; formerly is formal and sounds like a report or title.
Asks about any occasion in questions and negatives, as in 'Have you ever been there?' while once means a single occasion.

examples.everyday: I've only been to that restaurant once, but the pancakes were fantastic.
examples.professional: We only need to submit the report once, so please upload the final version to the shared drive by Friday.
examples.analytical: The argument turns on the claim that the sacrifice happened once, and that claim depends on how the word once is read in Hebrews.

nuance.analogy: Like a single photo versus a video loop: once is one frame, not something that repeats.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English ones, the genitive form of one, worn down in pronunciation and spelling to once.
common_mistakes: Saying it with a long o, as 'ohnss'; the word is WUNS.
Using once as a conjunction in formal academic writing, where 'when' or 'after' is preferred.
Confusing once with one time when you want to stress the count; 'one time' is more emphatic.

once.etymology: From Middle English *ones*, from Old English *ānes*, a remodelling (after *ān* (“one”)) of *ǣnes*, itself an extension of *ǣne* (“once”) with the genitive suffix *-es*.

senses.definition: Conclusively, finally, permanently.
senses.example: They replaced the entire door, in hopes of correcting the sticking and squeaking once and for all.

core.definition: Finally and permanently, so that the matter will never need to be raised again.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the word ALL most strongly. In speech 'and' reduces to 'und' and 'for' to 'fer', so the phrase runs together quickly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly strong; it can signal frustration when used to end an argument.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase in everyday talk and at work, as in 'Let's settle this once and for all.' It often expresses tiredness with repeated discussion, so it can sound firm or impatient. A natural reply is 'Fine, let's decide it now.' It pairs with verbs such as settle, resolve, end, and put to rest.

distinctions.note: Means permanently and is often used for leaving or stopping, while once and for all emphasizes ending a dispute.
Means at the end of a sequence and does not guarantee the matter is permanently settled.
Is formal and used in academic or scientific claims, so it is less common in casual speech.

collocations: settle this once and for all
end the debate once and for all
resolve it once and for all
put the rumor to rest once and for all
make it clear once and for all

examples.everyday: Let's settle this once and for all: are we going to the lake or the mountains this weekend?
examples.professional: I need us to agree on the naming convention once and for all, so the team stops changing it every sprint.
examples.analytical: The essay argues that the debate over causation cannot be resolved once and for all, because the evidence keeps shifting with new data.

nuance.analogy: Like pulling a weed up by the root instead of trimming the top: the problem stops growing back.
nuance.etymology: Built from once and the phrase for all, meaning for all time; the idiom is established in English.
common_mistakes: Dropping 'and' and saying 'once for all', which is not the standard American idiom.
Using it for a single action; 'I finished it once and for all' means it is finished permanently, not just once.
Pronouncing 'and' with a full vowel; in speech it is usually reduced to 'und' or 'n'.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word behind the English idea is ephapax, meaning once for all or once and for all, used in the New Testament to describe Christ's sacrifice as complete and not repeated. Romans 6:10 says Christ died to sin once for all. Hebrews 10:10 says believers are sanctified through the offering of Christ's body once for all. Jude 3 speaks of the faith once for all delivered to the saints.

traditions.view: The Divine Liturgy makes the one sacrifice of Christ present rather than repeating it, so Christ's offering is understood as complete once for all and made present in the Eucharist.
The Mass is understood as the same sacrifice of Christ made sacramentally present, not a new sacrifice, which is central to Catholic teaching on the Eucharist.

Most Protestants reject the Mass as a repeated sacrifice and teach that Christ's atonement is finished once for all, with the Lord's Supper as remembrance; Lutherans affirm a real presence, while Reformed views differ.

senses.definition: Alone in a category.
senses.example: He is the only doctor for miles.

senses.definition: Singularly superior; the best.
senses.example: She's the only lawyer worth hiring in this whole city.

senses.definition: Without sibling; without a sibling of the same gender.
senses.example: He is their only son, in fact, an only child.

senses.definition: Without others or anything further; exclusively.
senses.example: My heart is hers, and hers only.

senses.definition: No more than; just.
senses.example: The cat only sat on the mat. It didn't scratch it.

senses.definition: As recently as.
senses.example: He left only moments ago.

senses.definition: Emphasizing something that is just or necessary.
senses.example: It's only fair to let him borrow your kite, after you've had his toys all day.

senses.definition: Used to express surprise or consternation at an action.
senses.example: She's only gone and run off with the milkman!

senses.definition: Introduces a disappointing or surprising outcome that renders futile something previously mentioned.
senses.example: They rallied from a three-goal deficit only to lose in the final two minutes of play.

senses.definition: Introduces a clause with negative polarity, often one which upsets the listener's expectations.
senses.example: You're welcome to borrow my bicycle, only please take care of it.

senses.definition: Under the condition that; but. (clarification of this definition is needed)
senses.example: You're welcome to borrow my bicycle, only please take care of it.

senses.definition: But, except; but in fact. (clarification of this definition is needed)
senses.example: I would enjoy running, only I have this broken leg.

senses.definition: An only child.
senses.example: As an only, Lena spent most of her childhood reading alone in her room.

senses.definition: Placed at the end of a sentence to emphasize that something is trivial, small, undemanding or deserving of belittlement.
senses.example: Just need to replace the filter only.

core.definition: No more than; just; nothing beyond the amount, number, or thing mentioned.

pronunciation.tip: It is one stressed syllable followed by an unstressed 'lee' sound, so do not split it into two stressed syllables. Avoid making the first vowel a long 'oh' followed by a separate 'n' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can sound like a limit or a small amount, which may be disappointing or reassuring depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: In American speech, 'only' is placed directly before the word it modifies, which can change the meaning: 'I only ate the salad' means I did nothing else except eat it. Placement matters in writing, so 'I ate only the salad' is clearer. Americans often use 'just' in casual speech in the same way.

distinctions.note: 'Just' is more casual and common in speech and can mean 'exactly' or 'recently'; 'only' more strongly signals a limit or restriction.
'Merely' is more formal and emphasizes that something is unimportant; 'only' is neutral and everyday.

examples.everyday: I only have five dollars, so we can get coffee but not lunch.
examples.professional: We only have budget for two more engineers this quarter, so let's prioritize the data pipeline.
examples.analytical: The theory holds only under strict assumptions about independence, and its conclusions do not generalize beyond that setting.

nuance.analogy: 'Only' is like a fence around a sentence: it marks the boundary of what is included and excludes everything beyond it.
nuance.etymology: From Old English 'anlic,' meaning 'one-like' or 'unique,' over time shortened to 'only.'
common_mistakes: Placing 'only' too far from the word it modifies, which changes the meaning, as in 'I only saw Maria' versus 'I saw only Maria.'
Confusing 'only' with 'lonely' in pronunciation; the first sound in 'only' is a clear vowel, not an 'L.'

only.etymology: From Middle English *oonly*, *only*, from Old English *ānlīċ*, *ǣnlīċ* (“only; singular; solitary”), from Proto-Germanic **ainalīkaz*.

senses.definition: In an opportunistic manner.

core.definition: In a way that takes advantage of a chance or situation, often without regard for principle or for others.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on NIS, the syllable before -tic. Americans keep the r in 'per' and end with a light 'lee', so don't stress the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies self-interest and willingness to exploit circumstances, sometimes at others' expense.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this in news, business and political commentary to criticize someone who grabs advantage without principle, such as a company or politician. In casual talk people more often say 'taking advantage' or call someone 'an opportunist'. As an adverb it modifies a verb: 'he acted opportunistically'.

distinctions.note: Opportunely means at a convenient or timely moment with no moral criticism; opportunistically implies selfishly exploiting a situation.
Strategically describes deliberate planning toward a goal and is often neutral or positive; opportunistically suggests acting on whatever arises, sometimes without a plan.

examples.everyday: Some sellers raised their prices opportunistically when the storm hit, and people were really angry about it.
examples.professional: The vendor opportunistically raised its renewal price once our deadline was locked in, so we're renegotiating.
examples.analytical: Machiavelli's prince often acts opportunistically, treating every shift in alliances as a chance to strengthen his own position.

nuance.analogy: Like a surfer who waits for whatever wave comes along and rides it only for their own benefit.
nuance.etymology: From opportunistic, from opportunist, which comes from French opportuniste and ultimately Latin opportunus 'fitting, timely'.
common_mistakes: Using it as a neutral synonym for 'at the right time'; use 'opportunely' for that meaning.
Stressing the first syllable, as in OP-por-tu-nis-tic, instead of the NIS syllable.

senses.definition: The exercise of authority or power in a burdensome, cruel, or unjust manner.
The act of oppressing, or the state of being oppressed.
senses.example: Extreme freedom is followed by extreme oppression, said Plato.

senses.definition: A feeling of being oppressed. Special usage may include a sense of heaviness or obstruction in the body or mind; depression; dullness; lassitude.
senses.example: Our oppression was lifted by the reappearance of the sun.

core.definition: The exercise of cruel or unjust authority over people, or the state of being treated that way; also a heavy, suffocating feeling.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, PREH. The first syllable is a weak schwa, and the final -sion is pronounced like 'shun' with a reduced vowel, not 'shon'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes injustice or a crushing burden, and the word carries strong moral weight.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use oppression for political, social or economic injustice, such as oppression of minorities or workers. In casual speech people also say a heat wave or a mood feels like oppression. Saying it about a small annoyance can sound dramatic, so reserve it for serious situations.

distinctions.note: Suppression means forcibly stopping something, such as a revolt, a publication or a feeling. Oppression is the broader, ongoing unjust domination of a group.
Repression is mainly a psychological or political term for holding back feelings or dissent. Oppression describes the unjust exercise of power over people.

examples.everyday: The heat this afternoon is pure oppression, so let's stay inside until it cools down.
examples.professional: Several engineers described the manager's constant micromanaging as a kind of oppression that drained the whole team.
examples.analytical: Theories of oppression examine how economic and social structures systematically deny certain groups dignity, voice and rights.

nuance.analogy: Like a heavy blanket that you cannot throw off, oppression weighs on people until they cannot move freely.
nuance.etymology: From Latin opprimere, to press down or crush.
common_mistakes: Using oppression for minor inconvenience, which sounds exaggerated in casual talk.
Stressing the second syllable wrongly as OP-preh-shun; the stress is on PREH, the second syllable of the word oppression.

oppression.etymology: From Middle English *oppression*, from Old French *oppression*, from Latin *oppressiō* (“a pressing down, violence, oppression”), from *opprimō*; see *oppress*.

senses.definition: The best or most favorable condition, or the greatest amount or degree possible under specific sets of comparable circumstances.
Any long period of time marked by a persistently warm climate; a climatic optimum.
senses.example: Paleoclimate records show that the Holocene climatic optimum brought warmer summers to much of Europe.

senses.definition: The best or most advantageous; surpassing all others.
senses.example: optimum conditions for climbing

core.definition: The best or most favorable condition, or the greatest amount or degree possible under given circumstances.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and reduce the middle vowel to 'ih.' Do not pronounce the final 'um' as 'am' or 'om.'

nuance.connotation: Positive. It names a best point or level, usually in a scientific or planning context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'optimum' mostly in science, engineering, and formal writing, as in 'the optimum temperature.' In everyday conversation people usually say 'best' or 'ideal.' The plural is 'optima' in technical writing, though 'optimums' also appears.

distinctions.note: 'Optimal' is the adjective; 'optimum' is the noun for the best point or level itself.
'Maximum' is the highest possible amount; 'optimum' is the best amount, which may be less than the maximum.

examples.everyday: The bread is at its optimum right after it cools for about twenty minutes.
examples.professional: We need to find the optimum price point before we launch in the new market.
examples.analytical: Aristotle's mean names the optimum between excess and deficiency, though locating it in a given case requires judgment.

nuance.analogy: Like the sweet spot on a tennis racket, where the ball feels best and goes farthest.
nuance.etymology: From Latin optimum, neuter of optimus, 'best.'
common_mistakes: Using 'optimum' as an adjective, as in 'an optimum choice'; use 'optimal' there.
Mispronouncing it as 'op-TEE-mum' with stress on the second syllable.

optimum.etymology: From New Latin, neuter of Latin *optimus* (“best, very good”), from the root in *ops* (“work”) or *omnis* (“all”).

senses.definition: Serving as an ornament; having no purpose other than to make more beautiful.
senses.example: Some think it most ornamental to wear their bracelets on their wrists; others, about their ankles.

senses.definition: Bred for aesthetic or decorative purposes.
senses.example: Those cranberry bushes are ornamental, so they're not edible.

senses.definition: An ornamental plant.
senses.example: The garden center sold a rare ornamental that bloomed with purple flowers in spring.

core.definition: Serving mainly to decorate; decorative rather than useful, such as a plant grown for its flowers or leaves.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the third syllable, MEN. The final -al is a weak syllable, so the word ends in a reduced vowel, not a full a sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it can sound positive for beauty but slightly negative if the implication is that something is useless.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ornamental most often for plants, trees and grasses grown for their appearance, as in ornamental cabbage or ornamental grasses. For a decorative item in a home, they often say decorative. Describing a person as ornamental, meaning useless but attractive, is a pointed remark and can sound dismissive.

distinctions.note: Decorative is the everyday word for anything designed to look nice; ornamental suggests a purely visual purpose, often in gardens or architecture.
Useful means serving a practical purpose; ornamental means its purpose is only appearance, so the two words are opposites.

examples.everyday: We planted some ornamental grasses along the driveway just for the look.
examples.professional: The landscaping budget covers ornamental plantings but not vegetables for the staff garden.
examples.analytical: The author treats the ornamental details of the cathedral as a theology made visible, not merely as surface decoration.

nuance.analogy: An ornamental plant is like a painting hung on a wall: it is there to be looked at, not to do a job.
nuance.etymology: From ornament, from Latin ornamentum, equipment or adornment.
common_mistakes: Using ornamental for any decorative object in a home, where decorative is more natural.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in 'or-nah-MEN-tal' with the second syllable heavy.

senses.definition: Yawning or gaping.
Sleepy; drowsy; sluggish; careless.
senses.example: After the long, heavy lunch, the oscitant clerk stared blankly at his spreadsheet all afternoon.

core.definition: Yawning, or drowsy and inattentive, as if bored and not really paying attention.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and reduce the final '-ant' to 'uhnt'. Do not say 'os-SIGH-tant' with stress on the middle syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it suggests boredom and lack of attention.
nuance.usage_note: This is a rare, literary word that you will meet mostly in older novels, essays, or sophisticated writing. Americans would normally say 'sleepy,' 'drowsy,' or 'inattentive' in conversation. Using it in ordinary talk may sound showy, so use it in writing when you want a precise, somewhat old-fashioned tone.

distinctions.note: Drowsy is the everyday word for sleepy; oscitant adds the idea of yawning or gaping from boredom and is far more literary.
Ostentatious means showy or pretentious; it looks similar to oscitant, but the meanings are completely different.

examples.everyday: After a long lunch, my grandfather got oscitant in his armchair and nodded off during the game.
examples.professional: By the third hour of the review, the oscitant audience in the back row had stopped taking notes.
examples.analytical: Eighteenth-century moralists often portrayed the oscitant spectator as a figure of moral laziness and dull indifference.

nuance.analogy: Like a sleepy guard at a gate, half awake and not really watching who passes through.
nuance.etymology: From Latin oscitans, 'yawning,' from oscitare, 'to yawn.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the middle syllable (os-SIGH-tant).
Using it in casual conversation where 'sleepy' or 'bored' is more natural.

senses.definition: The normal process by which bone is formed.
senses.example: Doctors monitored the ossification of the baby's skull during her first year.

senses.definition: The calcification of tissue into a bonelike mass; the mass so formed.
senses.example: The scan revealed ossification in the artery wall, a sign of long-term damage.

senses.definition: The process of becoming set in one's ways or beliefs; rigid conventionality.

core.definition: The process of becoming rigid and set in old habits, beliefs, or structures that resist change.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the syllable 'kay' near the end of the middle, and reduce the 'os' to 'ah'. Do not say 'oh-sih-fih-CAY-shun' with an 'oh' vowel at the start.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it suggests rigidity and resistance to change.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use the figurative sense in political, religious, and cultural commentary, for example 'ossification of the bureaucracy.' In medicine it refers to bone formation, but in everyday speech the figurative sense is more common. In casual talk, 'rigidity' or 'getting set in your ways' is more natural.

distinctions.note: Rigidity is a state of being inflexible; ossification suggests a gradual process of hardening over time.
Stagnation means lack of growth or movement; ossification means becoming hard and fixed in form.

examples.everyday: My dad refuses to try any new restaurant, and I think that's a kind of ossification setting in.
examples.professional: Our approval process has suffered ossification, so every change to the schema needs three signatures.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that the church's doctrinal ossification made it slower to address new questions in science and society.

nuance.analogy: Like a riverbed that has hardened into stone, so the water can only follow the old channel.
nuance.etymology: From Latin os, ossis, 'bone,' plus -fication, 'making,' from facere, 'to make.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, as in 'oh-sih-fih-KAY-shun'.
Using the word only for literal bones in everyday talk, when the figurative sense is more common.

senses.definition: Resembling or characteristic of an ostrich; struthian.
senses.example: Her ostrich-like posture, head tucked low and neck stretched, made the children giggle.

senses.definition: Ignoring an imminent threat or unpleasant reality; head-in-the-sand.

core.definition: Ignoring an unpleasant threat or reality, like an ostrich with its head in the sand; avoiding facing problems.

pronunciation.tip: In General American, ostrich starts with the open AH vowel, not AW, because of the cot-caught merger, and the -ich ending has a short i. The main stress is on the first syllable, with a lighter secondary stress on like.

nuance.connotation: Negative, because it criticizes someone for refusing to face a problem.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ostrich-like in commentary on politics, business, health or family problems, usually to criticize avoidance. It is more analytical than the idiom head in the sand, which is more casual and common in conversation. Use it with care, because calling someone ostrich-like can sound like an accusation.

distinctions.note: Head-in-the-sand is an idiom used in conversation, while ostrich-like is an adjective that sounds more analytical and suits written commentary.
In denial describes a psychological refusal to accept a fact, while ostrich-like focuses on avoiding action or looking away from a problem.

collocations: an ostrich-like refusal to look at the numbers

examples.everyday: Ignoring the check engine light is pretty ostrich-like, Dan, and it'll cost you more later.
examples.professional: Leadership's ostrich-like response to the security audit means we're still running the old servers.
examples.analytical: Their ostrich-like silence about the moral costs of the policy suggests a deliberate refusal to examine its consequences.

nuance.analogy: Like an ostrich hiding its head in the sand, the problem is still there, just out of sight.
nuance.etymology: Ostrich comes from Old French ostruce, from Latin avis struthio, from Greek strouthion; -like is native English.
common_mistakes: Saying AWS-trich with an aw vowel; in General American the first syllable is AH.
Using ostrich as an adjective instead of ostrich-like or ostrich-style.

senses.definition: Extroverted: talkative, friendly, and social, especially with respect to meeting new people easily and comfortably; outgiving.
senses.example: Tom is very outgoing and enjoys meeting people; his brother, on the other hand, is painfully shy.

senses.definition: Going out, on its way out.
senses.example: Is there any outgoing post?

senses.definition: Being replaced in office (while still in office but after election has determined that he/she will be replaced).
senses.example: The outgoing politician wasn't too disappointed he'd lost the election; he was tired of political infighting.

senses.definition: The act of leaving or going out; exit, departure.
senses.example: The outgoing of the ship from the harbor was delayed by fog.

senses.definition: Money that leaves one's possession; expenditure, outlay, expense.
senses.example: Our monthly outgoing for rent and utilities keeps growing faster than my salary.

senses.definition: The extreme limit; the place of ending.
senses.example: The map marked the outgoing of the trail at the far edge of the valley.

core.definition: Friendly, talkative, and comfortable meeting new people; sociable and easy to get along with.

pronunciation.tip: For the adjective, stress OUT. The verb "go" is stressed in the sense of leaving, out-GOING, so stress shifts with meaning. The final -ing is a short "ing."

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes a warm, social personality, and it is often used in job descriptions and introductions.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use "outgoing" to describe people who are easy to talk to, such as "She's very outgoing and makes friends fast." It is positive and friendly. For a person leaving a job, "outgoing" can mean the person is leaving office or a position, such as "the outgoing mayor."

distinctions.note: Extroverted is a psychological term and more formal. Outgoing is the everyday word for someone who is friendly and social.
Friendly describes warmth in general. Outgoing describes energy and comfort meeting new people.

examples.everyday: My neighbor is so outgoing that she already knows everyone on the block.
examples.professional: We need someone outgoing for the client-facing role, since they will be meeting new partners every week.
examples.analytical: Outgoing people are often assumed to be more confident, although social energy and inner confidence are distinct traits.

nuance.analogy: Like a door that opens easily to visitors, an outgoing person invites others in without hesitation.
nuance.etymology: From out and going.
common_mistakes: Stressing "going" when describing a friendly person; it is stressed on the first syllable.
Confusing "outgoing" with "outgoings" in a financial sense, which means expenses.
Using "outgoing" for "extrovert" in formal writing without the right register.

conversation.text: My wife is really outgoing; she talks to everyone at parties.
I'm not very outgoing, but I'm working on it.
You have to be pretty outgoing to work in sales.

senses.definition: An oxidizing agent, especially one used to oxidize the fuel of a rocket or a fuel cell.
senses.example: The rocket's fuel tanks hold liquid oxygen as the oxidizer for the engines.

core.definition: A substance that causes oxidation, especially one that supplies oxygen so that a fuel burns, such as in a rocket engine.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the final '-er' a weak, r-colored sound, not a full 'ur.' The middle 'i' is a weak vowel, and 'dy' rhymes with 'sigh.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term used in aerospace, chemistry, and safety contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use oxidizer most often in rocketry, aerospace, and fuel or safety talk, such as 'liquid oxygen is a common oxidizer.' In general chemistry, 'oxidant' is more common. Safety labels may warn that an oxidizer should be stored away from fuel.

distinctions.note: Both mean an oxidizing agent; oxidizer is especially used in rocketry, fire, and combustion, while oxidant is the general chemistry term.
A fuel is burned or consumed in a reaction; an oxidizer supplies the oxygen or electron-accepting material that allows burning.

examples.everyday: The fertilizer bag warns that it is a strong oxidizer, so keep it away from gasoline.
examples.professional: The propulsion team switched to nitrous oxide as the oxidizer to simplify the storage system.
examples.analytical: A combustion reaction needs both a fuel and an oxidizer, so the reaction rate is limited by whichever one is scarcer.

nuance.analogy: An oxidizer is like the air a campfire needs: the wood burns only when there is enough oxygen available to combine with it.
nuance.etymology: From oxidize, with the agent suffix -er, meaning 'one that does.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the last syllable as a full 'er' sound; it is a weak r-colored vowel.
Confusing an oxidizer with a fuel; the oxidizer supplies oxygen, while the fuel is the material that burns.

senses.definition: Put into a package.
senses.example: packed lunch

senses.definition: Filled with a large number or large quantity of something.
senses.example: packed with goodness

senses.definition: Filled to capacity with people.
senses.example: The bus was packed and I couldn't get on.

core.definition: Full of people or things, with no space left; crowded.

pronunciation.tip: The word is one syllable and ends in a hard t sound, so pronounce the -ed as a t, not as a separate syllable. Do not add a vowel after the k.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans say a place is packed to describe a crowd, such as a restaurant, a concert or a train. It can also describe a schedule or a lecture that is full of content. It is casual and very common in conversation. Packed with is used when something is full of a material or feature.

distinctions.note: Crowded focuses on too many people in a space; packed often emphasizes that there is absolutely no room left.
Full is more general and neutral; packed is stronger and more vivid for crowds or schedules.

examples.everyday: The coffee shop was packed this morning, so we got our order to go.
examples.professional: My calendar is packed next week, so please send me the notes by email.
examples.analytical: The essay is packed with claims, yet it rarely stops to test any one of them.

nuance.analogy: Like a suitcase stuffed so full that the zipper barely closes.
nuance.etymology: Past participle of pack, from Middle Dutch or Low German pakken.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as PAK-ed, with an extra syllable.
Confusing packed with package, which is a noun for a parcel.

conversation.text: The trail was packed with people on Saturday.
The restaurant is packed; we'll have to wait an hour.
Are you packed? We leave at six.

senses.definition: A village council meeting.
senses.example: The elders gathered under the baobab tree for the village palaver about the new well.

senses.definition: Talk, especially unnecessary talk; chatter.
A meeting at which there is much talk; a debate; a moot.
senses.example: The committee's palaver lasted until midnight and settled nothing.

senses.definition: Disagreement.
senses.example: I have no palaver with him.

senses.definition: Talk intended to deceive.
senses.example: Don't believe the salesman's palaver about miracle cures and guaranteed profits.

senses.definition: To discuss with much talk.
senses.example: The neighbors palavered for hours on the porch about the zoning dispute.

senses.definition: To flatter.
senses.example: He palavered the new manager with compliments until she promoted him.

core.definition: Unnecessary fuss, lengthy talk, or formalities that waste time.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, 'LAV'. The final syllable is reduced to a soft 'er' sound, so it does not sound like 'puh-LAV-ur'.

nuance.connotation: Negative or mildly humorous. It suggests needless complication or long-winded discussion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use palaver informally to complain about lengthy paperwork, meetings, or procedures, as in 'all that palaver for a simple refund'. It is not used for serious discussions or formal meetings. It sounds a bit old-fashioned, so it works best in relaxed conversation. A natural reply might be 'I know, it's a lot of palaver.'

distinctions.note: Fuss is about excitement or worry over something minor, while palaver is about long, unnecessary talk or procedure.
Red tape refers to official rules that slow things down, while palaver is more casual and can refer to any long talk or ceremony.

examples.everyday: Getting the car registered took forever, with all the forms and the waiting, what a palaver.
examples.professional: Let's skip the palaver in the meeting and get straight to the decision on the budget.
examples.analytical: Much of the political palaver was designed to delay a decision rather than to inform the public.

nuance.analogy: Palaver is like a long detour through a traffic jam of words: you arrive eventually, but you wish you had taken the direct road.
nuance.etymology: From Portuguese palavra, 'word', from Latin parabola.
common_mistakes: Using palaver for serious, productive discussion, when it usually implies wasted effort.
Pronouncing the first syllable as 'PAL' instead of 'puh'.

palaver.etymology: Originally nautical slang, from Portuguese *palavra* (“word”), from Late Latin *parabola* (“parable, speech”).

senses.definition: The alleviation of a disease's symptoms without a cure; temporary relief.
Extenuation; mitigation.
senses.example: The lawyer argued for palliation, pointing out that his client had acted under severe financial stress.

core.definition: Relief of a disease's symptoms, such as pain, without curing the underlying illness.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the -AY- of the -ation ending. The middle vowel is reduced to a short 'ih', so keep the word to four syllables.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and clinical; it describes comfort-focused care rather than a cure.
nuance.usage_note: In American medicine, palliation appears mostly in clinical and hospice settings. Most people say palliative care rather than using the bare noun. In casual talk, it can sound stiff, so families often say 'we are focusing on comfort' instead.

distinctions.note: Remission means the disease has receded or is controlled; palliation focuses on easing symptoms, whether or not the disease is controlled.
A cure removes the disease entirely; palliation only eases its effects.

examples.everyday: Honestly, the treatment is mostly palliation at this point, just to help him feel better.
examples.professional: The care team recommended a palliation plan focused on pain control and sleep.
examples.analytical: Palliation can be ethically distinct from treatment, since its aim is relief from suffering rather than reversal of disease.

nuance.analogy: Like turning down the alarm on a noisy machine without repairing the machine.
nuance.etymology: From Latin palliare, to cloak or conceal.
common_mistakes: Using palliation to mean a cure or healing.
Confusing palliation with palpation, the act of touching the body during an exam.

palliation.etymology: Middle French *palliation*, from Latin *pallio* (“to cloak; to conceal”), from Latin *pallium* (“cloak”).

senses.definition: Lavish with praise; admiring, approving, complimentary.

core.definition: Expressing lavish praise in a formal or exaggerated way; full of admiring, complimentary language.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on the 'jir' syllable. The final -al is weak and sounds like 'kul,' so don't pronounce it as a separate, strongly stressed syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive on the surface, but it often suggests excessive or insincere praise.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this adjective mainly in formal reviews, criticism, and academic writing. In casual speech, people say 'gushing' or 'over-the-top.' It sounds stiff in ordinary conversation, so reach for simpler words there.

distinctions.note: 'Laudatory' is a more common and less ornate word for praising, while 'panegyrical' suggests grand, ceremonial, or excessive praise.
'Complimentary' is everyday and mild, while 'panegyrical' is formal and much more emphatic.

examples.everyday: His panegyrical review made the restaurant sound like the best meal of my life.
examples.professional: The vendor's panegyrical slide deck ignored every limitation of the model.
examples.analytical: The essay's panegyrical tone obscures the author's real argument about the regime.

nuance.analogy: If praise were a volume knob, a panegyrical tone would be turned all the way up.
nuance.etymology: From panegyric, from Greek panēgyrikos, relating to a festival assembly.
common_mistakes: Using 'panegyrical' in casual speech, where it sounds overly formal or pretentious.
Confusing it with 'panegyric' as a noun, when the adjective form needs the -al ending.

senses.definition: Having panels.

core.definition: Having flat, rectangular sections of wood, glass or other material set into a frame, such as paneled walls, doors or ceilings.

pronunciation.tip: One stressed syllable, PAN. The -eled ending is one reduced syllable, 'uhld', and American spelling has only one l.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; sometimes positive when describing traditional wood interiors.
nuance.usage_note: This word is common in home, real estate and design talk: a paneled den, paneled door or paneled ceiling. Americans spell it with one l, as paneled; the British spelling is panelled. Wood-paneled describes walls covered with wood sheets, while paneled alone is used for doors, ceilings and walls.

distinctions.note: Panelled is the British spelling; in American English write paneled.
Wainscoted means walls with wood boards or panels covering the lower part, mostly in historic or traditional rooms.
Framed describes a structure built around a frame; paneled describes a surface divided into panels.

examples.everyday: Our new house has a paneled den, which is perfect for watching football with friends.
examples.professional: The architect asked for paneled doors in the conference room to match the historic lobby.
examples.analytical: The paneled interior of the eighteenth-century hall reflects a deliberate effort to project order and wealth.

nuance.analogy: A paneled wall is like a quilt of flat boards, each fitted into its own frame.
nuance.etymology: From panel, from Old French panel, ultimately from Latin pannus 'cloth'.
common_mistakes: Spelling it 'paneled' in American writing.
Treating paneled as a noun meaning a group of people; the adjective describes surfaces, and panel is the noun for both.

senses.definition: Synonym of papism.
senses.example: Nineteenth-century pamphlets accused the bishop of papalism, a charge he firmly denied.

senses.definition: (historical) Hierocracy; the doctrine of the pope’s supreme authority in temporal as well as spiritual affairs.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: The doctrine that the pope holds supreme authority over the church and, historically, over temporal rulers as well.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and keep the al reduced to a short schwa-like vowel. The final -ism is pronounced -izm, with a short i.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in historical or theological scholarship, but it can sound polemical in Protestant or ecumenical settings where papism is used as an insult.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use papalism mainly in historical or theological writing, and the everyday terms are papacy and papal authority. Papism is the more common synonym in older polemics and is often pejorative, so avoid it in ecumenical settings. In a conversation with Catholics you would say papal primacy or papal authority.

distinctions.note: Papism is a synonym of papalism, but it is often used as an insult by Protestant polemicists, so papalism is more neutral in scholarship.
The papacy is the office or institution of the pope, while papalism is the doctrine of the pope's supreme authority.
Ultramontanism is a 19th-century movement favoring strong papal authority beyond the Alps, a more specific historical term.

examples.everyday: My history professor said papalism was the big fight in the fourteenth century, when kings and popes argued over who had the final say.
examples.professional: The ecumenical team agreed to set aside the word papalism in our joint document and talk instead about the papacy's role.
examples.analytical: Medieval papalism grounded the pope's claim to rule over kings in an argument about the two swords of Christendom.

nuance.analogy: Papalism is like a chain of command in which the top officer also claims authority over the civilian government.
nuance.etymology: From papal, from Medieval Latin papa, pope, with the suffix -ism for a doctrine.
common_mistakes: Confusing papalism (the doctrine) with papal (the adjective), as in papal authority.
Using papalism as a neutral synonym for Catholicism in general, which overstates the doctrine's scope.
nuance.biblical_note: Papalism is not a biblical word, but its central claim rests on Matthew 16:18-19, where Jesus says 'you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church' and gives Peter the keys of the kingdom. The Greek words petros (a stone) and petra (bedrock) are central to the passage, and Catholics see Peter's successors as bearing that office. John 21:15-17, where Jesus tells Peter to feed his sheep, is also cited, while Protestants generally read these passages as not establishing a universal papal jurisdiction.

traditions.view: The pope, as successor of Peter and bishop of Rome, holds a primacy of universal jurisdiction over the whole church, given by Christ to Peter and his successors.
The bishop of Rome holds a primacy of honor among the bishops within a conciliar church, but not a universal jurisdiction over all Christians, which Orthodox Christians reject.

Most Protestants reject papal supremacy as unscriptural, though Anglicans keep bishops while rejecting papal jurisdiction, and Lutheran and Reformed traditions differ in how they read the Petrine texts.

senses.definition: To afflict with paralysis.
senses.example: The stroke paralyzed the left side of his body, so he needed months of physical therapy.

senses.definition: To render unable to move; to immobilize.
To render unable to function properly.
senses.example: The transport strike paralyzed the city.

core.definition: To make someone unable to move or act, or to stop something from working normally.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, PAIR. The final -ize sounds like 'eyes', and the middle syllable is weak and quick.

nuance.connotation: Negative
nuance.usage_note: Americans use paralyze in both the physical sense and the figurative sense, as in 'paralyzed with fear' or 'the city was paralyzed by the storm'. In American spelling it is paralyze, not the British paralyse. The phrase 'paralyzed with fear' is very common in everyday American speech.

distinctions.note: Immobilize usually refers to holding something in place, such as a broken leg, while paralyze can refer to a loss of function or of decisive action.
Freeze is informal and often describes a sudden stop in motion, while paralyze suggests a more complete or lasting inability to act.

examples.everyday: The snowstorm paralyzed the whole town, so nobody could get to work.
examples.professional: The unclear approval process paralyzed the project, and no one knew who could sign off.
examples.analytical: Fear of error can paralyze moral agency, since a person who cannot choose cannot take responsibility either.

nuance.analogy: Like a computer that freezes when too many programs are open at once.
nuance.etymology: From paralysis, with the verb-forming suffix -ize.
common_mistakes: Using the British spelling paralyse in American writing.
Confusing paralyze with parallelize, which is a technical computing term.

senses.definition: A variable of a model that is trained by a machine learning algorithm.
Any measured quantity of a statistical population that summarizes or describes an aspect of the population.
senses.example: Our analysis aimed to estimate the unknown parameter describing the true mean height of all adults.

senses.definition: An input variable of a function definition, that gets an actual value (argument) at execution time.
senses.example: In Python, the function requires one parameter, named threshold, which the caller must supply.

senses.definition: A value kept constant during an experiment, equation, calculation, or similar, but varied over other versions of the experiment, equation, calculation, etc.
senses.example: We held the temperature parameter fixed at 300 kelvin while varying pressure across all trials.

senses.definition: A variable that describes a property or characteristic of some system (material, object, event, etc.) or some aspect thereof.
senses.example: The model's damping parameter describes how quickly the bridge's vibrations decay after each load.

senses.definition: An actual value given to such a formal parameter.
senses.example: Setting the learning rate parameter to 0.01 made the training converge much more slowly.

senses.definition: A characteristic or feature that distinguishes something from others.
senses.example: Her calm, unhurried style is the parameter that sets her lectures apart from everyone else's.

senses.definition: In the ellipse and hyperbola, a third proportional to any diameter and its conjugate, or in the parabola, to any abscissa and the corresponding ordinate.
senses.example: The parameter of the principal axis of a conic section is called the latus rectum.

senses.definition: Clipping of uniformizing parameter.
senses.example: Riemann surfaces are often described using a uniformizing parameter that maps the disk conformally onto them.

senses.definition: The ratio of the three crystallographic axes which determines the position of any plane.
senses.example: The mineralogist measured the crystal's parameters to determine the orientation of each face.

senses.definition: The fundamental axial ratio for a given species.
senses.example: Mineralogists recorded the fixed parameter for this species, which distinguishes it from related minerals.

core.definition: A learned numerical value inside a model, such as a weight, that the training process adjusts to fit data.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on RAM, the second syllable, and the final -er is reduced to a quick 'ter' with an r-colored vowel. Non-native speakers often stress the last syllable or pronounce the middle as 'ah'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: In American data science and AI, parameter means a value learned from data, such as a weight, which is different from a hyperparameter set beforehand by the engineer. Americans also use the word in statistics and programming, but the AI sense is most common in team conversations about models. Saying 'parameters' in everyday talk usually means the settings of a system.

distinctions.note: A parameter is learned from the training data, while a hyperparameter, such as the learning rate, is chosen by the engineer before training.
A variable is a general term for something that can change, while a parameter is a specific, usually fixed, value that defines a model or function.

examples.everyday: My friend says the new chatbot has billions of parameters, which is why it sounds so smart.
examples.professional: We froze the first layers, so only the final layer's parameters get updated during fine-tuning.
examples.analytical: The expressive capacity of the network depends on how its parameters are structured and constrained by the architecture.

nuance.analogy: Like the dials on a sound mixer that a sound engineer adjusts until the song sounds right.
nuance.etymology: From Greek parametron, measuring alongside, from para- beside and metron measure, via Modern Latin.
common_mistakes: Confusing parameter with hyperparameter, which is set before training rather than learned.
Using parameter to mean a limit or boundary in everyday talk, which is more natural in technical contexts.

parameter.etymology: From French *paramètre*, from New Latin *parametrum* (“parameter”), from Ancient Greek *παρα-* (“beside”) + *μέτρον* (“measure”).

conversation.text: The model has seven billion parameters, which are learned during training.
The mean and variance are the two parameters of a normal distribution.
The function takes a parameter that sets the maximum number of retries.

senses.definition: In a passionate manner.

core.definition: In a way that shows strong emotion, deep commitment or great intensity of feeling.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the unstressed middle syllables reduce to a weak vowel. The 'ion' is pronounced 'shun,' not 'see-on,' and the ending is 'lee,' not 'lee-ate.'

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral overall, since it signals sincere feeling. It can sound negative when the feeling is anger or opposition, as in 'passionately opposed.'
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word all the time to describe people who care deeply about something, such as a cause, a hobby or a belief. The usual pattern is 'passionate about' as an adjective, but the adverb is natural after verbs like 'believe,' 'argue' or 'care.' A natural reply to someone who shows strong feeling is a simple 'Yeah, you clearly care about this.'

distinctions.note: Enthusiastically stresses eagerness and excitement, often in an upbeat way, while passionately stresses deep emotional commitment that can also be serious or even angry.
Fervently is more formal and often used for religious or political devotion, while passionately is more common in everyday American speech.

examples.everyday: My sister talks about rock climbing so passionately that I finally signed up for a class with her.
examples.professional: Our product lead argued passionately for keeping the feature, and the team agreed to test it first.
examples.analytical: Thinkers who write passionately about justice often reveal the values that their arguments take for granted.

nuance.analogy: Like a fire that burns hot and visibly fills the room, passionately describes a way of acting with full, visible energy.
nuance.etymology: From passionate, from passion, from Late Latin passio 'suffering,' from Latin pati 'to suffer.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'I am passionately about jazz' instead of 'I am passionate about jazz' (the adjective takes 'passionate' after 'am')
Stressing the second syllable of 'passion' as in 'pa-SHUN' instead of 'PASH-un'

senses.definition: A person who loves and zealously supports and defends their country.

core.definition: A person who loves their country, supports it loyally and is willing to defend or serve it, often at personal cost.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, PAY, with a long A sound, not the short 'pat' vowel. The last syllable is reduced to 'ut,' so it does not sound like 'pa-tree-OT.'

nuance.connotation: Positive. Americans usually admire a patriot, though the word can be used sarcastically or to claim exclusive ownership of national loyalty.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'patriot' often in conversation about veterans, the military, national holidays and political debate. Calling someone a patriot is generally a compliment, but a speaker may use it to suggest they alone love the country. In a casual setting, a natural reply is 'Absolutely' or a comment about their service.

distinctions.note: A nationalist emphasizes national interests, sometimes above others, while a patriot emphasizes love and loyalty to the country itself.
Chauvinist implies aggressive, blind pride in one's group, which is usually negative, whereas patriot is typically positive.

examples.everyday: My dad is a real patriot; he puts a flag out every Fourth of July and never misses a parade.
examples.professional: The nonprofit's volunteers see themselves as patriots of public service, so their training emphasizes civic duty.
examples.analytical: Whether a patriot loves the nation's people or its founding principles remains a contested question in political philosophy.

nuance.analogy: A patriot is like a loyal member of a team who believes in its mission and will stay to help when it struggles.
nuance.etymology: From Greek patriōtēs, 'fellow countryman,' from patris, 'fatherland,' via French patriote.
common_mistakes: Using 'patriot' as an adjective; say 'patriotic' instead.
Pronouncing the first vowel as short 'pat' instead of PAY.

patriot.etymology: From Middle French *patriote*, from Late Latin *patriōta* (“fellow countryman”) from the Ancient Greek *πατριώτης* (“of the same country”), from *πατρίς* (“father land", "country”), from *πατήρ* (“father”).

senses.definition: A paved surface; a hard covering on the ground.
A paved path, for the use of pedestrians, located at the side of a road.
A paving (paved part) of a road or other thoroughfare; the roadway or road surface.
The paved part of an area other than a road or sidewalk, such as a cobblestone plaza, asphalt schoolyard or playground, or parking lot.
Interior flooring, especially when of stone, of large buildings.
The interior flooring of a church sanctuary, between the communion rail and the altar.

core.definition: The hard, paved surface of a road, especially the part cars drive on in American English.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable is nearly silent, so the word has about two strong beats. Americans often flap the t lightly and blend the v and m, so say PAYV-muhnt, not PAY-vuh-ment.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical, descriptive word for ground surfaces.
nuance.usage_note: In American English, pavement means the road surface, the part where cars drive, and Americans usually say sidewalk for the walkway next to the road. In British English pavement means sidewalk, so Americans may find a British speaker confusing if they say walk on the pavement. If you want the walkway in the US, say sidewalk, and for a general paved area, say paved area or parking lot.

distinctions.note: Sidewalk is the American word for the paved walkway beside a road, while pavement in the US means the road surface, not the walkway.
Asphalt is a specific black material made from petroleum and aggregate, while pavement is the general word for any paved surface.

examples.everyday: Be careful walking your bike, because the pavement is wet and slippery after the rain.
examples.professional: The facilities team inspected the pavement in the parking structure and flagged several cracks for repair this quarter.
examples.analytical: In the Gospel of John, the place called the Pavement is linked with Pilate's judgment, and the setting carries symbolic weight for readers.

nuance.analogy: Pavement is like a skin over the ground: it protects the soil beneath and gives everyone a smooth, hard place to travel, though it can crack when the earth moves.
nuance.etymology: From Latin pavimentum, floor of beaten earth or rammed stone, from pavire, to beat down.
common_mistakes: Saying walk on the pavement to mean walking on the sidewalk, which sounds British to Americans.
Confusing pavement with payment or pavilion, which are different words with different meanings.
nuance.biblical_note: John 19:13 mentions a place called the Pavement, in Hebrew Gabbatha, where Pilate sat in judgment over Jesus. The Greek lithostrotos means a stone-paved place, and the Revised Standard Version uses the Pavement as the place name. The passage shows the setting of Pilate's judgment, and the paved floor is a detail that scholars link to the Roman praetorium.

pavement.etymology: From Middle English *pament*, from Anglo-Norman *pavement* and reinforced by Middle French *pavement*; both from Latin *pavīmentum* (“paved surface or floor”), from *paviō* (“to beat, to ram, to tread down”).

senses.definition: To give attention; to heed.
senses.example: You needn't pay heed to his antics.

core.definition: To give careful attention to a warning, advice or instruction, and take it seriously.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on HEED, the second word, which rhymes with 'need' and 'speed'. Keep the vowel long and clear, and do not reduce it to a short 'i' as in 'hid'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it suggests serious and respectful attention.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use pay heed mostly in writing, speeches, news reports or dramatic speech, such as 'Pay heed to the warning signs.' In everyday talk, Americans say pay attention to, which is more natural. Pay heed sounds elevated, so use it when you want to sound serious or thoughtful. Heed is usually used with to and a noun.

distinctions.note: Pay attention is everyday and general; pay heed suggests taking a warning or advice seriously.
Take note means register information for later; pay heed implies acting on it.
Obey means follow an order; pay heed is broader and can apply to advice or warnings that are not commands.

examples.everyday: You had better pay heed to what the doctor said about your blood pressure.
examples.professional: The team should pay heed to the security review before we ship the update to customers.
examples.analytical: Scholars who pay heed to context rarely mistake a poetic metaphor for a literal claim.

nuance.analogy: Like a driver who sees the speed-limit sign and slows down right away.
nuance.etymology: Heed comes from Old English hedan, to take care; pay comes from Latin pacare.
common_mistakes: Saying 'pay heed of' instead of 'pay heed to'.
Using heed as a verb with 'to' omitted, as in 'pay heed the warning'; the usual form is 'pay heed to the warning'.

senses.definition: The act of reconciling two people or groups who disagree.

core.definition: The work of reconciling people or groups who disagree, often through negotiation or dialogue.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on PEACE, with secondary stress on MAKE. The final '-ing' is short and unstressed, so do not stretch the vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes constructive work to end disputes.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this noun in news, politics, faith communities and workplace talk about settling disputes. It is more formal than the everyday 'peacemaker', and it often describes ongoing effort rather than a single act. A natural reply is 'That's important work,' or 'Yeah, somebody has to do it.'

distinctions.note: Peacemaking focuses on negotiation to end conflict, while peacekeeping keeps an existing peace in place, often with troops.
Mediation is a formal process with a neutral third party, while peacemaking can be informal and involve many actors.
Peacebuilding aims at long-term reforms, while peacemaking focuses on the immediate work of reconciling the parties.

examples.everyday: Thanks for the peacemaking at dinner, Mom, the brothers finally stopped yelling.
examples.professional: Her peacemaking between the design and engineering teams saved the launch.
examples.analytical: Peacemaking, in the Christian tradition, is understood as active reconciliation rather than mere avoidance of conflict.

nuance.analogy: Peacemaking is like mending a torn fence with both neighbors standing there.
nuance.etymology: Peace comes from Latin pax through Old French pais; making comes from Old English macian, to make.
common_mistakes: Confusing peacemaking with peacekeeping, which involves troops and maintaining an existing truce.
Stressing the 'king' syllable too strongly at the end.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word eirēnopoios behind peacemaker comes from eirēnē (peace) and poieō (to make). In Matthew 5:9 Jesus says the peacemakers are blessed, for they will be called sons of God. In James 3:18 those who make peace sow in peace a harvest of righteousness. In 2 Corinthians 5:18-19 Paul describes God reconciling the world and entrusting believers with the message of reconciliation.

senses.definition: The state or condition of being pearlescent; a pearly appearance.
senses.example: The paint's pearlescence shifted from silver to pale pink as the car rolled into sunlight.

core.definition: The soft, shifting, pearl-like sheen on a surface, where color seems to glow from within and change with the angle of light.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the ES syllable, the same as in pearlescent. The final -ence reduces to a weak 'uns', and the r in the first syllable is strongly rhotic, so do not drop it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It praises a subtle, luxurious shine, and is used mostly in product descriptions for cosmetics, car paint, and packaging.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use pearlescence mainly in technical or commercial writing, such as paint catalogs, makeup labels, and design reviews. In everyday talk they usually say that something looks pearly or has a pearly shine. The word names the quality itself, so it fits a sentence about a finish.

distinctions.note: Iridescence is strong, rainbow-like color that shifts as you move, while pearlescence is softer, whiter, and more milky.
Luster is any gentle shine on a surface, whereas pearlescence specifically suggests the layered, milky glow of a pearl.

examples.everyday: The new car has a pearlescence that looks different in the sun than it does under the parking lot lights.
examples.professional: The packaging team wants more pearlescence in the lipstick shade without making it look glittery.
examples.analytical: The essay argues that the pearlescence of the shell comes from thin layers of aragonite that scatter light.

nuance.analogy: Like the soft gleam inside a seashell, pearlescence is color that seems to glow from underneath the surface.
nuance.etymology: From pearl plus -escence, 'the quality of becoming pearly'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing pearl like 'pear' (the fruit); the vowel is the r-colored ER sound of 'bird'.
Using pearlescence for a plain white surface with no shimmer; the word requires a layered, shifting sheen.

senses.definition: The state or quality of being peccable; liability to sin.
senses.example: Theologians debated whether the human peccability of Adam was a flaw or a freedom.

core.definition: In theology, the human capacity or liability to commit sin; the condition of being able to sin.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on BIL, the same syllable as in peccable. The final -ity is a light 'ih-tee', and the word is rare, so practice the stress shift from the adjective.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical in theology. It names a condition without judging a particular person.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use peccability mainly in theological, pastoral, and philosophical writing about human nature. In everyday talk they say 'our capacity to sin' or 'human weakness'. It is not used for ordinary mistakes, which are better described as errors or faults.

distinctions.note: Peccability is the liability or potential to sin, while peccancy is the actual sin or sinful quality.
Impeccability means being without sin or flaw, the opposite of peccability.
Fallibility is the general ability to be wrong, whereas peccability specifically concerns the capacity to sin.

examples.everyday: My friend said our peccability is the reason we all need grace every single day.
examples.professional: In the sermon series, the pastor explained that human peccability is why we rely on grace rather than on our own strength.
examples.analytical: Augustine's account of the will suggests that peccability alone does not explain sin, since sin arises from a corrupted choice.

nuance.analogy: Like a glass that can crack, peccability describes a state of being breakable by sin, even before any crack appears.
nuance.etymology: From Latin peccabilis, from peccare 'to sin'.
common_mistakes: Confusing peccability with impeccability, which is its opposite.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in 'PEK-uh-bil-i-tee', instead of 'pek-uh-BIL-ih-tee'.
Using peccability for everyday errors or mistakes instead of sin.
nuance.biblical_note: The English word does not appear in Scripture, but the idea does. Hebrew chata' and Greek hamartia both carry the sense of missing the mark. Romans 3:23 says that all have sinned and fall short of God's glory, Romans 5:12 explains that sin came into the world through one man, and Psalm 51:5 confesses a human frailty present from birth. 1 John 1:8 warns that claiming to have no sin deceives ourselves.

traditions.view: Humans are mortal and inclined to sin because of ancestral sin, understood as a corruption of nature rather than an inherited guilt, yet they remain free to choose good with God's help.
Original sin deprives human nature of original justice and leaves an inclination called concupiscence, which remains after baptism but is not itself sin; grace enables people to resist it.

Reformed Christians teach total depravity, that sin corrupts the whole person so the will cannot choose good apart from grace, while Lutherans stress inherited corruption and Wesleyans stress that grace enables real resistance to sin.

senses.definition: The usually informal hierarchy of authority, command, or social status, as determined by the especially natural propensity for domination of different members of a specific group over each other, such as older brothers and sisters over their younger siblings.
senses.example: In our family, the older siblings sit at the top of the pecking order.

senses.definition: The natural ranking of social status and dominance occurring in a group of birds.

core.definition: The informal ranking of people in a group by status or dominance, with those at the top having more power over those below.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on OR in 'order', and 'pecking' has a lighter secondary stress. The -ing is a short, unstressed sound, not a long ee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative, depending on context; it implies unfair or unspoken dominance but is often said with humor.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'pecking order' for families, offices, sports teams and friend groups, often in a light, joking way. It is informal and sometimes used as a complaint about who gets the best assignments. A common reply is 'Yeah, I'm at the bottom of the pecking order, so I get the early shifts.'

distinctions.note: 'Hierarchy' is a more formal, neutral term for a system of ranks, while 'pecking order' is informal and suggests an informal or even animal-like struggle for dominance.
A 'chain of command' is an official structure of authority, while a 'pecking order' is unofficial and based on status or personality.

collocations: at the bottom of the pecking order
at the top of the pecking order

examples.everyday: I'm not getting the window seat this time; I'm at the bottom of the pecking order.
examples.professional: Before we change the approval process, we need to understand the pecking order on this team.
examples.analytical: Sociologists describe status hierarchies as a kind of pecking order, though such rankings are rarely as fixed as the metaphor suggests.

nuance.analogy: Like a chicken yard where some hens reliably peck others, but are themselves pecked by hens above them.
nuance.etymology: Coined in the 1920s from observations of hierarchies among hens, with 'peck' from Middle English pekken.
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing 'pecking' like 'peking' or stressing the -ing syllable.
Using 'pecking order' for a formal, written chain of command.

senses.definition: A person who makes an excessive or tedious show of their knowledge, especially regarding rules of vocabulary and grammar.
senses.example: Nobody wanted to correct the typo with him because he was such a pedant about grammar.

senses.definition: A person who is overly concerned with formal rules and trivial points of learning.
senses.example: As a pedant, she insisted the meeting minutes list every motion in exactly the bylaws' wording.

senses.definition: Pedantic.
senses.example: His pedantic corrections of our footnotes made the group project miserable.

senses.definition: (rare) To be or act as a pedant.
senses.example: He pedanted over the serial comma until everyone on the team groaned.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: Someone who shows off their knowledge and insists on minor rules, especially of grammar, spelling or word meaning.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The second vowel is a weak schwa, so it sounds like 'PEH-dunt,' not 'pe-DANT.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. Calling someone a pedant is an insult, implying they are tiresome and care too much about trivial correctness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'pedant' to criticize someone who corrects small points, like a grammar fix in a casual email or a date detail in a story, when the point doesn't matter. Saying 'Don't be a pedant' is a common, mildly sharp comeback. Calling yourself a pedant is a playful self-deprecation, often used when you know you are being picky.

distinctions.note: A perfectionist wants his own work flawless; a pedant insists on correctness in other people's work and talk, often over trivia.
An expert knows a field deeply and applies knowledge usefully; a pedant displays knowledge in ways that irritate others.

examples.everyday: My brother is such a pedant; he corrected my spelling of 'definitely' in a birthday text.
examples.professional: In the code review, Dana was a pedant about variable names, so we spent an hour on naming instead of the logic.
examples.analytical: The critic is a pedant whose objections, however accurate, rarely engage the work's argument.

nuance.analogy: A pedant is like a referee who stops a friendly game every minute to point out a tiny rule violation.
nuance.etymology: From Italian 'pedante,' a teacher, originally a schoolmaster who drilled students on grammar.
common_mistakes: Using 'pedant' as a neutral word for a scholar; it is almost always disparaging.
Pronouncing the stress on the second syllable as in 'pe-DANT.'

pedant.etymology: From Middle French *pedant*, *pedante*, from Italian *pedante* (“a teacher, schoolmaster, pedant”), associated with unrelated.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to the Pentateuch, also known as the Torah.

core.definition: Of or relating to the Pentateuch, the first five books of the Bible, also called the Torah in Judaism.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the third syllable, TOO, and keep the 'tuh' before it reduced. Do not say 'pen-ta-TEUCH-al'; the 'ch' is pronounced like a 'k' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise scholarly and religious term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use pentateuchal mainly in Bible study, seminaries, universities and scholarly writing. In Jewish contexts people say Torah, and in general conversation they might say 'the first five books of the Bible' or 'the books of Moses'. The word is clear in religious settings but may sound academic in casual talk.

distinctions.note: Torah in Judaism can mean the five books and the wider teaching tradition; pentateuchal is a Christian and scholarly term for the five books alone.
Mosaic means related to Moses, often by tradition or authorship; pentateuchal refers to the five books regardless of who wrote them.

examples.everyday: Our Bible study group is reading through the Pentateuchal stories this year, starting with Genesis.
examples.professional: The seminar paper compares Pentateuchal law with legal codes from the ancient Near East.
examples.analytical: The documentary hypothesis reads the Pentateuchal narratives as layered compositions drawn from several sources.

nuance.analogy: Like the first five chapters of a long family history, which set the foundation for everything that follows.
nuance.etymology: From Greek pentateuchos, 'five-volumed', from penta- 'five' and teuchos 'scroll, book'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in 'PEN-ta-TOO-kal'.
Using Pentateuchal to mean the whole Bible rather than only the first five books.
Assuming Pentateuch and Torah are identical in every Jewish context; Torah can include the wider tradition of teaching.
