distinctions.note: Full of is a general, plain phrase; riddled suggests damage or flaws spread throughout something.
Ridden means dominated or plagued by something; riddled focuses on holes, errors, or infestations spread through an object.

examples.everyday: The old fence is riddled with holes, so the dog keeps getting out.
examples.professional: The first draft of the report was riddled with errors in the data tables.
examples.analytical: Her theory, riddled with contradictions, cannot explain the very evidence it was built to explain.

nuance.analogy: A riddled object is like a sieve: something that has been pierced so many times it no longer holds together.
nuance.etymology: From riddle (verb), from Old English hriddel, meaning sieve.
common_mistakes: Using 'riddled by' instead of 'riddled with'; 'with' is the natural preposition.
Using 'riddled' only for physical holes; Americans also say 'riddled with doubt' or 'riddled with errors.'

senses.definition: To transport oneself by sitting on and directing a horse, later also a bicycle etc.
senses.example: I ride to work every day and park the bike outside the office.

senses.definition: To be transported in a vehicle; to travel as a passenger.
Of a ship: to sail, to float on the water.
senses.example: The little fishing boat rode gently at anchor while the tide slowly rose beneath it.

senses.definition: To be carried or supported by something lightly and quickly; to travel in such a way, as though on horseback.
senses.example: The witch cackled and rode away on her broomstick.

senses.definition: To traverse by riding.
To convey, as by riding; to make or do by riding.
senses.example: How many races have you ridden this year?

senses.definition: To exploit or take advantage of (a situation).
senses.example: Some executives rode the housing boom and cashed out before the market crashed.

senses.definition: To support a rider, as a horse; to move under the saddle.
senses.example: A horse rides easy or hard, slow or fast.

senses.definition: To mount (someone) to have sex with them.
senses.example: Everyone at the party knew he had been riding her in the back room all night.

senses.definition: To nag or criticize; to annoy (someone).
senses.example: My mother rides me about my grades every single week, and it's exhausting.

senses.definition: Of clothing: to gradually move (up) and crease; to ruckle.
senses.example: The waistband of his slacks kept riding up whenever he sat down at the desk.

senses.definition: To rely, depend (on).
senses.example: The whole project rides on whether the federal funding comes through this spring.

senses.definition: Of clothing: to rest (in a given way on a part of the body).
senses.example: The necklace rides low on her collarbone, just where the dress is cut.

senses.definition: To play defense on the defensemen or midfielders, as an attackman.
senses.example: In lacrosse, the midfielder must ride the opposing defenseman to slow the clearing pass.

senses.definition: To manage insolently at will; to domineer over.
senses.example: Her older brother rides her relentlessly and treats every decision as his to make.

senses.definition: To overlap (each other); said of bones or fractured fragments.
senses.example: On the X-ray, the two fractured bone fragments ride over each other slightly.

senses.definition: To monitor (some component of an audiovisual signal) in order to keep it within acceptable bounds.
senses.example: vocal riding

senses.definition: In jazz, to play in a steady rhythmical style.
senses.example: The bassist rode a steady swing groove while the horns traded solos over the changes.

senses.definition: An instance of riding.
senses.example: Can I have a ride on your bike?

senses.definition: A vehicle.
senses.example: That's a nice ride; what did it cost?

senses.definition: An amusement ridden at a fair or amusement park.
senses.example: the kids went on all the rides

senses.definition: A lift given to someone in another person's vehicle.
senses.example: Can you give me a ride home?

senses.definition: A steady rhythmical style.
senses.example: The pianist's laid-back ride gave the whole quartet a relaxed, swinging feel.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of ride cymbal.
A wild, bewildering experience of some duration.
senses.example: That story was a ride from start to finish.

senses.definition: An act of sexual intercourse.
senses.example: I gave my boyfriend a ride before breakfast.

senses.definition: A district inspected by an excise officer.
senses.example: The excise officer's ride covered forty villages along the river, each visited monthly.

senses.definition: (historical) A fault caused by the overlapping of leads, etc.
senses.example: The glazier pointed out a ride in the window, where two lead strips overlapped.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: To sit on and control a horse or bicycle, or to travel as a passenger in a vehicle.

pronunciation.tip: Use a long 'i' diphthong and end with a clear 'd.' Do not confuse it with 'rid,' which has a short vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive: riding suggests freedom, travel, or fun, and getting a ride suggests a kind favor.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'ride' for riding a bike, riding a horse, and getting a lift in someone's car. 'Can I get a ride?' or 'Want a ride?' are common everyday offers. 'Ride shotgun' means to sit in the front passenger seat, a very American phrase. For public transport, Americans say 'ride the bus' or 'ride the subway.'

distinctions.note: Drive means you control the vehicle, while ride means you are transported, either as a passenger or on a bike or horse.
Take is used for public transport and routes, as in 'take the train'; ride focuses on the experience of being carried.

examples.everyday: Want a ride to the airport, or are you taking a cab?
examples.professional: I ride the Metro to the office most days, which gives me time to review code.
examples.analytical: Mounted riding in medieval Europe shaped social hierarchy, since only those who could afford horses could wield armored power.

nuance.analogy: Riding is like being carried by a current: you can steer a little, but the vehicle or animal carries you along.
nuance.etymology: From Old English ridan, meaning to ride on horseback or travel.
common_mistakes: Saying 'ride to' a car; Americans say 'ride in a car' but 'ride on a bus' or 'ride a bike.'
Confusing 'ride' with 'rid' in 'get rid of,' which is a different verb.
nuance.biblical_note: Riding in Scripture often signals kingship, power, or divine presence. Hebrew 'rakab' means to ride, and Greek 'epibaino' means to mount. Zechariah 9:9 describes a king riding on a donkey, which Matthew 21:1-11 connects to Jesus's entry into Jerusalem. Psalm 18:10 describes God riding on a cherub and flying, showing divine movement and majesty.

ride.etymology: From Middle English *riden*, from Old English *rīdan*, from **rīdan*, from Proto-Germanic **rīdaną* (“to ride”), from Proto-Indo-European **Hreydʰ-* (“to ride”), from **h₃reyH-* (“to move”), from **h₃er-* (“to move, stir”).

senses.definition: A plot of true positive rate against false positive rate across decision thresholds.
senses.example: The data scientist plotted the ROC curve to compare the classifier's performance across thresholds.

core.definition: A plot of a classifier's true positive rate against its false positive rate across all decision thresholds, used to judge performance.

pronunciation.tip: Say ROC as the word 'rock', not as separate letters. The stress falls on curve in the phrase, while ROC carries a lighter secondary stress.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It is a standard term in machine learning, medicine and statistics.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say ROC curve, pronounced like rock curve, in data science and medical research. The name comes from receiver operating characteristic, but almost nobody says the full phrase in conversation. Colleagues often mention the AUC, the area under the curve, as a summary number.

distinctions.note: A precision-recall curve is more informative for imbalanced data, while the ROC curve can look optimistic when negatives greatly outnumber positives.
A confusion matrix shows counts at one chosen threshold, while the ROC curve shows performance across all thresholds.

collocations: choose a threshold from the ROC curve

examples.everyday: My friend who works in medicine said the test looked good on the ROC curve, but he still wanted to see the actual false alarms.
examples.professional: Please add the ROC curve to the review deck so we can compare the two classifiers before choosing a threshold.
examples.analytical: The ROC curve summarizes discrimination across thresholds, but it does not by itself tell us how well calibrated the probabilities are.

nuance.analogy: An ROC curve is like a dial test: it shows how many real cases you catch as you accept more false alarms.
nuance.etymology: ROC is an abbreviation of receiver operating characteristic, a term from World War II radar analysis.
common_mistakes: Saying the letters R-O-C instead of pronouncing it as 'rock'.
Treating the ROC curve as a single score; the curve shows many thresholds, and the AUC is only one summary of it.

conversation.text: The ROC curve plots the true positive rate against the false positive rate across all thresholds.
We pick the operating point on the ROC curve based on how costly false alarms are.
On very imbalanced data, the ROC curve can look great while precision is poor, so check the precision-recall curve too.

core.definition: Revised Standard Version, an English Bible translation published in 1952 (complete in 1971) by American Protestant and Jewish scholars.

pronunciation.tip: Say the letters one by one: 'ar', 'ess', 'vee'. Stress falls on the final letter, V.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it names a specific Bible translation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say the letters, and the term is common in churches, seminaries, and Bible study. It is a mainstream Protestant translation known for a more formal, literary style. Many people now prefer the newer ESV or NRSV, but RSV is still used in academic and church settings.

distinctions.note: NRSV is the revised version of RSV from 1989, with more inclusive language in some passages.
KJV is the 1611 King James Version, older and more archaic; RSV uses modern English.

examples.everyday: My Bible study group reads from the RSV because it is easier to follow than the old King James.
examples.professional: Our seminary course on the Gospels requires students to compare the RSV with the original Greek.
examples.analytical: The RSV's translation of this verse reflects a debate among 20th-century scholars about the Hebrew text.

nuance.analogy: Like a well-known map that has been updated, giving the same terrain in a clearer style.
common_mistakes: Saying the word as 'ritz-vee' instead of spelling out the letters.
Confusing RSV with NRSV or ESV, which are different translations.
nuance.biblical_note: The RSV was produced by American Protestant and Jewish scholars under the National Council of Churches, first as a New Testament in 1946 and then as a complete Bible in 1952 and 1971. It is widely used across Protestant churches and includes an edition with Catholic books, the RSV Catholic Edition.

senses.definition: That rules; predominant; chief; reigning; controlling.
senses.example: the ruling monarch

senses.definition: An order or a decision on a point of law from someone in authority.

core.definition: An official decision on a legal or procedural question, made by a judge, referee, or other person with authority.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the 'u' is a long 'oo' sound. The ending is the short American /ɪŋ/, not a long 'eeng' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes an authoritative decision and does not signal approval or disapproval.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'ruling' most often in courts, sports, and news reports, as in 'the judge's ruling' or 'the referee's ruling'. In casual talk, people often say 'the call' or 'the decision'. As an adjective, 'ruling' appears in phrases like 'ruling party' or 'ruling class', mainly in political news.

distinctions.note: Decision is a general word for any choice, while a ruling is a formal judgment by someone with authority to decide a question.
A verdict is the decision of a jury on guilt or liability, while a ruling is an authoritative decision on a point of law or procedure.
An order is a command to do something, while a ruling is a judgment about what is correct or allowed.

examples.everyday: The ref's ruling on that tackle was ridiculous, and the whole bar booed when he made the call.
examples.professional: The compliance office's ruling means we can't release the product until the audit is complete.
examples.analytical: The Court's ruling in Marbury established judicial review, although the Constitution does not state that power explicitly.

nuance.analogy: A ruling is like a referee's whistle in a game: it ends the debate on that play, at least until a higher authority reviews it.
nuance.etymology: From rule (verb) with the suffix -ing, forming a noun for the act or result of ruling.
common_mistakes: Using 'ruling' for any kind of opinion, when it really means an authoritative decision.
Pronouncing the first vowel as in 'rule' but then stressing the final syllable, which shifts the rhythm away from the American pattern.

senses.definition: To flee or depart quickly.
senses.example: Don't run off before the end of the event.

senses.definition: To make photocopies, or print.
senses.example: Please run off a couple dozen more flyers to pass out.

senses.definition: To write something quickly.
senses.example: Shakespeare could run off a play in just a couple of days.

senses.definition: (of a liquid) To pour or spill off or over.
senses.example: They kept a barrel to store rainwater that has run off the roof.

senses.definition: To cause to flow away.
senses.example: to run off a charge of molten metal from a furnace

senses.definition: To chase someone away.
senses.example: If anyone comes into this field, the bull will soon run them off.

senses.definition: To operate by a particular energy or fuel source.
senses.example: This radio runs off batteries.

senses.definition: To have diarrhea. (Can we add an example for this sense?)
senses.example: I think the bad burrito made me run off all night.

senses.definition: To recite, especially items on a list.
senses.example: He ran off the checklist one by one but still missed a couple of items.

senses.definition: To steal (horses).
senses.example: He ran off a pony from the ranch.

core.definition: To leave quickly, usually to get away from a person, place, or difficult situation.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on OFF. The vowel is the 'aw' of caught, which many American speakers pronounce the same as the vowel in cot, and the f should be clear with no added 'oh' glide.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It describes leaving quickly, sometimes after an argument or to avoid responsibility.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say run off for a child who takes off, a dog that bolts, or someone who leaves after a fight. In offices, run off is also the everyday term for making copies, as in 'Can you run off ten copies?' Run off with means to elope or steal, which is a different sense.

distinctions.note: Run away suggests a longer escape, often from home, while run off is quicker and can be temporary.
Leave is the neutral general word, while run off is more informal and implies hurrying.

examples.everyday: The dog ran off when the doorbell rang, so I'm chasing him around the yard.
examples.professional: Can you run off the handouts for the 2 p.m. meeting before the conference room fills up?
examples.analytical: Some critics argue that a reformer who runs off at the first sign of resistance has confused the desire for change with a need for comfort.

nuance.analogy: Like a balloon slipping from a child's hand, it drifts away fast before anyone can grab it.
nuance.etymology: Run from Old English rinnan; off from Old English of, meaning away from.
common_mistakes: Using run off with to mean just leave, when it means elope or steal
Saying run off the copies in formal writing, where make copies or print is clearer

senses.definition: Without pity or compassion; cruel, pitiless.
Uncompromising; unrelenting.

core.definition: Willing to hurt or harm others to get what you want, showing no pity or mercy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and use a long 'oo' sound. The second syllable is reduced to 'luss', and the final 's' is a soft 'us'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes cruelty, ambition or a willingness to harm others without concern.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'ruthless' for businesspeople, politicians, competitors, or dictators who will hurt others to win. It is strong and can be used in news and everyday talk. In business it can also describe a positive approach, such as 'ruthless efficiency', meaning someone who cuts waste without sentiment.

distinctions.note: Cruel describes deliberately causing pain; ruthless describes being willing to do harm for a goal, without caring about the cost to others.
Merciless is close in meaning but is more literary, while ruthless is common in American speech and business.

examples.everyday: My brother says his new boss is ruthless about deadlines, so nobody gets any slack.
examples.professional: We need to be ruthless about cutting features that don't serve the core product before the release.
examples.analytical: A ruthless ethic of self-interest may achieve short-term gains, but it undermines the trust on which lasting communities depend.

nuance.analogy: A ruthless person is like a bulldozer clearing a field: it moves forward with no regard for what it knocks down along the way.
nuance.etymology: From ruth, meaning pity or compassion, plus the suffix -less.
common_mistakes: Using 'ruthless' for a neutral strict rule; it implies cruelty, not just firmness.
Saying 'rutheless' or stressing the second syllable; the stress is on the first syllable.

senses.definition: The state of being a saint.
Saints collectively.
A religious practice or institution involving the recognition and veneration of saints.
senses.example: The historian's book traces the development of sainthood from early martyr cults to modern canonization procedures.

core.definition: The state or status of being a saint, a holy person officially recognized by a church after a formal process.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and say the nt clearly before the hood ending, which rhymes with good. The t in saint is often silent in fast speech, so it sounds like SAYN-hood.

nuance.connotation: Positive and respectful. It is used about holy people, but it can also be used humorously about someone with great patience.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sainthood mainly in religious, historical, or formal contexts, such as discussions of canonization or church history. In casual speech they more often say saintly or describe someone as a saint. Calling someone's patience sainthood is a playful exaggeration that friends would understand.

distinctions.note: Sanctity is the quality of holiness, while sainthood is the formal status of being recognized as a saint.
Holiness is the sacred quality of being set apart for God, while sainthood is a recognized status of a person who has lived holy.

examples.everyday: My grandmother joked that raising five kids should earn her sainthood, and everyone at the table laughed.
examples.professional: The postulation office is preparing the documents for the bishop to advance the cause for sainthood.
examples.analytical: Medieval sainthood was often conferred through local acclaim and popular devotion long before the formal procedures of the papacy developed.

nuance.analogy: Like a hall of fame for holiness, where recognition follows a long and carefully checked record.
nuance.etymology: From saint and the suffix -hood, from Old English -hād, meaning state or condition.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as SAINT-hood with an extra syllable, or dropping the d.
Using sainthood as a verb form or confusing it with saintliness, which describes a quality rather than a status.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture the word saints translates the Greek hagioi, meaning holy ones or people set apart for God, and it refers to all believers in Christ rather than a select group. Romans 1:7 addresses the Christians in Rome as those called to be saints, Ephesians 1:1 greets the saints at Ephesus, and Philippians 1:1 greets all the saints in Christ Jesus at Philippi.

traditions.view: The church formally recognizes saints through a canonization process that includes investigation of the candidate's life, verification of miracles, and a papal decision, after beatification.
The church recognizes saints through long-standing veneration by the faithful and decisions of bishops or synods, without a single formal legal process like Rome's.
Most Protestant churches do not formally canonize saints and use saint for all believers, though Anglican and Lutheran churches often honor historic saints in their calendars without canonization.

senses.definition: The price at which something is offered for sale.
The reduced price of something during a sale.

core.definition: The reduced price of an item during a sale, usually lower than the regular or original price.

pronunciation.tip: Price gets the main stress, while sale has a lighter secondary stress. Say the r in price as the American rhotic r and keep the vowel diphthong clear.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests a good deal, though it can also suggest a bargain or lower quality if overused.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sale price in stores, ads and online shopping, and it usually appears next to a crossed-out original price. In a store, you might ask 'Is this the sale price?' before buying. The phrase is common in everyday retail talk, while businesses sometimes use 'sales price' in formal contexts.

distinctions.note: Regular price is the normal, non-discounted price, while sale price is the temporary reduced price.
List price is the official published price set by the manufacturer, which may be higher than what a store actually charges.
A discount is the amount taken off a price, while sale price is the final amount you pay after the reduction.

examples.everyday: The jacket was marked down, but the sale price still felt a bit high for what it is.
examples.professional: Please list the sale price in the catalog and show the original price in smaller type next to it.
examples.analytical: A sale price signals a temporary reduction, which shapes how customers judge the true value of a product.

nuance.analogy: A sale price is like a shortcut on a road map: it gets you to the destination faster, but only for a limited time.
nuance.etymology: Sale comes from Old Norse sala; price comes from Old French pris, from Latin pretium, 'value'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'sales price' in everyday shopping, when 'sale price' is the more natural American phrase in stores.
Stressing 'sale' equally with 'price', which makes the phrase sound flat; the main stress is on 'price'.

senses.definition: In a sapient manner.

core.definition: In a wise, discerning way, showing good judgment and sound understanding.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, SAY, and the middle syllables are quick and reduced. Don't pronounce the -ent- as a full vowel; it sounds like 'unt' and the word ends in -lee.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises wise, careful judgment, but the word is rare and can sound bookish or slightly ironic in casual speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this adverb in conversation. You will meet it mostly in essays, book reviews, sermons, and literary writing. In everyday speech, say 'wisely' or 'with good judgment' instead. Using 'sapiently' in a meeting may sound pretentious unless the context is clearly formal.

distinctions.note: 'Wisely' is everyday and common; 'sapiently' is rarer and more formal, and it suggests a thoughtful, almost scholarly kind of wisdom.
'Sagely' often describes an old, wise-seeming manner and can sound mock-serious, while 'sapiently' is a more neutral word for sound judgment.

examples.professional: The review committee sapiently postponed the launch decision until the audit results were in.
examples.analytical: Aristotle's practically wise person is one who sapiently weighs particular circumstances rather than applying fixed rules.

nuance.analogy: Like a seasoned pilot who reads the weather before takeoff, someone who acts sapiently looks ahead before deciding.
nuance.etymology: From Latin sapiens, 'wise, discerning,' from sapere, 'to taste, be wise.'
common_mistakes: Confusing 'sapient' (wise) with 'sentient' (able to feel or perceive), which is a different word.
Using 'sapiently' in casual speech, where 'wisely' sounds more natural.

senses.definition: The state of being satiated.
senses.example: Eating half of that loaf of bread has left me in a state of utter satiety.

core.definition: The feeling of being full and no longer hungry, or the state of having had enough of something.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on TY, the second syllable. Keep the first syllable weak, and the final syllable ends in a short 'ee' sound. The 'ti' is a light 'tee.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise term, used in nutrition and psychology.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use satiety in nutrition, diet, and health writing, as in 'high-satiety foods' or 'signals of satiety.' In everyday talk they say 'feeling full.' The word is standard in medical and dietary discussions.

distinctions.note: Fullness is the everyday word for having eaten enough; satiety is the technical term for the feeling of having had enough, often in diet research.
Satiation is the act or process of filling a desire; satiety is the state that results.

examples.everyday: Oatmeal gives me a lot of satiety, so I'm not hungry again until lunch.
examples.professional: The nutrition team tracked satiety scores to see which breakfast menu kept shoppers full longest.
examples.analytical: Philosophers of appetite have long asked whether satiety is a bodily signal or a moral lesson about desire.

nuance.analogy: Satiety is like the lid clicking shut on a full box: the sense that you have had enough.
nuance.etymology: From Latin satietas, 'fullness,' from satis, 'enough.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as SAY-shi-ety.
Using satiety as a casual synonym for 'hungry' or 'full stomach' without context.

senses.definition: Having a jagged edge like a saw.

core.definition: Having a jagged edge like the teeth of a saw.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TOOTHT, and the final -ed is a /t/ sound after the unvoiced th, so it sounds like 'tootht'. Do not add an extra vowel before the t.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a descriptive term for edges, leaves or ridges.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use saw-toothed mostly to describe natural or physical shapes, such as leaves, ridges, mountain outlines or blades. It sounds more descriptive and literal than casual, so it fits writing, science and careful description better than everyday talk.

distinctions.note: Serrated usually describes a fine, regular row of teeth on a blade or leaf, while saw-toothed describes a broader zigzag outline.
Jagged suggests an irregular, broken edge, while saw-toothed suggests a more regular, repeated pattern.

examples.everyday: The leaves on that bush have saw-toothed edges, so you can tell it apart from the plants next to it.
examples.professional: The new blade design has a saw-toothed edge that cuts faster through frozen food.
examples.analytical: The saw-toothed ridgeline in the poem images the tension between order and chaos in the speaker's mind.

nuance.analogy: Like a row of sharp teeth set side by side, the edge keeps catching and cutting the eye along its length.
nuance.etymology: From saw plus toothed, meaning having teeth like a saw.
common_mistakes: Dropping the final -ed sound, saying 'toothe' instead of 'tootht'.
Using saw-toothed as a noun instead of an adjective.
Confusing it with serrated for every kind of toothed edge.

senses.definition: Characterized by scratches.
senses.example: The old lens was scratchy from years of wiping with a dirty cloth.

senses.definition: Irritating; itchy.
Noisy, lossy; marred by white noise or static as a result of poor or low signal, interference or unfavorable atmospheric conditions.
senses.example: The FM station two hundred miles away was receivable, but the audio was too scratchy to positively identify.

senses.definition: Having popping and/or crackling sounds due to excessive wear, especially from scratch marks.
senses.example: The jazz record sounded warm but scratchy, with crackles from years of play.

senses.definition: Irritable; tetchy.

core.definition: Feeling rough, itchy, or irritating to the skin or throat; or sounding crackly, as a recording or a bad phone line.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final -y is a long ee. Do not stretch the first vowel, which is short, as in 'cat'.

nuance.connotation: Negative but mild. It describes an unpleasant feeling or sound.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use scratchy for wool clothes, sore throats, and poor phone or radio connections. For a sore throat, scratchy is more natural than irritated. On the phone, 'The line is scratchy' is a common complaint. A natural reply is 'Hang on, let me find a better signal.'

distinctions.note: Itchy describes the urge to scratch, while scratchy describes a rough texture or an irritating sound or throat.
Crackly suggests popping noises, while scratchy suggests a rough, grating sound or static on a line.

examples.everyday: My throat feels scratchy, so I'm going to make some tea.
examples.professional: The call was scratchy, so I'll resend the summary by email.
examples.analytical: A scratchy recording of an old sermon can still carry the speaker's theological urgency.

nuance.analogy: Like a radio station that fades in and out with static.
nuance.etymology: From scratch with the adjective suffix -y.
common_mistakes: Using scratchy for a damaged surface; use scratched for a table or a phone screen with marks.
Pronouncing the final -y as 'eye'; it is a long ee.

senses.definition: An application that searches for, and retrieves, data based on some criteria, especially one that searches the Internet for documents containing specified words.
senses.example: The search engine ranked the most relevant articles at the top of the results.

core.definition: A program or website that searches stored information, especially web pages on the internet, and returns results matching the words you type.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on "SEARCH" in this compound noun, and "engine" is reduced to "en-jin," with the final syllable very light. Don't stress both words equally.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It names a tool and carries no positive or negative judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use "search engine" for Google, Bing, and similar sites, and also for the search function inside a shopping site or app. In casual talk, people often say "Google" as a verb or noun, but "search engine" is the standard general term. In technical contexts, it can refer to the software behind a search function, such as a database or an internal enterprise search tool.

distinctions.note: A "browser" displays web pages you already know how to reach; a "search engine" finds pages that match your words.
A "database" stores structured data; a "search engine" is the tool that searches and ranks results, often across many sources.

examples.everyday: Just type the store's name into a search engine and you'll find the hours right away.
examples.professional: We need to improve how our internal search engine ranks product results for common queries.
examples.analytical: A search engine is less an oracle than a ranking system, and its criteria quietly shape what users come to believe is relevant.

nuance.analogy: A search engine is like a librarian who has read every book in the building and can point you to the right shelf in seconds.
nuance.etymology: "Search" comes from Latin "circare," to go around; "engine" comes from Latin "ingenium," meaning skill or cleverness, later a machine.
common_mistakes: Stressing both words equally or putting the main stress on "engine."
Confusing it with "browser": people sometimes say "I'll open my search engine" when they mean their web browser.

senses.definition: Synonym of look for.

core.definition: To look in a place or among things in order to find something or someone, often with effort or over a period of time.

pronunciation.tip: In this phrasal verb, the stress usually falls on "FOR," the particle, not the verb. Say "surch FOR" with a clear r in "for," and don't reduce it to a weak "fer" when speaking it alone.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes an action and can be positive, such as searching for a solution, or neutral, such as searching for keys.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use "search for" in everyday speech for lost objects, people, jobs, and answers, and in business for hiring or looking for information. It is close to "look for" but usually sounds a bit more deliberate. You can answer with "Found it!" or "Any luck?" to ask whether the search succeeded.

distinctions.note: "Look for" is more casual and common in daily talk; "search for" suggests a more careful or systematic effort.
"Search" takes a place as its object, as in "search the car"; "search for" takes the thing you want, as in "search for the keys."

examples.everyday: I'm searching for my keys, and I've looked everywhere. Have you seen them?
examples.professional: We're searching for a senior engineer who can lead the data platform team next quarter.
examples.analytical: The philosopher searches for a foundation for ethics that does not depend on a single revealed authority.

nuance.analogy: Searching for something is like walking through a dark room with a flashlight, pointing it at each corner until the thing you want appears.
nuance.etymology: "Search" comes from Latin "circare," to go around; "for" is an ordinary English preposition of purpose.
common_mistakes: Adding "for" after "search" when the object is a place: say "search the house," not "search for the house."
Using "search for" when you mean "look up" a word in a dictionary; Americans usually say "look up" for dictionaries and records.

senses.definition: A person's term in office with a title including the term secretary, such as secretary of state.
senses.example: His secretaryship was marred by accusations of corruption, but the next secretary of state was called incompetent.

senses.definition: The office or position of being secretary.

core.definition: The office, position, or term of service of a person holding the title of secretary.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, with a weaker stress on 'tair.' The final syllable is a short 'ship,' not 'sheep.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes an official position or period of service and does not carry emotional weight.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'secretaryship' in everyday speech. You are more likely to see it in news, history, or formal writing, as in 'during her secretaryship' or 'his secretaryship at the state department.' Usually people say 'term as secretary' or 'secretary of [department].'

distinctions.note: 'Term' is the everyday word for a period in office, while 'secretaryship' specifically refers to the office of a secretary.
'Office' is a general word for any official position, while 'secretaryship' is limited to the post of secretary.

examples.everyday: My grandfather's secretaryship of the local union lasted almost twenty years.
examples.professional: During her secretaryship, the committee adopted new rules for public comment.
examples.analytical: The historical significance of his secretaryship lies less in its length than in the precedents it set for executive power.

nuance.analogy: Like a term of office on a ballot: it is the period of time someone holds a role, often with a title attached.
nuance.etymology: From 'secretary' and the suffix '-ship,' meaning 'office or position.'
common_mistakes: Using 'secretaryship' for everyday office work; 'secretary' or 'job' is more natural.
Stressing the last syllable as 'ship' with a long vowel; the ending is short.

senses.definition: Related to, or caused by an earthquake or other vibration of the Earth.
senses.example: seismic activity

senses.definition: Subject to earthquakes.
senses.example: a seismic area

senses.definition: Of very large or widespread effect.

core.definition: Relating to earthquakes or the vibrations of the Earth; also, describing a change that is very large and far-reaching.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The z sounds like a voiced s, and the final -ic is a short, unstressed syllable, not 'eek'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use seismic literally for earthquakes and figuratively for big shifts, such as a seismic change in the tech industry or a seismic election result. Figurative use is common in news and business writing, but it is strong, so avoid it for small changes. Seismologist is the everyday word for the scientist who studies earthquakes.

distinctions.note: Tectonic refers to the large plates of the Earth's crust, while seismic refers to the shaking or vibrations themselves.
Dramatic describes something striking or noticeable, while seismic implies a deep, structural change that affects a whole system.

examples.everyday: Did you feel that seismic jolt last night? I thought a truck hit the house.
examples.professional: Moving the whole billing system to the cloud was a seismic shift for our team, so we planned the rollout carefully.
examples.analytical: Kuhn argued that scientific revolutions are seismic events, breaking the paradigm that had organized normal research.

nuance.analogy: A seismic change is like an earthquake under a building: the ground moves, and everything built on it has to adjust.
nuance.etymology: From Greek seismos, 'earthquake', from seiein, 'to shake'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first syllable as 'SEE-' instead of 'SIGHZ-'.
Using seismic for small or ordinary changes, where gradual or notable is better.

seismic.etymology: Based on Ancient Greek *σεισμός* (“shaking, earthquake”) + *-ic*, equivalent to *seismo-* + *-ic*.

senses.definition: Send a text message.
senses.example: I'll send a text to your brother so he knows we're running late.

core.definition: To send a short written message electronically to someone's cell phone.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the noun 'text', not 'send'. The 'a' is a reduced schwa, and the words link smoothly, so say it as 'sen-duh-TEKST'. The t in 'text' is a clear, unflapped t.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and friendly; it is ordinary, everyday language.
nuance.usage_note: This is the normal American phrase for sending any short phone message, whether by SMS or by an app like iMessage. In casual speech you can also say 'text me' or 'shoot me a text'. Americans rarely say 'send an SMS' in conversation. A natural reply is 'Okay, I'll text you' or 'Got it.'

distinctions.note: A call means speaking on the phone in real time, while a text is written and can be read later.
Message is broader and can mean any communication; a text is specifically a short message sent by phone.

examples.everyday: I'll send you a text when I leave the store, so you know when to start dinner.
examples.professional: I'll send a text to the team once the build passes, so nobody has to check the dashboard.
examples.analytical: When we send a text, the content often matters less than the wish to stay connected.

nuance.analogy: Like passing a note in class, except it travels instantly from one pocket to another.
nuance.etymology: From Latin textus, 'something woven', via Middle English; the messaging sense dates from the 1990s.
common_mistakes: Saying 'send an SMS' or 'send a message by text' in casual speech; 'send a text' is the natural form.
Pronouncing the t in 'text' weakly or as a flap; it is a clear, crisp t.

conversation.text: I'll send a text when I'm on my way.
Send a text to the group so everyone knows we're late.
She sent a text instead of calling because she was in a meeting.

senses.definition: The state of being senseless; unsense.

core.definition: The quality of being pointless, cruel or without reason; also a state of being unconscious or unable to feel.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'SEN', and the rest of the word is quick and reduced, with the final 'ness' sounding like 'nuhs'. Do not add an extra vowel after the 'sl'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It names the tragic or absurd quality of an act, event, or situation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use senselessness in news, grief, and reflective writing, as in 'the senselessness of the shooting'. It often expresses shock or frustration that something had no good reason. In casual speech, people often say 'it makes no sense' or 'it's so pointless' instead.

distinctions.note: Foolishness refers to a person's lack of wisdom, while senselessness refers to the pointless or cruel quality of an act or situation.
Absurdity suggests something ridiculous or contradictory, while senselessness suggests harm or waste without purpose.

examples.everyday: I still can't get over the senselessness of that accident, especially since the driver was only two blocks from home.
examples.professional: The postmortem highlighted the senselessness of repeating the same failed deployment three times without changing the process.
examples.analytical: Ecclesiastes repeatedly confronts the apparent senselessness of human labor under the sun, asking whether any gain remains from toil.

nuance.analogy: The senselessness of an act is like a clock with no hands: it moves and ticks, but it tells you nothing.
nuance.etymology: From senseless plus the noun suffix -ness, 'state or quality of'.
common_mistakes: Using senselessness for a simple mistake, where 'foolishness' or 'pointlessness' is more natural.
Confusing senselessness with 'insensibility', which refers to unconsciousness or a lack of feeling.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word hebel means breath, vapor or vanity, and it captures the sense of something fleeting and without lasting purpose. Ecclesiastes 1:2 opens with the phrase 'Vanity of vanities', showing the book's central theme. Ecclesiastes 2:17 describes the author's weariness with life, because the labor done under the sun seems to lead nowhere.

senses.definition: Characterized by sentiment, sentimentality or excess emotion; appealing to the emotions (especially tender emotions) rather than reason, morality, aesthetic taste, etc.
senses.example: The movie's sentimental ending, with the lost dog returning home, made the whole theater cry.

senses.definition: Derived from emotion rather than logical reason.
Romantic.

core.definition: Showing or appealing to tender feelings and emotions more than logic. Often describes nostalgia or romantic attachment.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the third syllable, MEN. The final syllable is a syllabic l, so say it as 'tul' without an extra vowel.

nuance.connotation: Mixed. It can be warm and affectionate, but it can also suggest excessive or naive emotion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say sentimental about an old object, a gift, or a place: 'It's sentimental value.' In criticism, calling a book or movie sentimental suggests it manipulates emotions. Be careful, because in other contexts sentimental can sound like a compliment about kindness.

distinctions.note: Emotional describes feeling in general, which can be neutral. Sentimental implies that the feeling is tender, nostalgic, or sometimes excessive.
Nostalgic means longing for the past. Sentimental can describe that longing but also a general softness about feelings.

examples.everyday: That old coffee mug is not worth much, but it has sentimental value because my grandfather used it every morning.
examples.professional: I'm not being sentimental about the old dashboard, but the new one is clearer and faster for the team.
examples.analytical: Critics often call a novel sentimental when it asks readers to feel grief without earning that grief through its details.

nuance.analogy: Sentimental feeling is like a warm light in an old photo: it glows because of memory more than the brightness of the scene.
nuance.etymology: From sentiment, from Latin sentire, to feel.
common_mistakes: Using sentimental to mean sensitive in a neutral way, when it usually sounds like nostalgia or softness.
Saying sentimental feelings when sentimental value is the more natural American phrase for objects.

senses.definition: To put (something such as a knife or sword) into a sheath.
To encase (something) with a protective covering.
Of an animal: to draw back or retract (a body part) into the body, such as claws into a paw.
senses.example: When the cat feels relaxed, it will sheathe its claws and rest its paws on the couch.

senses.definition: (dated, poetic) To thrust (a sharp object like a sword, a claw, or a tusk) into something.
senses.example: Let the knight sheathe his blade in the dragon's heart, as the old ballad promised.
senses.label: dated, poetic

core.definition: To put a blade, such as a knife or sword, into its protective cover; also, to cover something with a protective layer.

pronunciation.tip: The verb ends in a voiced 'th' (as in 'breathe'), while the noun 'sheath' ends in an unvoiced 'th' (as in 'teeth'). Americans often blur this, so practice the difference: sheathe /ʃið/, sheath /ʃiθ/.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, with a slightly elevated tone in ordinary writing.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech people more often say 'put the knife away' or 'put the sword back.' Sheathe is most natural for swords, knives, and sometimes cables or pipes covered in a jacket. You will see it in writing, technical descriptions, and fiction more than in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: Encase suggests fully enclosing something in a hard shell, while sheathe often describes a close-fitting cover that can be pulled off again.
Cover is the everyday general word, and sheathe is more specific and more formal, implying a protective case or jacket.

examples.everyday: After he cut the rope, my dad sheathed the knife and put it back in his belt.
examples.professional: The contractor sheathed the exposed pipes in foam insulation before the winter inspection.
examples.analytical: The poet sheathes a sharp political critique in the soft language of the pastoral, so the reader must look closely to find it.

nuance.analogy: Sheathing a sword is like slipping a phone into a case: the protection fits closely, and you can take it out again.
nuance.etymology: From sheath, from Old English scēath, a case for a blade.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the verb with an unvoiced 'th' like the noun 'sheath,' which makes it sound like 'sheeth' with a hard ending.
Using 'sheathe' in casual talk where 'put away' or 'cover' sounds more natural.

sheathe.etymology: From Late Middle English *shethen* (“to put into a sheath, sheathe; to provide with a sheath; to have sexual intercourse”), then:

senses.definition: Land adjoining a non-flowing body of water, such as an ocean, lake or pond.
senses.example: lake shore; bay shore; gulf shore; island shore; mainland shore; river shore; estuary shore; pond shore; sandy shore; rocky shore

senses.definition: Land, usually near a port.
senses.example: The seamen were serving on shore instead of on ships.

senses.definition: A prop or strut supporting some structure or weight above it.
senses.example: The shores stayed upright during the earthquake.

senses.definition: Not followed by up: to provide (something) with support.
senses.example: The engineers shored the trench walls with steel braces before workers entered.

senses.definition: Usually followed by up: to reinforce (something at risk of failure).
senses.example: My family shored me up after I failed the GED.

senses.definition: To threaten or warn unpleasant consequences (for someone); to threaten or warn off or scare away.
senses.example: The old sheriff's stern glare shored the rowdy teenagers away from the diner.

senses.definition: To threaten (to rain).
senses.example: Dark clouds shored all afternoon, so we cancelled the picnic.

senses.definition: To offer or present (someone something).
senses.example: The landlord shored the tenants a generous deal to renew their leases.

core.definition: The land along the edge of an ocean, lake, or other large body of water.

pronunciation.tip: The single syllable is stressed and uses the 'aw' vowel with a clear American r. Do not make it sound like 'show' or 'shore' with a long o.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is pleasant and everyday in beach or travel talk, and more poetic in literature.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'on the shore,' 'the Jersey Shore,' or 'at the shore' for going to the beach, especially in the Northeast. 'Beach' is more common for sandy places where people swim, while 'shore' refers to the coastline or edge in general. The verb 'shore up' is common in business for reinforcing something weak.

distinctions.note: 'Beach' is the sandy area people use; 'shore' is the broader boundary between land and water.
'Coast' refers to the land along the sea over a wide region; 'shore' is more local and specific to the water's edge.

examples.everyday: We walked along the shore and watched the kids build sandcastles.
examples.professional: The survey team mapped the eroding shore before the new pier was approved.
examples.analytical: The poet imagines the self as a stranded boat, thrown back again and again upon the shore of the unknown.

nuance.analogy: Like a border where a soft line of sand meets the endless blue.
common_mistakes: Using 'shore' for the sea itself, when the sea is the body of water.
Pronouncing the r as silent, which makes it sound like 'saw' with no r.

shore.etymology: From Middle English *schore*, from Old English **sċora*, from Proto-Germanic **skurô* (“rugged rock, cliff, high rocky shore”).

conversation.text: Stay close to the shore, okay? The waves are getting bigger.
We walked along the shore looking for shells until sunset.
The kids built a fort right near the shore, and the tide washed it away.

senses.definition: One who, or that which, shortens.

core.definition: A tool, service or thing that makes something shorter, especially a service that turns a long web address into a short link.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, and the -en is a reduced vowel. The final -er is a reduced 'er' sound, so the word does not end in 'ur' with a strong vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical, technical term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Outside tech, Americans rarely use shortener alone; they say 'link shortener' or 'URL shortener', which is common in marketing and social media. For the general idea of making something shorter, people say 'something that shortens' or name the specific tool, such as a hemmer for pants.

distinctions.note: An abbreviation is a shortened form of a word, such as 'Dr.' for 'Doctor', while a shortener is the tool or service that does the shortening.
Shortening can mean the process of making something shorter or a solid cooking fat, while shortener refers to the agent or tool that shortens.

examples.everyday: Use a link shortener so the address fits in the text message without breaking.
examples.professional: We use a link shortener so the tracking URLs fit in SMS campaigns and print materials.
examples.analytical: A URL shortener is essentially a lookup service: it stores a long address and returns a short key that redirects to it.

nuance.analogy: Like a nickname for a long name: everyone still knows who you mean, but it fits in less space.
nuance.etymology: From shorten, with the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Using shorten or shorteners as a common noun for any short form; use abbreviation for a shortened word.
Confusing it with shorthand, which is a writing system or short way of expressing something.

senses.definition: A case for displaying merchandise or valuable items.
senses.example: The jeweler placed the diamond necklace in a glass showcase near the door.

senses.definition: A setting, occasion, or medium for exhibiting something or someone, especially in an attractive or favorable aspect.
senses.example: The fair was a showcase for local farms and their best products.

senses.definition: To display, demonstrate, show, or present.
senses.example: I think the demonstration really showcases the strengths of the software.

core.definition: To display or present something so that its best qualities are clearly seen by others.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the first syllable, 'SHOH', and the second syllable is light. Do not stress 'case' as 'kayss' with strong emphasis; keep the final 's' as a clear /s/.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it implies that something is being shown in its best light, though it can sound like marketing when used too often.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'showcase' very often in business, school and arts settings, as in 'showcase our new product' or 'showcase student work.' It is a neutral to positive word and sounds natural in meetings, emails and presentations. In casual talk you might say 'show off' instead, which can sound a little boastful.

distinctions.note: Show off is informal and often suggests bragging or wanting attention, while showcase is neutral and professional.
Display is a more general word for putting something where it can be seen, while showcase implies choosing it to present its best features.
Demonstrate focuses on proving how something works or that it is true, while showcase focuses on attractive presentation.

examples.everyday: My daughter wants to showcase her new painting at the family dinner tonight.
examples.professional: Let's showcase the new dashboard in tomorrow's client meeting so the sales team can see the key features.
examples.analytical: Many religious communities showcase their traditions in worship, yet the deeper question is whether such display reveals or hides the truth.

nuance.analogy: Like a jeweler placing a diamond on velvet under a bright light, showcase makes the best parts easy to see.
nuance.etymology: From 'show' and 'case', a glass container for displaying objects.
common_mistakes: Using 'showcase' to mean only a physical glass case; as a verb it means presenting qualities.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'show-KAYSE'.

senses.definition: The act or process of signing off (approving with a signature).
The process of exiting a computer system; logoff.
A bid indicating that one's partner should pass.
A valediction, such as at the end of a letter or broadcast.

core.definition: A formal approval of a plan, decision, or product, usually given by a person with authority.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable 'OFF', with a light secondary stress on 'sine'. The hyphenated noun is pronounced differently from the verb phrase 'sign off' in some uses, but the stress stays on 'OFF'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a formal step in a process and is usually used in a business or organizational setting.
nuance.usage_note: In American offices, 'sign-off' is a common noun for the final approval needed before something proceeds. You might hear 'We need a sign-off from legal' in a meeting. It can also mean the closing of a message or broadcast, but in everyday workplace talk the approval meaning is most common.

distinctions.note: 'Approval' is the general word for permission, while 'sign-off' often emphasizes the final, formal step in a workflow.
'Authorization' is more formal and is often used for legal or security permissions, while 'sign-off' is typical in business and project work.

examples.everyday: I can't book the trip until my boss gives the sign-off.
examples.professional: We need final sign-off from the product team before the release goes out on Monday.
examples.analytical: A formal sign-off procedure creates a clear record of who bears responsibility for a decision.

nuance.analogy: A sign-off is like a final inspection before a building opens: no one moves in until the approval is stamped.
nuance.etymology: Formed from the phrasal verb 'sign off', from 'sign' (Latin 'signum', mark) and 'off'.
common_mistakes: Writing 'signoff' as one word in formal documents, when the hyphenated form 'sign-off' is more common in American writing.
Confusing the noun with the verb: say 'get sign-off' rather than 'get sign off' as a noun.

conversation.text: We're just waiting for sign-off from legal.
Can you give final sign-off on the design today?
The launch needs sign-off from both directors.

senses.definition: One's exclusive romantic partner.
A person with whom one has an important bond of some kind.
senses.example: She brought her significant other to the company holiday party last December.

core.definition: One's steady romantic partner, used when you do not want to name a boyfriend, girlfriend, husband, or wife.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on OTH in other, while significant is lighter and its first syllable reduces to suh. Say other with a voiced th, as in the, and a clear r at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to warm, but it can sound clinical or evasive when someone avoids a more specific word.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use significant other in dating, on forms, and in polite introductions when they do not want to specify gender or marital status. It is common among adults, and it can sound playful or cautious if used too often. A natural reply is Nice to meet you, or Bring them along, and you can also use the partner's name.

distinctions.note: These are more specific and casual, while significant other is a neutral placeholder that covers any gender.
Spouse means a married partner, while significant other can refer to someone you are dating without being married.
Partner can be professional or romantic, but significant other is used only for romantic or intimate relationships.

examples.everyday: Bring your significant other to the barbecue on Saturday, we would love to meet them.
examples.professional: Are we allowed to bring a significant other to the company holiday party?
examples.analytical: Survey forms that ask only for a significant other often fail to capture the many forms that intimate partnership can take.

nuance.analogy: Significant other is like a placeholder name: it holds the spot for someone important without revealing the details.
nuance.etymology: A modern American phrase combining significant, from Latin significans, and other, from Old English oþer; the exact first use is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Using significant other for any important person, such as a mentor or friend, when it means only a romantic partner.
Saying the word other with a hard t or ah sound instead of UH-ther.

senses.definition: Clipping of simulator.
senses.example: They played a flight sim all afternoon.

senses.definition: Clipping of simulation.
A simulation session or scenario.
senses.example: (Can we add an example for this sense?)

senses.definition: Clipping of simulate.
senses.example: Let's sim the warehouse layout to see whether the new robots actually reduce wait times.

core.definition: Short for simulation: a computer or training model that imitates a real system or situation.

pronunciation.tip: Use a short i, like in 'sit', and close the word with a clear m. Do not stretch it into 'seem'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is casual shorthand used mainly in technology, gaming, training, and engineering conversations.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sim informally with coworkers, gamers, or engineers, especially for flight sims, physics sims, or training sims. In formal reports, people usually write simulation or simulator. The word can also be a verb in casual shop talk, but simulate is the standard form.

distinctions.note: Simulation is the formal word for the process or model, while sim is informal shorthand in speech and casual writing.
A simulator is usually a device or software that runs the model, while sim can refer to the scenario itself.
Emulation copies the behavior of another system, often hardware, while simulation models how something behaves in general.

examples.everyday: My brother spends every weekend playing a flight sim in his basement.
examples.professional: Let's run the sim again with the updated inventory numbers before we commit to the schedule.
examples.analytical: The sim lets us test the model's assumptions without the cost and risk of a real-world trial.

nuance.analogy: Like a practice field for a sports team, where they can try plays before the real game.
nuance.etymology: Clipping of simulation, from Latin simulare, to imitate.
common_mistakes: Using sim in formal reports where simulation is expected.
Pronouncing it with a long e sound like 'seem'.

senses.definition: To be in a position in which the upper body is upright and supported by the buttocks.
senses.example: After a long day of walking, it was good just to sit and relax.

senses.definition: To move oneself into such a position.
senses.example: I asked him to sit.

senses.definition: To occupy a given position.
senses.example: The dishes are still sitting on the table!

senses.definition: To remain in a state of repose; to rest; to abide; to rest in any position or condition.
senses.example: After the long flight, I just wanted to sit on the couch and do nothing.

senses.definition: To be a member of a deliberative body.
senses.example: I currently sit on a standards committee.

senses.definition: To lie, rest, or bear; to press or weigh.
senses.example: The heavy snow sat on the flat roof until the crew shoveled it off.

senses.definition: To be adjusted; to fit.
senses.example: Your new coat sits well.

senses.definition: To be accepted or acceptable; to work.
senses.example: How will this new contract sit with the workers?

senses.definition: To cause to be seated or in a sitting posture; to furnish a seat to.
senses.example: Sit him in front of the TV and he might watch for hours.

senses.definition: To accommodate in seats; to seat.
senses.example: The dining room table sits eight comfortably.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of babysit.
senses.example: I'm going to sit for them on Thursday.

senses.definition: To cover and warm eggs for hatching, as a fowl; to brood; to incubate.
senses.example: The hen sat on her eggs for three weeks until the chicks hatched.

senses.definition: To take a position for the purpose of having some artistic representation of oneself made, such as a picture or a bust.
senses.example: I'm sitting for a painter this evening.

senses.definition: To have position, as at the point blown from; to hold a relative position; to have direction.
senses.example: Our apartment sits just north of the river, near the old bridge.

senses.definition: Of a legislative or, especially, a judicial body such as a court, to be in session.
senses.example: In what city is the circuit court sitting for this session?

senses.definition: An act of sitting.
senses.example: That first sit in the new office chair felt surprisingly comfortable.

senses.definition: Subsidence of the roof of a coal mine.
senses.example: Engineers monitored the sit of the roof after the coal seam collapsed.

senses.definition: Clipping of situation.
senses.example: Okay, so what's the sit with the server outage this morning?

senses.definition: (rare) An event, usually lasting one full day or more, where the primary goal is to sit in meditation.
senses.example: I signed up for a weekend sit at the zen center near Boulder.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: To rest your body on your buttocks with your upper body upright, usually on a chair, bench, or the floor.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is short and relaxed, like the i in 'bit', and the t is clearly released at the end. Do not add a vowel after the t, and do not stretch the vowel into 'seet'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Sit is one of the most basic verbs in American English and is used constantly, from 'Please sit down' to 'Mind if I sit here?' Americans often say 'have a seat' as a more polite invitation in offices or restaurants. In everyday talk 'sit' is also used loosely for being located, as in 'the car sits in the driveway'.

distinctions.note: Seat is usually transitive, as in 'seat the guests', while sit is intransitive, describing the action of the body itself.
Stand describes being upright on your feet, the opposite posture, while sit describes resting on the seat of the body.

examples.everyday: Please sit down, dinner will be ready in a few minutes.
examples.professional: Let's sit down together after the meeting so I can walk you through the model results.
examples.analytical: Descartes's meditator sits by the fire in his dressing gown, and that stillness becomes the setting for his radical doubt.

nuance.analogy: Sitting is like settling into a boat: your weight rests fully on the seat, and the upper body stays upright.
nuance.etymology: From Old English sittan, from a Germanic root related to Latin sedere, meaning to be seated.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'sit' with 'seat' and saying 'Please sit the guests' instead of 'Please seat the guests'.
Adding an extra vowel, as in 'sitt' or 'seet', instead of a short vowel and a clear final t.

sit.etymology: From Middle English *sitten*, from Old English *sittan*, from **sittjan*, from Proto-Germanic **sitjaną*, from Proto-Indo-European **sed-* (“sit”).

senses.definition: A slut, a sexually promiscuous woman.
(dated) One who is uncareful or unconcerned about appearance or surroundings, usually said of a dirty and untidy woman.
senses.example: Her landlady called the untidy tenant a slattern who never cleaned her rooms.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: A dated word for an untidy, careless woman; in old usage, also an insult for a sexually promiscuous woman.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SLAT-ern. The t between vowels is a quick American flap that sounds like a soft 'd,' and the final syllable is a reduced vowel with no 'z' sound.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative and insulting; it judges a woman's appearance and morals.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'slattern' in speech today. It appears mostly in older novels, literary criticism, or historical writing. Because it can be a sexual insult, avoid it in conversation. Modern speakers would say 'sloppy,' 'messy,' or, for appearance, simply describe what they see.

distinctions.note: 'Slob' is an informal, general word for a sloppy person of any gender; 'slattern' is archaic and gendered.
'Slut' is an offensive modern insult; 'slattern' is an older, literary word, but its sexual sense is still insulting.

examples.professional: In the manuscript, the editor flagged the word slattern as archaic and possibly offensive for a modern audience.
examples.analytical: The novel's use of slattern reveals Victorian assumptions that linked a woman's domestic order with her moral character.

nuance.analogy: Calling someone a slattern in the old sense is like wearing a corset to a casual barbecue: the word belongs to an earlier era and now feels out of place.
nuance.etymology: Probably from a dialect verb meaning to be untidy or slovenly; origin uncertain.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final syllable as 'slat-ERN' or adding a 'z' sound at the end.
Using the word in modern speech without realizing it is archaic and offensive.

slattern.etymology: Dating from the 17th century; related to *slattering* (“slovenly”), from the dialectal verb *slatter* (“to slop, to spill”).

senses.definition: Covered in sleet; full of sleet.
senses.example: sleety weather

core.definition: Covered with sleet, or describing weather with sleet falling.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, SLEE, and the final -y is a clear, unstressed ee. Do not pronounce the final syllable as ai.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative, since it describes unpleasant weather conditions.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sleety in casual talk and in weather descriptions, such as sleety roads or a sleety morning. Weather reports more often say sleet-covered or describe sleet directly, so sleety is more conversational than technical. It is common in the Midwest and Northeast during winter.

distinctions.note: Icy means covered with ice, while sleety refers specifically to sleet, so roads can be sleety without being completely glazed with ice.
Slushy describes partly melted snow, while sleety describes weather or surfaces affected by sleet.

examples.everyday: The roads are sleety, so please drive slowly on the way home.
examples.professional: We are pausing deliveries because the sleety conditions make the highway unsafe.
examples.analytical: A sleety afternoon can turn a clear sky gray and bring a damp chill that feels colder than the thermometer shows.

nuance.analogy: Sleety weather is like a thin glaze of cold frosting on everything outside, making every surface slippery.
nuance.etymology: From sleet plus the adjective suffix -y.
common_mistakes: Using sleety for ice that has no sleet involved; icy is better for pure ice.
Stressing the second syllable, which makes the word sound unnatural.

senses.definition: The act of mounting on the wing, or of towering in thought or mind; intellectual flight.
senses.example: Her essay showed a soaring of imagination that left the committee speechless.

senses.definition: Assurgent, ascending.
senses.example: Soaring smoke rose from the chimney in a thin gray column.

core.definition: Rising very high or increasing very quickly, such as prices, temperatures, or demand.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable. The vowel in 'soar' is the same as in 'door' or 'store,' not the long o in 'soak'; the r is pronounced clearly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative when describing rising costs; positive when describing ambition or achievement.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'soaring' often in news and business for prices, rents, rates, and stock values, and it is standard in writing. For a more dramatic, informal effect, people say 'skyrocketing.' In literary contexts it can describe a bird, an idea, or a soaring spirit.

distinctions.note: Rising is neutral and general, while soaring suggests a large, fast climb.
Skyrocketing is more informal and dramatic, while soaring is more common in news and formal writing.

examples.everyday: Gas prices are soaring again, and I'm dreading the next fill-up.
examples.professional: Cloud storage costs are soaring, so we need to review our contracts before next quarter.
examples.analytical: The essay's soaring rhetoric lifts the question of grace above the mechanics of the argument.

nuance.analogy: Soaring is like a kite that catches a strong wind and climbs without effort.
nuance.etymology: From Old French essorer 'to soar,' from Latin ex- 'out' and aura 'air.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing soar with a long o, like 'soh-ar'; the vowel is the same as in 'door.'
Using 'soaring' for a small or gradual increase; it implies a large, rapid rise.

senses.definition: The skill, tendency or property of being sociable or social, of interacting well with others.
senses.example: He was a true introvert, and his sociability lagged behind others of his age in the school.

core.definition: The ability or tendency to enjoy being with other people and to interact easily and pleasantly with them.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on BIL, the third syllable from the end of the -ity pattern. Say the middle syllables quickly and reduce the vowels to schwa, so the word sounds like 'soh-shuh-BIL-ih-tee' rather than 'so-sha-BEE-li-ty'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes a pleasant, friendly quality, though it can sound slightly formal compared with 'friendliness'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sociability mostly to describe a person's general capacity for friendly interaction, often in job descriptions, evaluations or reflective talk. In casual conversation people usually say 'she's so friendly' or 'he's really outgoing' instead. It is rarely used as a compliment on its own in everyday speech.

distinctions.note: Sociability is a personal trait of enjoying company; sociality is the broader quality of being social, often a property of humans or animals as a group.
Friendliness describes warm, kind behavior toward people; sociability adds the enjoyment of group interaction and conversation.

examples.everyday: Her sociability makes her the first person everyone wants to sit next to at a party.
examples.professional: Her sociability helped her build relationships with clients across three time zones.
examples.analytical: Aristotle's account of human nature suggests that sociability is not merely a convenience but a constitutive feature of the good life.

nuance.analogy: Sociability is like a warm room that people naturally drift into, because the atmosphere itself invites them to stay.
nuance.etymology: From Latin sociabilis, from socius meaning companion.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, saying 'so-sha-BIL-i-tee' with extra vowels rather than reduced ones.
Using sociability for a single friendly act; it names a general trait.

senses.definition: Causing pain or discomfort; painfully sensitive.
senses.example: Her feet were sore from walking so far.

senses.definition: Sensitive; tender; easily pained, grieved, or vexed; very susceptible of irritation.
Dire; distressing.
senses.example: The school was in sore need of textbooks, theirs having been ruined in the flood.

senses.definition: Feeling animosity towards someone; annoyed or angered.
senses.example: Joe was sore at Bob for beating him at checkers.

senses.definition: Sorely.
An injured, infected, inflamed or diseased patch of skin.
senses.example: They put ointment and a bandage on the running sore.

senses.definition: Grief; affliction; trouble; difficulty.
A young hawk or falcon in its first year.
A young buck in its fourth year.
To mutilate the legs or feet of (a horse) in order to induce a particular gait.
To grow sores; to be beset with skin lesions.

core.definition: Painful, tender or aching when touched or moved, especially a part of the body after injury, illness or exercise.

pronunciation.tip: This one syllable rhymes with 'more' and 'store', with the diphthong 'oh' and a clear r at the end. Don't say it like 'soar' or 'saw'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes physical pain, but 'sore loser' and 'sore spot' carry a mild negative sense about emotional sensitivity.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'sore' constantly for everyday aches: 'my legs are sore' after a workout, or 'I have a sore throat' when sick. In informal talk, a 'sore loser' is someone who sulks after losing. Adverb and noun uses are much less common in everyday speech.

distinctions.note: Painful describes something that causes pain in general; sore describes a part of the body that hurts when touched or used.
Tender means sensitive to touch but not necessarily hurting; sore usually means it actually aches or hurts.

examples.everyday: My legs are so sore after the hike that I can barely climb the stairs.
examples.professional: I'm not feeling well and my back is sore, so I'll join the call from home today.
examples.analytical: The poem treats the body as a site of memory, each sore joint marking a loss the speaker cannot name.

nuance.analogy: Like a bruise that shows you exactly where the blow landed.
nuance.etymology: From Old English sār, 'painful, wounded', from Proto-Germanic *sairaz.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'sore' like 'soar' or 'sewer'; in General American it has the 'oh' vowel.
Using 'sore' for emotional hurt in everyday talk; Americans usually say 'hurt' or 'upset' for feelings.

sore.etymology: From Middle English *sor*, from Old English *sār* (“ache, wound”) and *sār* (“painful, grievous”), from **sair*, from Proto-Germanic **sairaz* from Proto-Indo-European **seh₂iro-*, enlargement of **seh₂y-* (“to be fierce, afflict”).

senses.definition: The sensation of a sour taste.
senses.example: (Can we add an example for this sense?)

senses.definition: A sweet/candy having a sharply sour taste.
senses.example: My son bought a bag of sours, and the first one made him wince.

senses.definition: A drink made with whiskey, lemon or lime juice and sugar.
senses.example: (Can we add an example for this sense?)

senses.definition: Any cocktail containing lemon or lime juice.
senses.example: The bartender suggested a whiskey sour, shaken with fresh lemon juice and a dash of bitters.

senses.definition: A sour or acid substance; whatever produces a painful effect.
senses.example: Her cutting remarks were a constant sour that made every family dinner unbearable.

senses.definition: The acidic solution used in souring fabric.
senses.example: The dyer soaked the wool in a sour before rinsing it in clean water.

senses.definition: Of a person's character, hostile or unfriendly.
senses.example: He gave me a sour look.

senses.definition: Tasting of acidity.
senses.example: Lemons have a sour taste.

senses.definition: Made rancid by fermentation, etc.
senses.example: Don't drink that milk; it's turned sour.

senses.definition: Tasting or smelling rancid.
senses.example: His sour breath makes it unpleasing to talk to him.

senses.definition: Excessively acidic and thus infertile.
senses.example: sour land

senses.definition: Of petroleum, containing excess sulfur.
senses.example: sour gas smells like rotten eggs

senses.definition: Unfortunate or unfavorable.
senses.example: The negotiations took a sour turn when the buyer walked out without a word.

senses.definition: Off-pitch, out of tune.
senses.example: The violin was sour all through the concert, and the audience could hear it.

senses.definition: To make sour.
senses.example: Too much lemon juice will sour the recipe.

senses.definition: To become sour.
senses.example: The milk will sour quickly if we leave it out on the counter all afternoon.

senses.definition: To spoil or mar; to make disenchanted.
senses.example: Years of office politics soured him on the company, and he started looking for a new job.

senses.definition: To become disenchanted.
senses.example: We broke up after our relationship soured.

senses.definition: To make (soil) cold and unproductive.
senses.example: Poor drainage and constant flooding had soured the field, so the corn barely grew.

senses.definition: To macerate (lime) and render it fit for plaster or mortar.
senses.example: Historic masons would sour lime in pits for weeks before mixing it into mortar.

senses.definition: To process (fabric) after bleaching, using hydrochloric acid or sulphuric acid to wash out the lime.
senses.example: After bleaching, the mill will sour the cotton in dilute sulfuric acid to remove residual lime.

core.definition: Having a sharp, acidic taste, like that of lemon, vinegar, or unripe fruit; not sweet.

pronunciation.tip: It sounds like 'sow' in cow, followed by a light American r. Do not confuse it with sower, the person who plants seeds, which is pronounced SOH-er.
