senses.definition: To convey (information, a message, news, etc.) using a telephone (noun sense 1).
senses.example: She telephoned the test results to the patient's family before lunch.

senses.definition: To (attempt to) contact (someone) using a telephone.
senses.example: Please telephone me tomorrow morning so we can review the budget together.

senses.definition: To provide (a place) with a telephone system.
senses.example: The company telephoned the entire third floor before the renovation was finished.

senses.definition: To transmit (sounds) over a distance.
senses.example: The old radio telephoned faint voices across the valley every evening.

senses.definition: To (attempt to) contact someone using a telephone; to make a telephone call.
senses.example: Please telephone me tomorrow morning so we can review the budget together.

core.definition: A device, usually with a handset, used to talk with someone at a distance over phone lines or wireless networks.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and reduce the middle to a quick 'uh'. Don't add an extra syllable at the end, as in 'fo-NEE'; the last syllable is just 'fohn'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. The word itself carries no tone; context and tone of voice do the work.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech people usually say 'phone' or 'call' rather than 'telephone'. 'Telephone' sounds more formal or official, as in 'Please telephone our office,' and it appears in phrases like 'on the telephone' and 'telephone number'. Americans also say 'cell phone' or 'cell' for a mobile device, and 'landline' for a wired home phone.

distinctions.note: 'Phone' is the everyday short form and is used in almost all casual speech; 'telephone' is more formal or official.
'Call' is the usual verb for contacting someone by phone ('I'll call you'), while 'telephone' as a verb sounds formal.
A 'cell phone' is a wireless mobile device, while 'telephone' can refer to any phone, including a landline.

examples.everyday: Sorry I missed your call. I was on the telephone with my mom.
examples.professional: Please telephone the front desk if you need a room change before check-in.
examples.analytical: Bell's telephone transformed social life by letting distant families and businesses coordinate in real time, which changed expectations of immediate response.

nuance.analogy: A telephone is like a bridge built of wire or radio waves, carrying a voice across a gap that a shout could never cross.
nuance.etymology: From Greek tēle 'far' and phōnē 'sound, voice'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable as in 'te-le-PHONE'; the stress is on the first syllable.
Saying 'telephone to him' in casual speech; say 'call him' or 'telephone him' with no 'to'.

telephone.etymology: The is derived from *tele-* + *-phone*, modelled after dated.

senses.definition: A pavilion or portable lodge consisting of skins, canvas, or some strong cloth, stretched and sustained by poles, used for sheltering people from the weather.
senses.example: We were camping in a three-man tent.

senses.definition: A trouser tent; a piece of fabric, etc. protruding outward like a tent.
senses.example: The loose fabric of his jacket formed a tent over his hips.

senses.definition: A roll of lint or linen, or a conical or cylindrical piece of sponge or other absorbent, used chiefly to dilate a natural canal, to keep open the orifice of a wound, or to absorb discharges.
senses.example: The nurse inserted a sterile tent into the wound to keep it open and draining.

senses.definition: A probe for searching a wound.
senses.example: The surgeon used a tent to explore the depth of the wound before stitching.

senses.definition: To go camping.
senses.example: We’ll be tenting at the campground this weekend.

senses.definition: To prop up aluminum foil in an inverted "V" (reminiscent of a pop-up tent) over food to reduce splatter, before putting it in the oven.
senses.example: Before roasting the chicken, tent the pan with foil so the skin doesn't splatter.

senses.definition: To form into a tent-like shape.
senses.example: The sheet tented over his midsection.

senses.definition: Synonym of fumigate.
senses.example: The exterminators will tent the house next week to kill the termites.

senses.definition: To probe or to search with a tent; to keep open with a tent.
senses.example: to tent a wound

core.definition: A portable shelter made of fabric stretched over poles or stakes, used for camping or outdoor events.

pronunciation.tip: It is a single syllable with a short e, the same vowel as in 'bed'. Do not pronounce it like 'taint' or 'tint'. Keep the final t crisp.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and positive in most contexts. It suggests camping, outdoor fun, or a temporary event space.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'tent' for camping shelters and also for large event structures at weddings, fairs or circuses. For a pop-up canopy over a patio or picnic, people often say 'canopy' or 'pop-up'. Saying 'we pitched a tent' is a natural way to describe setting one up.

distinctions.note: A canopy is a roof-like cover that is usually open on the sides, while a tent is enclosed on all sides and designed for sleeping or shelter.
A tarp is a flat waterproof sheet used as a cover, while a tent has walls and is designed to be occupied.

examples.everyday: We pitched the tent near the lake before it got dark, so we would not have to set it up in the rain.
examples.professional: The company rented a large tent for the outdoor product launch, and the event coordinator confirmed the power connections.
examples.analytical: The tent, as a temporary shelter, reveals how people in the past balanced mobility with protection from the elements.

nuance.analogy: A tent is like a turtle's shell you can carry and set up anywhere, giving you a home that folds away.
nuance.etymology: From Old French tente, from Latin tendere, 'to stretch'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'tint' for the vowel, which makes the word sound like a different word.
Using 'tent' for a pop-up canopy over a patio, where Americans usually say 'canopy'.

tent.etymology: From Middle English *tente*, borrowed from Old French *tente*, from Vulgar Latin **tenta* (“tent”), from the feminine of Latin *tentus*, ptp.

conversation.text: It took us an hour to put up the tent.
Our tent leaked during the storm last night.
Is this tent big enough for four people?

senses.definition: To end something, especially when left in an incomplete state.
senses.example: to terminate a process before its completion

senses.definition: To conclude.
To set or be a limit or boundary to.
senses.example: to terminate a surface by a line

senses.definition: To form an appropriate end on (a wire, cable, hose, pipe, etc), such as by applying a cable terminal or a hose ferrule.
senses.example: We'll rough them all in before we start terminating any of them.

senses.definition: To end the employment contract of an employee; to fire, lay off.
To kill someone or something.
senses.example: The enemy must be terminated by any means possible.

senses.definition: To end, conclude, or cease; to come to an end.
Of a mode of transport, to end its journey; or, of a railway line, to reach its terminus.
senses.example: This train terminates at the next station.

senses.definition: To issue or result.
Terminated; limited; bounded; ended.
Having a definite and clear limit or boundary; having a determinate size, shape or magnitude.
senses.example: Mountains on the Moon cast shadows that are very dark, terminate and more distinct than those cast by mountains on the Earth.

senses.definition: Expressible in a finite number of terms; (of a decimal) not recurring or infinite.
senses.example: One third is a recurring decimal, but one half is a terminate decimal.

core.definition: To bring something to a formal end, especially a contract, job, agreement or process.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle vowels are weak, and the final syllable rhymes with 'mate'. Do not say 'ter-MIN-ate' with the stress in the middle.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It is formal and often refers to ending something abruptly or officially.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'terminate' in business, legal and technical contexts, such as terminating a contract or an employee. In everyday speech they usually say 'end', 'cancel' or 'stop'. The verb is transitive, so you terminate something or someone, not 'terminate from' something.

distinctions.note: End is everyday and general, while terminate is formal and often implies a formal or official ending.
Cancel usually means calling off a plan or event, while terminate is used for ongoing arrangements such as contracts or employment.

examples.everyday: The landlord said he would terminate the lease if we kept missing rent payments.
examples.professional: HR will terminate his system access at the end of the day on Friday, so please hand over your credentials.
examples.analytical: The argument terminates in an aporia, since neither premise can be defended without assuming the conclusion.

nuance.analogy: To terminate a contract is like pulling the plug on a machine: the process stops, and it will not restart unless someone rebuilds it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'terminare', to set a limit, from 'terminus', boundary.
common_mistakes: Saying 'terminate from the job' instead of 'terminate someone's employment' or 'terminate the employee'.
Stressing the middle syllable, as in 'ter-MIN-ate'.

terminate.etymology: From Middle English *terminaten* (“to bring to an end; to adjudicate; to end, stop; to border, confine, contain”) from *terminat* + *-en*, Latin *terminātus*, perfect passive participle of *terminō* (“to set bounds to, bound, limit, end, close, terminate”)…

senses.definition: Very; extremely.
senses.example: He's terribly busy and you really shouldn't bother him.

senses.definition: Very badly.
senses.example: She took part in the karaoke, but sang terribly.

senses.definition: (dated) So as to cause terror or awe.
senses.example: The lion roared terribly.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: Very, extremely, or in a very bad way; often used as an intensifier in polite speech.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, 'TER'. The middle syllable is a reduced 'ih', and the final syllable is 'lee', not 'lay'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral as an intensifier, and negative when it means very badly. It can sound a little British in intensifying use.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'terribly' mainly in the sense of 'very badly' or as a polite intensifier, such as 'I'm terribly sorry'. In everyday American speech 'really', 'so' or 'so sorry' is more common. The intensifying use sounds more British, so it may draw a smile in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: Really is the everyday American intensifier, while terribly sounds more formal or British.
Awfully is informal and common in Americans' speech, but may sound old-fashioned.

examples.everyday: I'm terribly sorry I missed your call, but my phone was on silent.
examples.professional: The release is terribly behind schedule, so we need to cut scope this sprint.
examples.analytical: The argument is terribly compressed, which makes its premises hard to test.

nuance.analogy: Terribly is like turning the volume knob all the way up on an adjective: it makes the feeling louder, for better or worse.
nuance.etymology: From 'terrible', from Latin 'terribilis', frightening, from 'terrere', to frighten.
common_mistakes: Using 'terribly' to mean only 'badly' when a positive intensifier is intended, such as 'terribly good', which sounds odd to Americans.
Saying 'TER-ib-lee' with an extra stressed syllable.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Bible, the adjective 'terrible' often describes God's awe-inspiring majesty, as in Deuteronomy 10:17 in the RSV, which speaks of 'the great, the mighty, and the terrible God'. The adverb itself has no special biblical meaning.

senses.definition: Singular of thanks (“an expression of appreciation or gratitude; grateful feelings or thoughts; favor, goodwill, graciousness”)
senses.example: He gave a quick thank to the volunteers before leaving the stage.

senses.definition: To express appreciation or gratitude toward (someone or something).
senses.example: She thanked him for the lift.

senses.definition: In the future tense in the form one will thank someone to do something, chiefly expressing a command or criticism: to request that (someone) do something.
senses.example: I’ll thank you not to smoke in my house!

senses.definition: To respond to (someone) out of, or as if out of, appreciation or gratitude.
senses.example: Whenever I buy her coffee, she thanks me with a hug.

senses.definition: Chiefly followed by for: to credit or hold (someone or something) responsible, especially for something negative; to blame.
senses.example: We can thank global warming for this freak weather.

senses.definition: (rare) To express appreciation or gratitude for (something).
senses.example: I thanked the nurse for the careful, patient care she gave my father.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: To express gratitude to someone for something they did or gave you.

pronunciation.tip: Start with the voiceless th, with the tongue tip between the teeth and no voice, not a d sound as in 'this'. Keep the vowel short, like 'bank', and don't add a g after the ng.

nuance.connotation: Positive and warm. In the future-tense form 'I'll thank you to...' it can sound irritated or like a firm reprimand.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use thank constantly, but usually in the set phrases 'thank you' and 'thanks' rather than 'I thank you'. A natural reply to thank you is 'you're welcome' or 'no problem'. The construction 'I'll thank you to stop' signals a firm request or mild scolding, so use it carefully.

distinctions.note: Appreciate can mean valuing something or being grateful; thank is directed at a person and expresses gratitude in words.
Grateful is an adjective describing the feeling; thank is the verb that expresses it to someone.

examples.everyday: I just wanted to thank you for picking up my kids after school.
examples.professional: I want to thank the team for pulling together the report on such a short deadline.
examples.analytical: Paul repeatedly urges his readers to thank God in every circumstance, tying gratitude to his understanding of divine providence.

nuance.analogy: Like a receipt for a gift: it acknowledges that something valuable was received.
nuance.etymology: From Old English thancian, from thanc 'thought, gratitude', related to think.
common_mistakes: Saying 'thank you for to help me' instead of 'thank you for helping me'; use the -ing form after for.
Pronouncing the th as voiced, as in 'this', instead of voiceless as in 'think'.
Saying 'I thank to you'; the person thanked comes directly after the verb.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture, giving thanks is rendered from Hebrew yadah (hodah), 'to give thanks, to confess', often in the Psalms, and from Greek eucharisteo, 'to give thanks', the root of 'Eucharist'. 1 Thessalonians 5:18 urges believers to give thanks in all circumstances. Psalm 100:4 invites worshipers to enter God's gates with thanksgiving. In Luke 17:11-19, of ten lepers healed by Jesus, only one returns to give thanks.

thank.etymology: From Middle English *thank* (“gratitude; expression of gratitude, thanks; attractiveness; commendation, praise; God’s grace; goodwill; merit, reward; mind, thought”), from Old English *þanc*, *þonc* (“gratitude; expression of gratitude, thanks; favour,…

senses.definition: Used to add emphasis to a question or statement.
senses.example: What the devil are you doing here at this time of night?

core.definition: Used as an intensifier in questions to express surprise, irritation, or strong curiosity, as in 'What the devil is that?'

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on DEV, and the second syllable is a weak uhl. Say 'the' as a weak thuh before the word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative. It expresses irritation or surprise, and it is a mild oath.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this almost always in questions with what, who, where, how, or why, as in 'What the devil are you doing?' It sounds somewhat old-fashioned and folksy, and it is heard more from older speakers or in Southern and rural speech. A natural reply is simply an answer, or 'Good question' or 'I have no idea.'

distinctions.note: The hell is stronger and more profane, so it is avoided in polite company where the devil is acceptable.
The heck is milder and more family-friendly; the devil sounds more emphatic but still mild.

examples.everyday: What the devil is that smell coming from the fridge?
examples.professional: Who the devil scheduled this review for seven in the morning?
examples.analytical: What the devil does objective mean in a model that inherits its labels from human judgment?

nuance.analogy: Like a dramatic underline added to a question, pressing harder on the words.
nuance.etymology: From Old English deofol, from Late Latin diabolus, from Greek diabolos, 'slanderer'.
common_mistakes: Taking the phrase as a serious reference to the devil; here it is a mild exclamation.
Using it in formal writing; it belongs to casual speech.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture, 'devil' translates Greek diabolos, 'slanderer' or 'accuser', which renders Hebrew ha-satan, 'the adversary.' Job 1:6-12 shows the adversary among the heavenly beings, Matthew 4:1-11 describes Jesus being tempted by the devil in the wilderness, and Revelation 12:9 identifies the ancient serpent as the Devil and Satan. The idiomatic intensifier draws on the figure of the devil, but it does not reflect these passages' meaning.

senses.definition: From there, from that place or from that time.
senses.example: I came thence.

senses.definition: Deriving from this fact or circumstance; therefore, therefrom.
senses.example: I had a really bad car accident, and thence came all my backpains.

core.definition: From that place or time; for that reason. Mainly found in formal, legal or literary writing.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a voiced th at the start and a clear, voiceless s at the end. Do not add an extra vowel between the n and s.

nuance.connotation: Neutral but dated; it sounds stiff or old-fashioned in ordinary speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely say thence in daily conversation. You will see it in legal documents, academic writing, or literary prose, as in 'The river flows north and thence east.' In casual speech, say from there or so instead. Using it casually can sound pretentious.

distinctions.note: From there is the everyday phrase, while thence is formal and mainly written.
Thence can mean 'from that place or time', while therefore means 'as a logical result' and is used in arguments.

examples.professional: We migrated the database in March, and thence the reporting dashboards were rebuilt over two sprints.
examples.analytical: The argument begins from human finitude and thence derives its account of grace as a gift that exceeds human merit.

nuance.analogy: Thence is like a river that flows from its source and carries the same water onward from there.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English thennes, from then plus the adverbial genitive ending -s.
common_mistakes: Using thence for ordinary time, as in 'We ate thence,' when then is correct.
Assuming it is a common everyday word; it sounds stilted in casual American talk.

thence.etymology: From Middle English *thennes*, from *thenne* + *-es*, the former from Old English *þanan*, from **þananā*.

senses.definition: With regard to thermodynamics.

core.definition: In terms of thermodynamics; with respect to the laws of heat, energy and work. It describes how a system behaves according to those principles.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on 'NAM', and the secondary stress falls on 'THUR'. The 'dy' is pronounced like 'dye', and the final syllable 'lee' is light. Learners often stress the 'dy' or pronounce the middle vowels too strongly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It sounds precise, but it can seem overly formal or showy in casual talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'thermodynamically' mainly in physics, chemistry, engineering and academic writing. In everyday speech they would rarely use it, or might say 'in terms of energy' or 'the way heat works' instead. Use it only when you are discussing the laws of thermodynamics or a system that depends on them.

distinctions.note: 'Thermally' refers to heat in general, while 'thermodynamically' refers specifically to the laws of energy and heat conversion.
'Energetically' means with energy or vigor in a general sense. 'Thermodynamically' is technical and refers to heat and energy within physical systems.

examples.everyday: My brother-in-law is an engineer, and he says the house is built badly, thermodynamically speaking.
examples.professional: The model is thermodynamically consistent, so the energy balance should close across each simulation run.
examples.analytical: A reaction is thermodynamically favorable when the change in free energy is negative, regardless of how fast it proceeds.

nuance.analogy: 'Thermodynamically' is like a rule of a game: it tells you what is allowed to happen in a system, even if it does not say how fast it happens.
nuance.etymology: From 'thermodynamic' plus the adverb suffix '-ally'.
common_mistakes: Using it in casual speech where simpler words are more natural.
Stressing the 'dy' syllable instead of 'NAM'.
Confusing 'thermodynamically' with 'thermally'; the first refers to the laws of thermodynamics, the second to heat in general.

senses.definition: A device that automatically responds to changes in temperature by activating a heating or cooling system to maintain the temperature at a desired setting.
senses.example: The thermostat clicked on when the living room dropped below sixty-eight degrees.

senses.definition: An algorithm used to maintain a simulated system at a set temperature by absorbing or releasing heat.
senses.example: In the simulation, the thermostat keeps the virtual cluster at a fixed temperature.

core.definition: A device that senses temperature and switches heating or cooling on or off to keep a room at a set temperature.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable. The middle vowel is reduced to a quick uh, and the final syllable rhymes with cat.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and everyday.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say thermostat for the wall unit in a home or office, and people often say turn up the thermostat or the heat is set on the thermostat. In a technical context it can also mean a control algorithm. It is very common in everyday life and in home repair talk.

distinctions.note: A thermometer only measures temperature, while a thermostat also controls the heating or cooling system.
A heater produces heat; a thermostat tells the heater or air conditioner when to turn on or off.

examples.everyday: Could you turn the thermostat up a few degrees? It's freezing in here.
examples.professional: We integrated the smart thermostat with the building management system so energy use drops after hours.
examples.analytical: In a feedback control model, the thermostat acts as the comparator, measuring the error between the set point and the actual temperature.

nuance.analogy: A thermostat is like a referee for the room: it watches the temperature and calls for the heater or air conditioner when the score drifts too far from the target.
nuance.etymology: From Greek thermos (hot, warm) and statos (standing, stable), a device that keeps temperature steady.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable (thur-MAH-stat).
Confusing thermostat with thermometer in everyday speech.

conversation.text: Can you turn up the thermostat? It's freezing in here.
We keep the thermostat at sixty-eight in the winter.
The landlord put a lock on the thermostat.

senses.definition: Without thorns.

core.definition: Having no thorns, especially of a cultivated plant variety bred so it is easier to pick or handle.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, THORN-less, and let the 'or' sound rhotic as in 'store'. The ending '-less' is a reduced 'luhs', not a full 'lees'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and descriptive; it is usually a positive feature for plants people want to harvest.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly use it for plants, especially garden and grocery talk such as thornless blackberries or thornless honey locust. It is not used for people, and 'easy to handle' or 'gentle' is more natural for a person. Gardeners often say 'thornless variety' in catalogs and conversation.

distinctions.note: Spineless means lacking spines or, figuratively, lacking courage; thornless applies only to thorns on plants.
Smooth describes any surface without roughness; thornless is more specific to a plant's lack of thorns.

examples.everyday: I bought thornless blackberries this year, so picking them won't scratch my arms.
examples.professional: The nursery catalog lists three thornless varieties that suit our commercial orchard.
examples.analytical: The thornless cultivar reflects a human selection that trades the plant's natural defense for ease of harvest.

nuance.analogy: Like a rose with its thorns sanded off: still a rose, but nothing to snag on.
nuance.etymology: From thorn (Old English þorn) plus the suffix -less, meaning without.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable as thorn-LESS
Using it for a gentle person, which sounds odd

senses.definition: Disregard for other's feelings or the consequences of one's actions.

core.definition: Failure to consider other people's feelings or the consequences of one's actions.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The '-less' weakens to 'lus', and the final '-ness' is short, 'nis'. Keep the 'th' voiceless and the 't' light.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a failing, though often a mild one rather than cruelty.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'thoughtlessness' to describe a careless mistake or rudeness that was not intentional: 'It was pure thoughtlessness, not cruelty.' It can sound a bit formal in very casual talk, where people often just say 'that was thoughtless.' In a conflict, saying 'I was thoughtless' is a sincere and effective apology.

distinctions.note: 'Carelessness' is failure to take care in doing something, often with practical errors; 'thoughtlessness' is failure to consider people's feelings or impact.
'Rudeness' is deliberately or openly impolite; 'thoughtlessness' is usually unintentional and comes from not considering others.

examples.everyday: It wasn't malice, just thoughtlessness, but she was still hurt when he forgot her birthday.
examples.professional: The rollout failed because of thoughtlessness about how the change would affect support staff.
examples.analytical: Ethical thoughtlessness is a serious failure, because it allows harm to occur without anyone choosing it.

nuance.analogy: Thoughtlessness is like walking through a crowded room without looking up: you bump into people you never meant to hurt.
nuance.etymology: Formed from 'thought', the suffix '-less' meaning 'without', and the noun suffix '-ness'.
common_mistakes: Using 'thoughtlessness' to mean 'thought' or 'deep thinking'; it names a lack of consideration.
Pronouncing the middle syllable with a full vowel; it reduces to a weak sound in American speech.

senses.definition: (historical) The floor of a threshing house or similar area where grain is threshed.
senses.example: Farmers beat the wheat stalks on the threshing floor to separate the grain from the chaff.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: A flat, hard-packed area where grain was beaten or trodden to separate the seeds from the straw.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on THRESH, with a lighter stress on floor. Floor rhymes with more and door, so the vowel is the aw sound, not oh, and the r is clearly pronounced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and historical. It carries a biblical or rural-heritage tone, with no judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use threshing floor mainly for ancient or historical farms, farm museums, and Bible passages. On a modern farm, people say field, barn, or threshing area, and they rarely use the phrase in casual talk. The term appears frequently in Scripture, so it is common in Bible study and preaching.

distinctions.note: A barn is a building for storing animals and equipment, while a threshing floor is an open, hard surface outdoors or in a special building for threshing.
A threshing house is a building with a threshing floor inside; threshing floor names the surface itself and can be used without a building.

examples.everyday: We visited an old farm museum where they showed an ancient threshing floor made from packed clay.
examples.professional: The archaeology team dated the threshing floor to the early Iron Age, which helps us understand local grain storage.
examples.analytical: The threshing floor in the story becomes a place of decision, where Boaz and Ruth meet and where the narrative turns toward redemption.

nuance.analogy: A threshing floor is like a hard, open patio where the harvest is beaten until the grain falls free.
nuance.etymology: From threshing, the process of beating grain free from its husk, plus floor, the level surface where the work is done.
common_mistakes: Saying floor with an oh vowel, as in flow, instead of the aw sound in more.
Using threshing floor for a modern harvest area, where field or threshing area is more natural.
nuance.biblical_note: In Hebrew the word is goren (גֹּרֶן), a flat surface where grain was threshed; in the Greek New Testament it is halōn (ἁλών), a threshing floor. Key passages in the RSV: 2 Samuel 24:18-25, where David is told to build an altar on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite, which becomes a sacred site; Ruth 3:2-6, where Ruth goes to the threshing floor at night to meet Boaz, who is winnowing barley; and Matthew 3:12, where John the Baptist describes the one who will clear his threshing floor and gather the wheat, separating the righteous from the chaff.

core.definition: The Greek form of the name Timothy, the companion of the apostle Paul, used in some Bible texts and in older English translations.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable. The th is voiceless, and the final syllable is reduced to us. Americans rarely use this form in speech and say Timothy instead.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a classical or scholarly form of a name.
nuance.usage_note: In American English the standard name is Timothy. Timotheus appears in Greek manuscripts, scholarly commentary, and some older translations. Use it only when you are discussing the Greek text, and say Timothy in conversation or in a sermon.

distinctions.note: Timothy is the standard English form used by American Bibles and churches; Timotheus is the Greek or scholarly form.

examples.everyday: We just call him Timothy at church, but his Greek name is Timotheus.
examples.professional: In the seminar handout, I used the Greek form Timotheus when comparing the manuscripts.
examples.analytical: The epistolary address in the Pastoral Epistles presents Timotheus as the recipient, which shapes the letter's authority.

nuance.analogy: Like a person's formal name on a passport versus the name everyone uses at work.
nuance.etymology: Greek Τιμόθεος (Timotheos), meaning honoring God, from timē (honor) and theos (God).
common_mistakes: Using Timotheus in everyday English where Timothy is standard.
Stressing the first syllable.
nuance.biblical_note: Timotheus is the Greek form of Timothy and appears in the Greek text of the New Testament, including Acts 16:1, 1 Thessalonians 3:2, and the opening verses of several letters attributed to Paul. The RSV uses the English form Timothy. The Greek name means honoring God.

senses.definition: In a tireless manner; without tiring, flagging, or ceasing.
senses.example: The volunteers worked tirelessly to improve the content.

core.definition: In a way that continues without stopping or slowing down, with great energy and persistence.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle syllable is a weak, reduced vowel, and the final -ly is a light 'lee', so the word has four syllables, not five.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises steady, persistent effort, and it is often used in tributes and reviews.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'tirelessly' with verbs of effort, such as 'work,' 'campaign,' or 'advocate.' It sounds slightly formal, so in everyday speech people might say 'nonstop' or 'without stopping' instead. Use it when you want to praise someone's steady commitment.

distinctions.note: Constantly means happening all the time, and can be neutral or negative. Tirelessly always implies effort and praise.
Relentlessly suggests pressure or force that does not let up, often in a harsh or intense way.

examples.everyday: My sister has been calling every hospital in the city, searching tirelessly for our lost dog.
examples.professional: The data engineering group worked tirelessly over the holiday to keep the pipeline running.
examples.analytical: The prophet's argument is that God acts tirelessly on behalf of the weak, and that this action grounds the hope of the community.

nuance.analogy: Working tirelessly is like a river that keeps flowing through every season, never pausing to rest.
nuance.etymology: From tireless, plus the suffix -ly; tireless is from tire, the verb, plus -less.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'tirelessly' with 'tiredly,' which describes a state of being tired rather than effort without stopping.
Pronouncing the middle syllable clearly, which makes the word sound stiff; keep it reduced.

senses.definition: Causing fatigue or boredom; wearisome.
senses.example: Eventually his long stories became tiresome.

core.definition: Annoying, boring or tiring in a way that makes you impatient or irritated.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The final -some is a reduced 'sum', not 'some' with a full vowel, and the middle syllable is quick and light.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes something that wears a person down, such as a repeated annoyance or a dull task.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'tiresome' to complain about a repeated annoyance, as in 'that tiresome noise.' It is more common in writing and older speech than in very casual talk, where people often say 'annoying' or 'a pain.' Saying it about a person can sound harsh.

distinctions.note: Tiring describes something that makes you physically or mentally tired. Tiresome describes something that irritates or bores you.
Annoying is the everyday word for irritating and is more common in conversation. Tiresome suggests something dull and repetitive that you have to put up with.

examples.everyday: Sorry, the traffic on the highway is so tiresome today that I'm going to be late.
examples.professional: Filling out the same expense form every week is tiresome, so I'd like to automate it.
examples.analytical: Critics have argued that the book's repetitive style becomes tiresome, even though its central claim is powerful.

nuance.analogy: A tiresome task is like a dripping faucet: it is not dangerous, but it keeps wearing on your patience.
nuance.etymology: From tire, the verb, plus the suffix -some, meaning tending to or causing.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'tiresome' with 'tiring'; a long hike is tiring, but a long meeting about formatting is tiresome.
Using 'tiresome' for a person in casual speech, which sounds unkind.

senses.definition: A traffic light.

core.definition: An electric light system at a road intersection that tells drivers when to stop, slow down, or go.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress goes on TRAF, not on SIG. The final syllable of 'signal' is reduced to 'nul' with no separate vowel sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical, everyday term.
nuance.usage_note: Most Americans say 'traffic light' in casual speech, and 'traffic signal' is more common in official notices, city websites, traffic engineering, and road safety writing. Both mean the same thing. If someone says 'the signal is out,' they mean the light is not working, and you should treat the intersection as a four-way stop.

distinctions.note: Traffic light is the everyday American term, while traffic signal is more formal and used in official and engineering contexts.
A stop sign is a fixed sign without a light, while a traffic signal changes colors to control the flow of cars.

examples.everyday: Turn left at the second traffic signal, then you'll see the grocery store.
examples.professional: The city engineer said the new traffic signal timing should reduce delays on Main Street by about twenty percent.
examples.analytical: A traffic signal coordinates the competing claims of many drivers, turning a chaotic intersection into a predictable sequence.

nuance.analogy: A traffic signal is like a metronome for cars, setting the beat that everyone follows.
nuance.etymology: Signal comes from Old French signal, from medieval Latin signale, from signum, 'sign.'
common_mistakes: Saying the second syllable of 'signal' as 'sig-NAL' instead of 'SIG-nul'.
Using traffic signal and stop sign as if they were the same thing.

senses.definition: Able to be transferred.
senses.example: To start a new career, you need transferable skills.

core.definition: Able to be moved, passed on, or used in a new job, situation or context.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on FUR, and the -able ending is a weak 'uh-bul'. The first r is pronounced fully, and the a in the last syllable is reduced to a quick 'uh'.

nuance.connotation: Positive in professional contexts, since transferable skills and credits are valued.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use transferable most often for skills, credits and tickets, as in 'transferable skills' on a résumé or 'nontransferable tickets' for a game. It's common in career changes and school applications. The standard spelling is transferable; the double-r form appears as a less common variant.

distinctions.note: Portable describes something that can be physically carried or used in different places, while transferable focuses on moving skills, rights or benefits between people or contexts.
Movable means able to be physically moved; transferable often implies a change of ownership, use or context.

examples.everyday: Don't worry about your restaurant job, because the customer service skills you learned are very transferable to an office.
examples.professional: Her project management experience is highly transferable, so she could move into a product leadership role.
examples.analytical: A skill is transferable only when its underlying principle applies in a new setting, not merely when the same surface task recurs.

nuance.analogy: Like a driver's license that works in another state, but only when the rules match well enough.
nuance.etymology: From transfer (Latin transferre, to carry across) plus -able (Latin -abilis, able to be).
common_mistakes: Calling a person transferable when you mean they were transferred; say a transferred employee or a transfer.
Pronouncing the stressed vowel like 'fair' instead of the 'fur' sound in the first r syllable.

senses.definition: An instance of ensnaring something or someone.
The capturing of furbearing animals in traps so as to harvest them for their pelts.
senses.example: Trapping muskrats and beavers was once a winter income for many families in the north.

senses.definition: An ornamental covering or harness for a horse; caparison.
senses.example: The knight's horse wore a trapping of crimson silk embroidered with the family crest.

core.definition: The activity of catching wild animals in traps, especially for their fur, or the act of ensnaring someone or something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the ending a light 'ing' sound, not 'eeng'. The middle vowel is short and reduced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most uses. It can sound negative in an ethical discussion of animal cruelty, or in a metaphor about being caught.
nuance.usage_note: In American English, trapping most often refers to catching animals for their fur or to wildlife management, and people talk about it in rural and outdoor settings. Figurative uses, like the trapping of a person in a bad situation, are less common. Americans may also say 'trapping season' or 'trapping license'.

distinctions.note: Trapping is the act of catching; trappings are the outward accessories or signs of a role or status.
Hunting is the broader pursuit of game, often with weapons, while trapping relies on devices that catch the animal.

examples.everyday: My uncle does some trapping in the winter, mostly for beaver and muskrat.
examples.professional: The state wildlife department regulates trapping during the fall season to control the population.
examples.analytical: The ethics of trapping depends on whether the practice is sustainable, humane, and necessary for managing the animal population.

nuance.analogy: Like a fishing net that closes around whatever swims into it, the trap waits for the animal to step in.
nuance.etymology: From Old English treppe or trappe, 'snare or trap', with the sense of 'trapping' developing in the 1400s.
common_mistakes: Confusing trapping with trappings, which means ornaments or signs of status.
Using trapping as a verb, when the verb is trap.
Assuming the word always refers to animals, when it can describe any ensnaring.
nuance.biblical_note: Scripture uses the image of the snare or trap to describe danger, deception, and ensnarement, but the English word trapping as such is rare. Psalm 91:3 speaks of God delivering the faithful from the snare of the fowler, and Proverbs 22:5 says that thorns and snares lie in the path of the perverse.

senses.definition: A net or dragnet used for trawling.
senses.example: The trawl came up full of cod and flounder, far more than expected.

senses.definition: A long fishing line having many short lines bearing hooks attached to it; a setline.
senses.example: The longline trawl stretched for two miles, baited with hooks every few feet.

senses.definition: An exhaustive search.
senses.example: I embarked on a trawl through my uncle's papers in search of his missing will.

senses.definition: To take (fish or other marine animals) with a trawl.
senses.example: The fisherman went out to trawl the deep sea for shrimp.

senses.definition: To fish from a slow-moving boat.
senses.example: They used a large net to trawl for fish along the coast.

senses.definition: To make an exhaustive search for something within a defined area.
senses.example: We need to trawl through the data to find meaningful patterns.

core.definition: To fish by dragging a large net along the sea floor, or to search thoroughly through a large amount of information.

pronunciation.tip: This is a one-syllable word. Say a smooth 'tr' followed by the vowel of 'law' and a clear final L, without adding an extra vowel after the L.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In the fishing sense it is technical; in the search sense it can be tiring or negative, for example when people trawl through records.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'trawl' for fishing with a large net and, more often, for searching through lots of material, like 'trawling through emails' or 'trawling the internet'. In a personal context, 'trawling for people' can imply looking for romantic or sexual partners, so use it carefully. The verb is often followed by 'through' or 'for'.

distinctions.note: Dredge can mean scraping up sediment from a riverbed or digging up old facts, while trawl specifically means dragging a net through water or searching widely.
Troll means fishing by pulling a baited line behind a moving boat, while trawl means dragging a net.

examples.everyday: I spent an hour trawling through old photos looking for that picture of us at the lake.
examples.professional: I'll trawl the logs for errors from last night's deployment before we talk to the client.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that the study trawls through a vast number of variables until something looks significant.

nuance.analogy: Trawling is like a fisherman pulling a huge net through the water, sweeping up everything in its path.
nuance.etymology: Probably from Middle Dutch traghelen, to drag or pull, possibly related to a word for a net.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to use through or for after trawl when searching, as in 'trawl the emails' versus 'trawl through the emails'.
Stressing a second syllable or adding an extra vowel after the L.

senses.definition: A rapid repetition of the same note, or an alternation between two or more notes. It can also be intended to mean a rapid and repetitive variation in pitch for the duration of a note. It is notated by a strong diagonal bar across the note stem, or a detached bar for a set of notes (or stemless notes).
senses.example: The violin's tremolo on the final note made the scene feel tense and fragile.

senses.definition: A variation in the volume of a note or a chord, evoking a tremor or quiver.
senses.example: The guitarist added a tremolo to the chord, so the sound quivered as it faded.

senses.definition: The device in an organ that produces a tremolo effect.
senses.example: The organist switched on the tremolo, and the pipes began to waver slightly.

core.definition: In music, a rapid repetition of one note or a quick alternation between notes, or a rapid variation in volume or pitch.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TREM, and the middle syllable is a reduced 'uh'. Americans say the final vowel as 'oh' with a clear long o. The initial t is often a tr sound, not a flap.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a musical term, sometimes used about guitar effects.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tremolo in music lessons, guitar and amplifier talk, and music theory. Guitarists often mean the tremolo arm or effect pedal, which varies volume or pitch. Outside music, the word is rarely used.

distinctions.note: Vibrato varies pitch slightly and smoothly, while tremolo repeats a note or varies its volume rapidly.
A trill is a rapid alternation between a note and the note above it; tremolo is repetition of one note or a rapid volume change.

examples.everyday: My brother put a tremolo pedal on his guitar, and now every song sounds a little wobbly.
examples.professional: The session guitarist used a tremolo effect on the bridge, so the track has a shimmering feel without extra instruments.
examples.analytical: In the Baroque string writing, tremolo sustains tension by repeating a single pitch rapidly over a moving bass line.

nuance.analogy: Think of a strobe light: the same color is switched on and off very quickly, creating a shimmer.
nuance.etymology: From Italian 'tremolo', trembling, from Latin 'tremulus', trembling.
common_mistakes: Confusing tremolo with vibrato, which changes pitch rather than volume.
Stressing the last syllable, saying 'tre-MO-lo'.

tremolo.etymology: Borrowed from Italian *tremolo*, first-person present indicative of *tremolare* (“to shake, to tremble”).

senses.definition: Insignificant trifles of little importance, especially items of unimportant information.
senses.example: These trivia take up too much of the day.

senses.definition: A quiz game that involves obscure facts.
senses.example: I joined the trivia club this semester!

core.definition: Unimportant facts and details, or a quiz game built on obscure facts; it is a mass noun and takes a singular verb.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, TRIV. The middle is a clear ee and the final syllable is a reduced uh, not ah. Pronounce the t clearly before r.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; often friendly when it means a trivia game, mildly dismissive when it means small details.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use trivia for little facts, like who sang a certain song, and for trivia night at a bar, where teams compete. It is a mass noun with a singular verb: Trivia is fun, not Trivias are fun. For one fact, say a fun fact or a trivia question.

distinctions.note: Trivia is the noun for little facts or the quiz game; trivial is the adjective meaning unimportant.
A fun fact is a single surprising detail, while trivia is the broader category or the game.

examples.everyday: We're doing trivia night at the bar on Thursday, so bring your movie trivia.
examples.professional: The onboarding deck is full of company trivia about history and office moves, so let's cut it down.
examples.analytical: A list of dates and names may be accurate, but without context it is only trivia and not understanding.

nuance.analogy: Like loose change in a pocket: each coin is real money, but none of it adds up to much.
nuance.etymology: From Latin trivia, the plural of trivium, place where three roads meet; English trivial comes from the same root.
common_mistakes: Adding an s to make trivias; trivia is a mass noun and takes a singular verb, as in This trivia is interesting.
Using trivia for a single fact; say a fun fact or a trivia question instead.

trivia.etymology: From Latin *trivia*, plural of *trivium* (“place where three roads meet”).

senses.definition: A metrical foot in verse consisting of a stressed or heavy syllable followed by an unstressed or light syllable.

core.definition: A metrical foot in poetry with a stressed syllable followed by an unstressed syllable, like 'TABLE' or 'HAPPY'.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, TROH. The second syllable is a light 'kee' with no strong stress. Americans say the final -ee sound, not 'ay'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical term from poetry and linguistics.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use trochee in English classes, poetry analysis, or linguistics. It is not used in everyday talk. When describing a poem, say 'the lines are in trochaic meter' or 'this is a trochee.'

distinctions.note: An iamb is an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed one, the reverse of a trochee.
A dactyl is one stressed syllable followed by two unstressed ones; a trochee has only one unstressed syllable after the stress.

examples.everyday: My poetry class is reading a poem written in trochees, so the lines go DUM-da, DUM-da.
examples.professional: In the training data for the poem classifier, each line was labeled by whether it contained trochees or iambs.
examples.analytical: Longfellow's Hiawatha is written in trochaic tetrameter, a meter that gives its lines a falling, chant-like rhythm.

nuance.analogy: A trochee is like a heartbeat pattern, strong then weak: DUM-da, DUM-da.
nuance.etymology: From Greek trochaios, running, from trechein, to run.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable (troh-KEE) instead of the first.
Confusing a trochee with a dactyl; a trochee has one unstressed syllable after the stress.

trochee.etymology: Borrowed from French *trochée*, via Latin *trochaeus* from the Ancient Greek *τροχαῖος*, derived from *τρέχω* (“run”).

senses.definition: Like a trollop.

core.definition: Like a trollop; untidy, careless about appearance, or sexually loose, in an old-fashioned and offensive way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and reduce the middle syllable to a quick 'luh.' End with the sh sound of 'fish.'

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative and sexist. The word insults a person, usually a woman, and it sounds old-fashioned.
nuance.usage_note: Americans seldom use this word now, and it mostly appears in older novels or literary criticism. Saying it about someone in person would sound very harsh and dated. If you need a neutral description of careless or messy dress, use 'sloppy' or 'unkempt.'

distinctions.note: Slatternly describes a messy, untidy person, while trollopish adds an implication of sexual looseness.
Tawdry describes something cheap and gaudy, while trollopish describes a person's manner or appearance with a sexual suggestion.

examples.everyday: Her costume was a little trollopish for a church picnic, and people definitely noticed.
examples.professional: The editor removed a trollopish description of the heroine because it did not fit the tone of the children's book.
examples.analytical: Victorian reviewers often read the heroine's dress as trollopish, treating her manner as a sign of moral decline.

nuance.etymology: From trollop, a term for a slovenly or disreputable woman; the origin of trollop is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Confusing trollopish with trollish, which means like a troll or a mischievous monster.
Using the word casually in ordinary conversation, where it sounds offensive.

senses.definition: Ready to use without further assembly or test; supplied in a state that is ready to turn on and operate (typically refers to an assembly that is outsourced for manufacture).
senses.example: They wanted a turnkey solution for the entire system, but we could only provide the enclosure.

senses.definition: A system that is supplied ready to switch on and operate.
senses.example: The hospital bought a turnkey imaging system that was installed and running within a week.

senses.definition: (dated) A warder or jailer; a keeper of the keys in a prison.
senses.example: The turnkey unlocked the cell door and led the prisoner down the long corridor.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: To supply a turnkey product; to supply something fully assembled and ready to use.
senses.example: We can sell you all the parts, or we can turnkey the entire unit.

core.definition: Ready to use as soon as it is delivered, with nothing left for the buyer to assemble, install or test.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, with the r-colored 'ur' vowel. The final syllable is a long e, like 'key', and there is no separate word 'turn key' in speech.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests convenience and reliability, so sellers often use it as a selling point.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use turnkey in business, construction, IT and software, as in 'a turnkey solution' delivered fully set up. It belongs to business and sales talk, not casual chat. The old noun sense for a prison guard is dated and rare in American English.

distinctions.note: Off-the-shelf means a standard product sold as is, while turnkey means the seller also installs, configures and tests it for you.
Custom-built means designed specially for one buyer, while a turnkey system may be standard but delivered fully working.

examples.everyday: My neighbor bought a turnkey hot tub, so it came fully set up and he just plugged it in.
examples.professional: We are offering a turnkey deployment, so the vendor handles installation and training.
examples.analytical: A turnkey system shifts the cost of integration to the vendor, which can reduce risk but also limits how much the buyer understands the design.

nuance.analogy: Like buying a car with the keys already in your hand: it is ready to drive away.
nuance.etymology: From turn and key; originally used for a building handed over ready to occupy, with its key turned over to the owner.
common_mistakes: Writing 'turn key' as two words in technical writing; the adjective is turnkey.
Using turnkey for anything easy to use; it means fully delivered and ready to run.

senses.definition: Not appealing.
senses.example: The soggy sandwich looked unappealing, so I left it on the counter.

core.definition: Not attractive or pleasant; does not make you want to have, see, or do something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on PEE, the third syllable. The first two syllables are weak and reduced, so do not say 'UN-ap-peal-ing'.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative; used for food, offers, places and ideas that do not attract you.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'unappealing' for food, offers, looks or ideas you don't want: 'The menu looked unappealing.' It's a polite, neutral way to say you don't like something; 'gross' is more casual and stronger. A typical reply is 'Yeah, I'd skip that one.'

distinctions.note: Unattractive usually refers to looks; unappealing covers looks, taste, offers and ideas.
Repulsive is much stronger and suggests disgust; unappealing is milder and more polite.

examples.everyday: The leftovers looked a bit unappealing after sitting in the fridge all week.
examples.professional: The vendor's terms were unappealing, so we asked them to revise the penalty clause.
examples.analytical: For many readers, the author's argument seems unappealing because it reduces moral life to incentives.

nuance.analogy: Like a stale sandwich on a plate: it's still food, but nobody wants to pick it up.
nuance.etymology: From un- 'not' and appealing, from appeal, from Latin appellare 'to address, call upon'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, saying 'UN-ap-peal-ing'; the stress is on PEE.
Using it for things that are dangerous or morally wrong; it only means not attractive.

senses.definition: Not ceremonial.

core.definition: Lacking the usual ceremony or formality; plain, informal or abrupt in manner or procedure.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on MOH, with a light secondary stress on un-. Reduce the middle -er- to a quick 'uh' rather than a clear 'air' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative; it can describe a plain, unfussy event or a rushed, impersonal one.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use unceremonial less often than unceremonious, especially for people's manners. It fits events, departures or practical procedures better, as in 'an unceremonial start to the meeting.' In everyday talk people say 'informal' or 'casual' for a relaxed tone. Used casually, the word can sound stiff.

distinctions.note: Unceremonious is usually negative about rude or abrupt behavior; unceremonial more often describes an event or procedure that lacks formal ritual.
Informal is a general, neutral word; unceremonial specifically stresses the absence of expected ritual or rites.

examples.everyday: The party started with an unceremonial shout of 'let's eat!' from the kitchen.
examples.professional: The product launch had an unceremonial start, with no keynote and only a short email update.
examples.analytical: The ritual's unceremonial conclusion, lacking the expected prayers and procession, invites scholars to question its original purpose.

nuance.analogy: Like a wedding held in a backyard with no music or speeches: the event happens, but without the usual rites.
nuance.etymology: From un- plus ceremonial, from ceremony, from Latin caerimonia, meaning religious observance.
common_mistakes: Confusing unceremonial with unceremonious; the second is more common for rude or abrupt manners.
Stressing the first syllable; the main stress falls on MOH.

senses.definition: Tending not to communicate; not communicating.
senses.example: He asked and asked, but she remained silent and uncommunicative.

core.definition: Unwilling or unable to talk or share information; reserved, guarded, or not forthcoming with answers.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on MYOO, and the final -ive is a short ih sound, not eye. Many learners stress the -cat- syllable or drop the middle -ca- vowel, so say each syllable clearly with the reduced uh vowel.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative; it suggests withholding information or emotion, which can be frustrating, though it can also describe someone simply private.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it to describe someone who answers in short phrases or keeps information to himself or herself, often with mild criticism. It is more formal than tight-lipped or closed off, and in casual talk people often say he doesn't say much. It can also describe a witness, a patient or a teenager neutrally.

distinctions.note: Quiet describes a low level of noise or a calm temperament; uncommunicative describes a refusal or inability to share information.
Reticent means reserved and slow to speak about feelings; uncommunicative covers any unwillingness to share facts or answer questions.
Taciturn describes a naturally silent temperament; uncommunicative can describe a situation-specific refusal to talk.

examples.everyday: My brother was pretty uncommunicative about his new job, so I still don't know what he actually does.
examples.professional: The vendor was uncommunicative about the outage, so we escalated the ticket to their account manager.
examples.analytical: A government that is uncommunicative about its methods invites suspicion, even when its motives are sound.

nuance.analogy: Like a locked door: the people inside may be fine, but nothing gets through.
nuance.etymology: From un- (not) plus communicative, from Latin communicare 'to share'.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with uncommunicated, which describes information, not a person's manner.
Using to with the adjective; say uncommunicative with someone or about something instead.

senses.definition: The state of being unexpected.

core.definition: The quality or state of being unexpected; the surprising or unforeseen nature of something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on PECT. The final -ness is a reduced 'nis' with no full vowel, and the -ed is a short 'id'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it names a quality and is often used in analysis or criticism.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this noun in casual speech. They say 'it was unexpected' or 'the surprise'. It appears in writing, critique and analysis, when you need to name the quality itself.

distinctions.note: Surprise is the feeling or the event itself; unexpectedness is the quality that causes it.
Unpredictability refers to an inability to forecast over time; unexpectedness refers to a single event that was not anticipated.

examples.everyday: I loved the twist, mostly for its unexpectedness.
examples.professional: The unexpectedness of the spike made the forecast hard to defend in the review.
examples.analytical: The unexpectedness of the event is part of what makes it persuasive as evidence rather than mere coincidence.

nuance.analogy: Like a missing step on a staircase: the jolt comes from the gap between what you expected and what happened.
nuance.etymology: un- + expectedness, from Latin exspectare 'to look out for'.
common_mistakes: Using 'unexpectedness' in casual speech, where 'surprise' or 'the unexpected part' sounds more natural.
Pronouncing the second syllable as 'eks' instead of the reduced 'ik'.

senses.definition: To remove a hindrance from; to free or unencumber.

core.definition: To remove an obstacle or hindrance from something, freeing it to move or progress.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on HIN, the first syllable of the root. The final -er is a reduced, r-colored vowel, so say 'HIN-der', not 'HIN-dur' with a heavy vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It describes removing obstacles, usually in a formal or literary tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'unhinder' in conversation; they say 'clear the way', 'remove the obstacles' or 'get rid of the roadblocks'. You will see it occasionally in formal writing, policy documents or older literature. If you need a common word, use 'remove' or 'clear'.

distinctions.note: Unhinge means to take a door off its hinges or to make someone mentally unstable; unhinder means to remove an obstacle.
Remove is common and neutral; unhinder is rarer and suggests clearing an obstacle that was blocking progress or free movement.

collocations: unhinder the free exchange of ideas

examples.professional: Our goal is to unhinder the approval process by removing the duplicate sign-offs.
examples.analytical: The reform aims to unhinder economic life by removing the regulations that have stalled investment.

nuance.analogy: Like pulling a fallen branch out of a river so the water flows freely again.
nuance.etymology: From un- (remove) + hinder; 'hinder' comes from Old English hindrian, to hold back.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'unhinge', which has a different meaning.
Using it in casual speech, where 'clear' or 'remove' would sound more natural.

senses.definition: Petty; not important or noteworthy.
senses.example: The committee spent an hour debating unimportant changes to the meeting agenda.

core.definition: Not significant enough to matter much or deserve attention.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on PORT, with a strong American r. The middle im is short, and the final -ant reduces to unt. Many learners wrongly stress the un or say un-im-por-TANT.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly dismissive; calling something unimportant can downplay a concern and may sound dismissive if said to someone who cares about it.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this in everyday talk and at work to say something does not matter much, as in That's unimportant, let's move on. It can sound harsh when applied to a person's concern, so That's not a big deal or It's minor is softer. In casual speech, it's fine or no big deal is even more common.

distinctions.note: Minor implies small in size or rank and is neutral; unimportant is a broader judgment about whether something matters at all.
Trivial is stronger and often means silly or petty; unimportant is more neutral.
Irrelevant means not connected to the topic at hand; something can be important in general but irrelevant to a particular question.

examples.everyday: Don't worry about the stain on your shirt; it's unimportant.
examples.professional: The formatting issues are unimportant for now, so let's focus on the model's accuracy.
examples.analytical: The author treats the marginal notes as unimportant, but her central argument depends on them.

nuance.analogy: Like a grain of sand on a beach: it is there, but it changes nothing.
nuance.etymology: From un- 'not' plus important, from French important, from Latin importare 'to bring in, be of concern'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable; say un-im-PORT-unt, not un-IM-por-tant
Saying that's unimportant bluntly to an upset colleague, which can sound dismissive; soften it with not a big deal

senses.definition: In an unreasonable manner.
senses.example: He behaved unreasonably.

senses.definition: To an unreasonable degree.
senses.example: The team was given an unreasonably short amount of time to put together a presentation.

core.definition: In a way that goes beyond what is fair, sensible, or expected; to an excessive degree.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on REE, and the middle syllables are reduced. Don't add an extra 'ay' sound at the end; the final syllable is a clear 'lee'.

nuance.connotation: Negative or emphatic: it usually criticizes excess, delay, or unfair treatment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'unreasonably' to describe behavior or prices that go too far: 'She was unreasonably angry about a small mistake.' It is often paired with adjectives like 'high', 'late', or 'strict'. It sounds formal in casual speech, so many people prefer 'way too' in conversation.

distinctions.note: 'Excessively' is neutral and general; 'unreasonably' adds the idea that the amount is unfair or unjustified.
'Overly' is common and informal; 'unreasonably' is more formal and carries stronger judgment.

examples.everyday: The restaurant charged us an unreasonably high price for a plate of fries.
examples.professional: The vendor's support fee is unreasonably high for a team of our size.
examples.analytical: He argues that the court behaved unreasonably by applying the rule without considering the context.

nuance.analogy: Like a tip that is so large it makes the bill ridiculous: the amount is not impossible, but it is far beyond what makes sense.
nuance.etymology: From unreasonable plus -ly, from Latin ratio, 'reason'.
common_mistakes: Using 'unreasonable' as an adverb; use 'unreasonably' before an adjective, as in 'unreasonably expensive'.
Pronouncing the middle syllables too strongly; they should be quick and reduced.

unreasonably.etymology: From Middle English *unresonably*, equivalent to *unreasonable* + *-ly*, after *resonably* (whence *reasonably*) and Late Latin *irratiōnābiliter*.

senses.definition: Machine learning that finds structure in data without labels, such as clusters.
senses.example: We used unsupervised learning to group customers by purchase behavior, since we had no labels.

core.definition: Machine learning that finds structure, such as clusters or patterns, in unlabeled data without being told the correct answers.

pronunciation.tip: The strongest stress falls on LEARN, with a secondary stress on SU in unsupervised. The r in 'learning' is a rhotic vowel, so say 'LUR-ning', not 'LER-ning'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical; it describes a method rather than an attitude.
nuance.usage_note: Data scientists use this phrase constantly in meetings, papers and interviews. Everyday speakers usually just say machine learning. A typical exchange: 'Are we doing supervised or unsupervised learning?' and 'Unsupervised, since we have no labels yet.'

distinctions.note: Supervised learning trains on inputs paired with correct labels; unsupervised learning finds structure without them.
Reinforcement learning improves through rewards and penalties over time, rather than from labels or from structure in the data alone.

examples.everyday: My cousin's photo app uses unsupervised learning to group pictures by place without anyone labeling them.
examples.professional: For the customer segmentation project, let's try unsupervised learning first, since we don't have labeled segments yet.
examples.analytical: Unsupervised learning raises a philosophical question: an algorithm can discover clusters, but whether they are meaningful depends on human judgment.

nuance.analogy: A librarian grouping new books into shelves by subject before any catalog exists.
nuance.etymology: From un- plus supervised, from Latin supervidere, to oversee, plus learning.
common_mistakes: Thinking unsupervised means the system is unattended; it means the training data has no labels
Weakening the stress on LEARN, which carries the main stress of the phrase

conversation.text: Unsupervised learning finds structure in data without labels, for example by clustering similar customers.
We don't have labels yet, so let's start with unsupervised learning to see what groups emerge.

senses.definition: In an unsuspecting manner.

core.definition: Without suspecting anything; in a way that shows no awareness of danger, deception or a trick.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on SPEK, with a lighter secondary stress on un-. The middle syllables reduce to a schwa, and the -ly ending is a quick, light lee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative for the person involved, since it often describes someone being fooled or harmed, though it can describe innocent openness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this mostly in news reports, crime stories and narratives, as in 'The man was struck while unsuspectingly walking home.' In daily talk people more often say 'without warning' or 'when nobody was paying attention.' It is rarely used about yourself in casual speech, where it can sound dramatic.

distinctions.note: Unknowingly means without knowing a fact; unsuspectingly stresses that the person had no reason to be wary or on guard.
Innocently describes a lack of bad intent; unsuspectingly describes a lack of suspicion, often about a threat.

examples.everyday: My friend unsuspectingly ordered the spiciest dish on the menu and then started sweating.
examples.professional: The client unsuspectingly signed the contract without noticing the auto-renewal clause.
examples.analytical: The subject unsuspectingly accepted the framing, which is precisely why the bias in the survey went undetected.

nuance.analogy: Like a hiker who strolls down a trail without noticing the bridge is out, stepping forward with no warning.
nuance.etymology: From un- (not) plus suspecting, from Latin suspicere, to look up at, to mistrust.
common_mistakes: Using unsuspectingly for a neutral surprise rather than a situation involving danger or deception.
Stressing the first syllable or pronouncing the -ing as a full syllable.

senses.definition: An instrument or device for domestic use, especially in the kitchen.
senses.example: We have convenient storage for all the kitchen/eating utensils.

senses.definition: Specifically, a eating utensil (fork, table knife, or spoon); a piece of flatware or cutlery.
senses.example: Please set the table with clean utensils: a fork, a knife, and a spoon for each guest.

senses.definition: A useful small tool, implement, or vessel.
senses.example: He stocked up on old-style writing utensils.

core.definition: Tools or devices used in cooking and eating, such as forks, knives, and spoons; flatware or cutlery.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, TEN. The middle vowel is a reduced schwa, so the word has only two full vowels and the final -ils sounds like 'ulz'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes ordinary objects with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use utensils mostly in everyday kitchen and restaurant talk, often with the phrase 'silverware' or 'flatware' for metal eating tools. A waiter might ask, 'Do you need utensils?' when giving takeout. Plastic forks and spoons from a takeout bag are also called utensils.

distinctions.note: Silverware refers specifically to eating tools made of silver or silver-plated metal, while utensils is the broad, everyday term for any eating or cooking tool.
Tools is a general word for hand instruments used for work; utensils are specifically for food preparation or eating.

examples.everyday: Could you grab some utensils from the drawer? The noodles are ready.
examples.professional: Please make sure the catering team brings enough serving utensils for the lunch meeting.
examples.analytical: The utensils a culture uses at the table reveal a great deal about its assumptions regarding manners and the body.

nuance.analogy: Utensils are the 'hands' of the kitchen: each one extends your fingers so you can handle food without touching it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin utensilia, 'implements, things for use', from utensilis, 'fit for use'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'utensil' for a single item when speaking of several; 'utensils' is the plural and is often used for a set.
Mispronouncing the stress as 'yoo-ten-SILS' rather than stressing the second syllable.

conversation.text: Do you need utensils with your takeout order?
The plastic utensils are by the napkins.
Please don't send utensils; we have some at home.

senses.definition: Very devoted and possibly submissive to one's wife; showing excessive uxorial devotion.

core.definition: Excessively devoted to one's wife, often to the point of being overly indulgent or submissive to her wishes.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable. The x is pronounced as a k plus s sound, so do not say it as a z, and the vowel in the stressed syllable is the American aw sound.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative to neutral; it can sound affectionate or mocking depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: You will rarely hear uxorious in everyday American speech. It appears in essays, book reviews, and witty commentary. It implies excess, so it suggests a husband who lets his wife dominate his decisions. Friends would say devoted or crazy about his wife instead.

distinctions.note: Devoted is positive and common; uxorious adds a sense of excess and sometimes submissiveness.
Doting describes affectionate overindulgence toward anyone, while uxorious is specific to a husband's devotion to his wife.

examples.everyday: He is so uxorious that he would drop everything to make his wife's coffee.
examples.professional: Our former CEO was so uxorious that he cleared every major decision with his wife before the board vote.
examples.analytical: Critics described the Victorian writer as uxorious, yet his letters reveal a more complicated dependence on his wife's judgment.

nuance.analogy: Like a compass needle that points only toward one person, showing devotion that has lost its independent direction.
nuance.etymology: From Latin uxorius, of a wife, from uxor, wife, with the English suffix -ous.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as uh-ZOR-ee-us; the x is pronounced k plus s.
Using uxorious for a wife's devotion; the word describes a husband.

uxorious.etymology: Latin *uxōrius* (“of or pertaining to a wife”), from *uxor* (“wife”) + *-ious*.

core.definition: A man in 2 Samuel 6 who was struck dead by God after reaching out to steady the ark of the covenant as it was carried.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final ah sound is weak and close to uh.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to solemn; it is a name linked to a serious lesson about holiness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mention Uzzah in Bible study when discussing the holiness of God and the ark. The story is often taught as a warning about reverence, not as a judgment on his intentions. The name is a proper noun, so use it as a name only.

distinctions.note: Uzza is a name for a family of temple servants in Ezra and Nehemiah; Uzzah is the man who touched the ark in 2 Samuel.

examples.everyday: Have you read the story of Uzzah touching the ark? It always surprises people.
examples.professional: Our devotional series includes a session on Uzzah, since that passage raises questions about reverence and obedience.
examples.analytical: The narrator in 2 Samuel 6 presents Uzzah's death as a judgment that makes David fearful and ultimately reshapes his plans for the ark.

nuance.analogy: Like a person who reaches for a falling vase, not realizing the object is too sacred to touch.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew ʿUzzāh, meaning strength.
common_mistakes: Confusing Uzzah with Uzza, a different name for another family.
Pronouncing the second syllable as a full ah.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew ʿUzzāh, meaning strength. 2 Samuel 6:6-7 describes Uzzah reaching out to steady the ark when the oxen stumbled, and God strikes him dead. 2 Samuel 6:8 says David was angry and named the place Perez-uzzah, meaning breach of Uzzah. 1 Chronicles 13:9-11 gives a parallel account.

senses.definition: An instance of verbalizing.
senses.example: His verbalization of the problem helped the team finally see where the model failed.

core.definition: The act or result of expressing a thought, feeling, or idea in words, especially spoken words.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on -zay-, and the last syllable is a light 'shun.' The unstressed vowels in the middle syllables are reduced to a weak 'uh' or 'ih.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a process, often in therapy, education, or psychology.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use verbalization in psychology, teaching, and formal writing, especially when describing how people put feelings or problem-solving steps into words. In everyday speech, people usually say saying it out loud or putting it into words.

distinctions.note: Articulation stresses clear and precise expression, while verbalization simply means turning something into words.
Expression is broader and can include gestures, art, or music, while verbalization specifically refers to words.

examples.everyday: Talking to my sister helped with the verbalization of what was bothering me.
examples.professional: The workshop uses verbalization of each step so the team can spot assumptions before writing code.
examples.analytical: Wittgenstein's worry is that verbalization can make an inner experience seem more fixed than it is.

nuance.analogy: Verbalization is like pouring water from a pitcher into a glass: the thought takes a definite shape once it is in words.
nuance.etymology: From verbalize, with the suffix -ation, from Late Latin verbalis, 'of words.'
